In a world dominated by demand cycles, rate setters could put some trust in their Taylor rules and/or DSGE models, and then debate the precise calibration of the policy tightening or easing. In a world of sudden negative supply shocks associated with high uncertainty (pandemics, trade wars, real wars, etc), such models offer very limited support. It leaves policymakers facing policy options that can imply significant trade-offs and ultimately forces them to take decisions under elevated uncertainty. 'Wait and see' and 'no rush' may be the instinctive response to uncertainty. On the surface, this has been the response this week, as all core central banks left their polices unchanged. However, a closer look reveals notable differences in how they approach the uncertainty around the ongoing global energy shock and the guidance this provides for markets. In a previous note, we had argued that the BCCh wasn't likely to react aggressively in a scenario of oil staying at $100 for a few months because the board would see the shock as a transitory cost-push negative for economic activity. After the March meeting and minutes, we revised our assessment: the bar for hikes looks lower, as some members are concerned about persistence risks. When oil came down with the first ceasefire announcement, chances of hikes went down again; but with the subsequent blockade and Brent futures above $110, persistence risks will likely play a relevant role in BCCh decisions going forward. In this context, we now expect a 25bp hike in June, and another 25bp hike in September. The duration of the Middle East conflict is hard to predict, but outcomes are skewed towards hikes even if a resolution happens soon. records.text: a delay. In both economies, we think rate hikes this year will be followed by cuts in 2027 to push policy rates below current levels. A week ago, we had argued that the probability of the central banks looking through the inflation shock was rising. That probability has reduced, both with the rise in oil price and communication this week. But we still think it is higher than the likelihood of more hikes than we expect. Euro area: food for the bears in us is growing There was a lot of data this week, and the general gist was early and obvious cracks in economic resilience. And, by this, we don’t particularly mean April inflation data. Headline inflation was as expected at 3.0% yoy and core at a marginally softer 2.2% yoy. We don’t refer to GDP growth either at weaker-than-expected 0.1% qoq for the Euro area average, vs our expectation of 0.2% or the ECB’s of 0.3%. Having said that, this data should have reduced the need for hawkishness (not least because partially available GDP details at the national level signal a fast domestic demand deterioration). We have been watching (and lamenting) the lacklustre credit cycle in the Euro area for a while. The March 2026 bank lending data was better than in February, but three-month moving averages are in line with flat momentum in 2025. The Bank Lending Survey points to further tightening in lending conditions and lower demand expectations. The SAFE survey (among companies) echoes that. Monthly sentiment data continues to deteriorate.

Page 17 Bond Market Strategy G10 Rates Chartpack: April 2026 Mingyue Xin | Strategist | +44-20-754-10002 Note: This note was originally published on 27 April 2026. Summary This report summarises key macroeconomic metrics and frameworks that we are closely monitoring. We provide a regular update on the evolution of developed market (DM) rates markets in the recent past. Considering the uncertainty surrounding trade and fiscal policy, we begin by comparing budget balances and current account balances across major DM countries. We then analyse the distribution of outstanding bonds by investor type to assess the proportion held by price-insensitive investors, such as domestic cen tral banks. Moving to market pricing, we examine pricing trends of major central banks, followed by recent market movements in key rates products. Finally, we update our cross -country PCA of term premia, as well as the seasonality of selected rates instrum ents. Definitions, methodologies, links to our key views, and recent publications are provided in the appendix. In contrast to the global hawkish repricing observed in G10 central banks during March, the market this month has unwound some of that repricing. Nevertheless, 2y, 10y, and 30y yield levels remain well above those seen at the end of February. Following the update of the IMF World Economic Outlook, we refreshed the independent variables within our cross -market valuation mapping.

records.text: US: Inflation to remain above 3% through year-end 1519 May 2026 ▪ We believe the US is facing a persistent inflation problem for three reasons: 1) there are more tariff-related price increases to come, 2) non-shelter core services will not return to its pre-pandemic trend, and 3) the oil shock from the Middle East conflict and supply chain strain will add further inflationary pressure. ▪ Our latest Global Outlook painted a picture of resilient US economic growth and a solid job market through 2027. Beneath the surface, our work on the economic impacts of artificial intelligence posits that the technology’s net effect on the job market will be to lower the unemployment rate over the near term rather than raise it. ▪ We see signs of this dynamic in recent statistics: weekly and daily data shows hints of acceleration in new hiring based on ADP figures and job openings, while initial claims touched their lowest level since 1969 in the week of 25 April. Meanwhile, job-cut announcements and sluggish hiring in AI-exposed sectors have not translated to widespread job losses. records.text: US Economics 04 May 2026 Citi Research 2 Core PCE in March rose 3.2%YoY, boosted by some modest upward revisions to January inflation. The next two months of core PCE inflation data for April and May will still look uncomfortably strong for Fed officials in our view, but with monthly readings slowing in the second half of the year in our base case. We are currently tracking core PCE at 3.0% Q4/Q4 2026. Factors influencing our inflation assessment last week: (↑) Core PCE inflation rose 0.29%MoM in March, matching our forecast following CPI and PPI data. On a year-on-year basis core PCE is up 3.20%, somewhat stronger than our forecast due to revisions higher to January. Core goods prices were strong as expected, rising 0.21%MoM. Recent strength in core goods has mostly to do with stronger computer software and accessories prices, rather than an effect of tariffs or higher energy prices (which remains an upside risk into the summer months). “Supercore” PCE rose 0.34%, with PCE legal services rising a modest 0.3% in line with PPI data, rather than falling ~4% in line with CPI. Uncertainty around this component will remain as the BEA has adjusted its methodology in some months but not others. The next two months of core PCE data will likely remain strong, with a 0.23% increase in April and a 0.36% in May in our latest forecasts. Morgan Official intervention in JPY this week saw USD/JPY fall from above 160 to 157, though we still see the yen’s fund- ing characteristics weighing on the currency from here. BoJ data confirmed intervention of around 5.4tn yen as the MoF pushed back on recent yen weakness. We see the yen’s prior weakness as fundamentally justified, with rate spread and terms of trade moves directionally consistent with a depreciating currency. After a level reset in spot from inter- vention, any correction in equity markets would play against JPY shorts from these levels, but a backtest (Figure 2O v e r r e c e n t y e a r s U S D / J P Y t e n d s t o r i s e e v e n i f e q u i t i e s f a l l a s l o n g a s b r e n t o i l p r i c e s a r e r i s i n g ) shows that equity drawdowns while oil prices head higher mean the yen is less likely to weaken. This speaks to the diminishing returns of JPY as a safe haven over recent years. FX interven- tion may have been conducted ahead of the golden week peri- od to get ahead of any yen weakness during the holiday peri- od. The BoJ meeting this week did have a hawkish tilt with three dissenting votes but the central bank remaining on hold ultimately means they should still be viewed as behind the curve, which can weigh on JPY via inflation expectations. • Neutralise short USD exposure as markets may be complacent towards the rise in energy prices. • USD seasonality, hawkish Fed, resilient US data are constructive US

Energy drove headline inflation higher, to 3.0% y/y, in April Euro area headline inflation accelerated to 3.0% y/y in April, up from 2.6% y/y in March, while core inflation edged down 0.1pp, to 2.2% y/y (for more, see April flash HICP review: Another step higher). Across components (Figure 1), the acceleration in headline inflation was driven almost entirely by energy inflation surging to 10.9% y/y from 5.1% y/y in March, likely mirroring developments in fuel prices. Pass-through to gas and electricity prices is expected to materialise only gradually over the coming months. Non-energy components showed diverging dynamics in April. Food, alcohol and tobacco inflation edged up 0.1pp, to 2.5% y/y, while the easing in core inflation was driven entirely by a decline in services inflation (-0.2pp to 3.0% y/y), most likely reflecting base effects from unusually strong airfares in April 2025. By contrast, core goods inflation increased 0.3pp, to 0.8% y/y. Rising inflation expectations raise persistence risks Two main factors will likely shape the trajectory of headline inflation in the coming months: the evolution of energy prices and the extent and magnitude of indirect and second-round effects. The Nikkei and other media outlets reported yesterday that the government and BoJ carried out a yen-buying intervention in forex markets. A further depreciation in the yen could lead to a huge increase in import costs given the rise in oil prices, and we suspect that authorities felt that the situation could no longer be overlooked. At the same time, the public has shown no significant worsening in dissatisfaction regarding the yen’s travails despite the extent of the slump. The Takaichi administration retains high approval ratings of 60-70%. I was asked on multiple occasions by investors during a recent European trip why the historic falloff in the currency has not sparked deep anger at the government and if and why the Japanese people are not discontent with the feeble state of the yen. While there is no definitive answer to this question, our hypothesis is that Japanese citizens largely lack the opportunity to experience directly the negative impact of the weak yen and may thus be less sensitive to its disadvantages. It is true that prices for goods and services have risen in Japan since 2022, but it is difficult to grasp intuitively in daily life how much of that is attributable to currency weakness. records.text: US front-end pricing of roughly balanced risks around the current policy rate is decidedly hawkish versus our economists’ Fed assessment. But with the FOMC drifting towards a more neutral assessment, we think the market is still lacking the components that would make a compelling near-term case for outright longs. Duration longs have value to hedging deeper growth downside, but as higher for longer oil prices can see US inflation pricing continue to mechanically increase as time passes without resolution, our preference remains for real rate longs on a beta versus nominals. While still subject to news on oil flows and the conflict in Iran, EUR front-end rates are now likely to settle into a 2-3 hike range as the ECB is set to move towards a June hike. Inflation risk now looks more balanced in the HICP curve, implying the same for core yields. EU debt may underperform on high supply, but the universe of bonds is deepening, and we think EU spreads will be resilient to higher rate volatility and hikes. In the UK, Gilt yields are near post-war highs, but will likely need a combination of macro, policy and political relief to outperform through May. The long-end of the JGB curve is not entirely free of bursts of volatility that suggest supply/demand imbalances, but we think broader behavior mainly reflects macro risks, with a greater likelihood that higher risk premia in the belly and long-end sustains. records.text: Japan Rates Weekly 01 May 2026 Citi Research 3 The vote was split 6-3 at the BoJ’s April MPM. Given that a hold was seen as certain, this was the most hawkish result possible. We see this as laying the groundwork for a rate hike in June and have brought forward our outlook for the next hike to June from July. However, the money market’s reaction has been muted. Interest rates reacted to the surprise by rising temporarily, but the pricing of a June rate hike did not reach the 80% we had expected previously, and fell back to around 65% after the press conference. Reasons could include poor visibility regarding the Bank’s reaction to stagflation should the real economy deteriorate as well as possible pressure from the government. There has been no marked change in the pricing of one rate hike roughly every six months from June onward. The yen weakened on concern that the BoJ is behind the curve, and with high crude oil prices and a hawkish Fed also playing a role the USDJPY topped the critical ¥160/$ level while the 10y yield exceeded 2.5%. In response, the MoF appears to have intervened in the FX market on April 30. The size will be revealed later, but the USDJPY initially fell to the ¥155/$ handle, which is seen as an initial target. However, terms of trade continue to deteriorate along with high oil prices, and the yen remains weak in historical terms. In addition, sustainability could be a problem for interventions. However, input-cost increases across the food value chain have clouded the outlook and added a layer of uncertainty around agricultural production. This has prompted us to revise our 4Q26-1Q27 food inflation projection to 4.3%oya (SARB: 4.1%), from 2.9% prior to the conflict. Moreover, a prolonged crisis that results in a multi- plicity of shocks (elevated input costs, FX depreciation and heightened global food prices) could see food inflation move closer to 6%, likely adding to the SARB’s difficulties in anchoring expectations to the 3% target. Here we highlight potential upside risks to the food trajectory, explore the pass- through across the value chain, and use regression analysis to map potential scenarios. (See: “Reserve demand and deregulations”.) FRN maturity date For FRNs that do not mature on a business day, the lack of accrued interest is a major concern for 2a7 investors. As a result, many 2a7 funds sell such securities back to the dealers as the maturity month approaches, which add pressure to dealer balance sheets. Treasury should therefore consider changing stated maturity dates for FRNs, so they always occur on a business day. We do not see the same need for non -FRN securities, which generally have a broader and more diversified investor base that is less affected by this issue. The primary benefit would be stronger FRN liquidity and reduced need for dealers to warehouse affected securities on their balance sheet. A potential drawback would be increased fragmentation between FRNs and other Treasury securities, potentially resulting in similar but not identical maturity dates leading to pricing distortions in the front end of the curve. Considerations when using analysts' price targets Accounting for analysts' coverage scope Analysts are not tasked with producing absolute valuations for every stock in the market. Instead, they typically specialise in specific industry sectors, often drawing on prior industry experience. Consequently, analysts are generally better equipped to rank stocks within an industry than to compare valuations across industries. Actually, analysts often cover only a subset of firms within a sector or a limited set of firms across multiple industries (Figure 16). As a result, they are likely most effective at ranking stocks within their own coverage universe. To use analysts' price targets effectively, investors should take these considerations into account. 1 May 2026 14 Barclays | QPS Equity

records.text: 1 May 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 69 Risks on the horizon for funding As we discussed last week, the upcoming seasonal drawdown in the Treasury General Account (TGA) is poised to extend the stable conditions experienced in funding markets since the start of the new year. However, we also identify several emerging risks that could disrupt current calm funding conditions and reintroduce repo volatility later this year. The first risk is reduced RMPs and increased bill supply. We currently project RMPs to decline further to $15bn per month, a pace we expect to continue through December. If realized, this slower pace would exacerbate the impact of summer bill issuance. Accounting for our RMP projections, our forecast is for ~$380bn in net bill issuance across July and August, which could pressure funding rates higher. Another potential risk on the horizon is the upcoming implementation of cross- margining, recently approved by the SEC and set to go live at the end of the month. Cross-margining programs across central counterparties (CCPs) allow for the recognition of offsetting exposures, such as repo-financed USTs and futures in treasury-futures basis trades, to meaningfully reduce initial margin costs. Research from the Chicago Fed indicates that savings could be roughly 50% from a baseline where dealers require no haircut in uncleared bilateral repo and may be up to 80% relative to cleared repo. Committee members were then able to align with different parts of those scenarios, but understandably, none did so with high conviction, stressing the uncertainty around geopolitics. That said, we think that the median voter is broadly around Scenario B, which assumes some slight upside to current energy prices and a some persistence in the shock still to come. The BoE laid out a series of policy rules that, under this scenario, imply that tightening by holding Bank Rate at 3.75% would be deemed sufficient to offset the energy price shock. This was made explicit by Governor Bailey at the press conference when he said there was sufficient tightening delivered by "reversing out these [previously] assumed cuts" . Adjusting the policy rule changes outlined by Chart 3.5 in the MPR for this tightening, as done by our colleague Moyeen Islam, demonstrates the governor's conceptual point (Figure 1). External factors remain crucial While input prices are important for bottom-up modelling, the medium-term outlook for South African food inflation is heavily dependent on import parity pricing of grains, and hence global food prices and the exchange rate are key driv- ers of the outlook. Similar to the domestic backdrop, upside risks to global food prices have emerged from trade disrup- tions, although these have been tempered by ample global cereal supplies. Our tracking, which uses futures contract pricing and harvest data from the Crop Estimate Committee, indicates that grain prices will likely move further away from import parity pricing, which we expect to cushion the poten- tial inflationary effects (Figure 3). Moreover, in South Africa, meat and cereals are the two larg- est components of the food basket, together accounting for close to 55% of the total (Figure 4). Meat prices are typically linked to cereal prices, given grains’ role as a key feed input and an important driver of livestock production costs. Hence, the combination of a benign global outlook for grains and a robust domestic harvest, together with early signs of success in the fight against foot-and-mouth disease, are likely to cap upside risks to meat inflation in 2026. ECB ready to set sail As expected, the ECB kept policy interest rates unchanged at its April meeting. The decision was unanimous and framed as an “informational hold” , reflecting the GC’s assessment that the information set was not yet decisive enough to justify the start of a tightening cycle. Still, a rate hike was discussed, and President Lagarde clearly signalled June as the meeting at which the GC will be able to update its projections and scenario analysis and take a more “informed” policy decision. records.text: f this year to a lift in business sentiment, amidst still strong tech demand. There are, thus, two important vulnerabili- ties related to an intensified energy price shock. First, prices pass through quickly to consumer inflation and crude oil prices at $150bbl or higher could push global CPI inflation to a 10%ar for three months. With confi- dence readings depressed, households may shift towards caution in the face of an intensified squeeze. Second, an energy price shock threatens to unwind the normalization in global business sentiment that has taken hold in recent months. The direct growth drag from a business sentiment slide would likely be magnified through slower household income gains as it stalls the recovery in labor demand now underway. • Central banks lose patience. As noted above, central banks have traditionally tightened policy during oil price shocks, contributing significantly to the growth drag dur- ing these events. While the oil price shock envisaged in the adverse scenario is expected to produce sub-par growth, the initial inflation spike will raise concerns for central banks of a repeat of the 2021-23 episode. Reac- tions to this scenario will likely vary, and we do not antic- ipate a Fed tightening in response to an oil price spike. But the risks of a broader, immediate turn towards tight- ening will be elevated in this environment and will likely play an important role in determining financial conditions and overall economic resilience. New BoK Governor Hyun Song Shin recently remarked that it is not prudent to respond to a temporary shock with monetary policy. We still believe that the BoK will prefer a data-dependent approach rather than being pre-emptive, which is reflected in the pace and timing of hikes in our base- case scenario. On second-round effects, we think the rises in core inflation could be relatively modest compared with the high inflationary period during 2022–23. Both measures are expected to rise further next month. Q1 GDP rose 2.0% (saar), driven by strong investment, with March capital goods orders excluding defense and aircraft suggesting momentum will continue in coming quarters. Real spending slowed to 1.6% (saar); some Q2 pickup is likely, but will depend on the offset between higher gasoline prices and tax refunds from the OBBBA. March income and outlays data reinforced prior trends: soft real disposable income (-0.1% m/m), solid real spending (+0.2% m/m), and a further drop in the saving rate (down 0.3pp to 3.6%), consistent with wealth effects supporting spending amid weak real income growth. The ECI indicates the moderation in compensation cost growth is slowing, with compensation per hour up 0.9% over the past 3 months and 3.4% over the past 12 months, little changed from recent readings. Orders of nondefense capital goods ex-aircraft (core orders) surged in March, were revised higher in prior months, and now sit 2.6% above shipments, underscoring strong equipment investment in Q1 and supportive momentum into Q2. The weak economic backdrop should provide some comfort to the Council that second round effects will be much weaker than in 2022/23. And this is where the 1Q growth numbers come in: slack in the euro area economy is increasing. This should help limit second round effects. And this limits the overall needed degree of tightening. From today’s perspective, more than two hikes seem unlikely. Second, hiking rates by more than 25bp in June would squarely fall outside yesterday’s policy positioning. This week, markets had started to price more than a 25bp move in June, and investors have asked us over the past days whether such a move could be in the cards. We think this is very unlikely. The Council would need to completely change its assessment of the situation. Specifically, it would need to see strong risks of significant second round effects and a de-anchoring of inflation expectations. To (collectively) arrive at this conclusion, the Council would need to see convincing evidence that growth is picking up from here strongly. Current data signals the exact opposite (see here). Yesterday’s messaging also served to dispel the notion that a larger hike was likely. Market pricing of total expected ECB hikes retreated somewhat. records.text: 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa Distributed on: 01/05/2026 12:31:23 GMT Distributed on: 01/05/2026 12:31:23 GMT 1 May 2026 Deutsche Bank Research Europe United Kingdom Economics UK Weekly Digest Date Fiscal Update – Less Headroom, More Pressure With the local elections taking the front page in the week ahead, we update our outlook for the public finances. The good news? Borrowing just about slipped below the OBR's official projections at GBP 132bn. The bad news? Market moves since the Iran conflict will have changed the outlook for the public finances dramatically. Indeed, a good chunk of the Chancellor's primary headroom, we estimate, will have vanished following market pricing. And spending pressures will push borrowing even higher through the remainder of the decade. As part of our weekly, we do two things: first, we run a mark-to-market on what the Chancellor's headroom looks like given recent market moves; two, we update our own fiscal projections, embedding the recent market moves whilst also accounting for rising fiscal pressures. Bottom line: something's got to give – Chancellor Reeves will likely need to go back to the tax drawing board over the next two years to deal with rising defence spending pressures and departmental spending envelopes for the next Spending Review. The Chancellor will also likely need to look at efficiency savings to square the fiscal circle. Either way, more will need to be done to get the public finances back to where it was pre-conflict. W

We have found that the wedge can explain a significant amount of the variation in sport breakevens over the past five years, with the factor’s significance rising as the wedge fell in March to its narrowest level over the past fifteen years. With components which have a higher weight in PCE expected to remain firm in coming months, a narrow core CPI/PCE wedge is likely to keep breakevens narrower than model-implied levels (see TIPS Strategy, US Fixed Income Markets Weekly, 4/17/26). While a shift to a softer trimmed mean or median PCE tracking by the Fed, as espoused by Fed Chair nominee Warsh, would provide relief on this front, we think it is unlikely such measures can sway current Committee opinions (see TIPS Strategy, US Fixed Income Markets Weekly, 4/24/26). records.text: Continued upward revisions to AI capex estimates continue to spur upward revisions to earnings estimates for AI infrastructure stocks. To estimate the earnings of AI infrastructure stocks we utilize S&P 500 companies that are constituents of the GS AI Semis (GSCBSMHX), GS AI Data Centers (GSTMTDAT), or GS Power Up Americas (GSENEPOW) basket. Analyst estimates for these stocks’ earnings in 2026 and 2027 have risen by 20% and 27% YTD in aggregate, driving upward revisions to EPS estimates for the S&P 500. The strength of the AI investment boom increases the upside risks to our S&P 500 EPS forecasts. Coming into the quarter, we estimated that AI infrastructure stocks would account for roughly 40% of S&P 500 EPS growth this year and 30% of growth in 2027, but that impulse appears larger today than it did just a few weeks ago. While rising input costs and slowing economic growth pose downside risks to corporate earnings, the boost to earnings from AI investment means risks around our forecast for 12% S&P 500 EPS growth in 2026 are skewed to the upside, and we will revisit those forecasts at the end of the earnings season. While surging AI investment spending has been a tailwind to earnings, it continues to weigh on S&P 500 buybacks. Among the companies that have reported results so far, capex spending in Q1 grew at a rate of more than 40% year/year. Dividend growth has remained relatively steady at 8%, but buyback growth continues to stagnate, tracking at just 1% year/year growth.

records.text: 1 May 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 65 How effective is Treasury’s forward guidance at anchoring issuance expectations? In February 2024, Treasury began signaling that nominal coupon auction sizes would likely remain unchanged for “at least the next several quarters.” Since then, this message has been repeated at every quarterly refunding announcement, effectively becoming a form of forward guidance around coupon issuance. To assess the effectiveness of this guidance, we constructed a time series of average dealer expectations for coupon auction sizes using Treasury’s semiannual Primary Dealer Auction Size Survey (found here). The results are illustrated in today’s charts. Across nominal coupons, average expected auction sizes for both year-end FY26 and year-end FY27 initially moved higher in 2024, but declined over 2025, particularly in the second half of the year. As of the most recent survey taken in November, dealers expected broadly unchanged sizes for the coming fiscal year- end (September), which aligns with Treasury’s guidance of no changes for “at least several quarters”. This shift is also reflected in Treasury’s pre-refunding conversations with dealers, where expectations for the timing of future coupon increases have steadily moved further out. In Q2 2024, dealers expected “modest coupon increases beginning in 2025 or 2026”. By Q2 2025, those expectations had shifted “more definitively into 2026”. In Q1 2026, expectations moved further out

The event is normally inflationary, particularly for food and ener- gy prices since Brazil’s energy matrix relies heavily on hydro- power. Aggregate GDP effects are typically slightly negative, depending on the magnitude and regional distribution of the shock, due to weaker agricultural output. As a result, the BI-FXPI provides a heuristic for the BI’s policy reaction function, which can be summarized as follows. • We construct the Bank Indonesia - FX Pressure Index (BI-FXPI) to gauge FX-driven policy bias • … by combining FX pressure, intervention capacity and effective policy response • This helps to assess FX-driven policy constraints and policy bias, heading into each BI meeting • We expect BI to remain on hold in 2026 but see rising risks of policy tightening in 2Q26 We introduce the Bank Indonesia - FX Pressure Index (BI- FXPI), a high-frequency, market-based indicator designed to gauge the degree of FX-driven constraints on the BI’s mone- tary policy decisions (Figure 1). In our view, BI’s near-term policy calibration is shaped primarily by FX stability consid- erations, with growth and inflation playing a secondary role when external pressures on the IDR intensify. This is consis- tent with the BI’s repeated emphasis on maintaining IDR sta- bility alongside inflation and growth objectives, with policy calibration contingent on external conditions and capital flows. The BI-FXPI should be interpreted as a gauge of FX- driven policy constraints and bias, rather than as a mechanical predictor of policy decisions, which have to also take into account other economic fundamentals. -0.25 0.00 0.25 -2.0 -1.5 -

records.text: nsmission: Direct, indirect and second- round Direct effects can be immediate (petrol prices). Some direct effects can be slower because of, for example, contracts (electricity prices). Indirect effects can take a little time , as higher energy cost s transmit into non - energy prices. Firms selling goods and services might not immediately try to protect margins by passing through their rising energy costs into output (selling) prices. The speed of price resets will affect how quickly this indirect passthrough occurs. Second-round effects occur as a result of the direct (and indirect) energy effects pushing inflation higher. Some of these can be quick (inflation expectations). Others tend to be slower (wages, indexation effects). Direct effects are by and large mechanical. Indirect and second-round effects are not automatic. They will be influenced by the size of the direct effects and whether general economic conditions are conducive to passthrough. Second-round effects, in particular, will be determined by persistence of the shock, cyclical conditions (labour market tightness) and structural features (indexation, central bank credibility, etc). Direct effects The direct effects are playing out as expected. Energy HICP jumped to 10.9% yoy in April from -3.1% pre-conflict (February). records.text: 1 May 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 50 Deutsche Bank AG Broadly speaking, the new eSLR calculation enables dealers to hold more Treasuries on balance sheet, which is supported by the weekly Fed data of dealer net positions which has shown a substantial increase since the rule change. Reduced eSLR constraints also make dealers more likely to engage in swap spread trades directly or facilitate them for clients, which increases demand for Treasuries and resulted in wider swap spreads. On the flip side, these activities lead to crowded positioning and thereby increases the risk of large price changes during volatility shocks. (See: “Swap spreads: Waiting to re-enter wideners”.) Bank capital rules proposed in March could add to demand for Treasuries at the margin, though likely less impactful than the eSLR easing. While this is a problem for investors in private credit vehi- cles, here we address whether this is also a problem for the broader macroeconomy. We see two major potential channels. The first is a reduction in credit supplied to non-financial businesses. The second is financial stability risks emanating from banks and other levered lenders to private credit. We see limited risks from either channel. Private credit accounts for only a small share of credit extended by the financial system to non-financial business borrowers. Perhaps more importantly, private credit doesn’t occupy a particularly unique role in credit extension. This contrasts with, say, the relation between community banks or CDFIs and the busi- nesses they serve. Moreover, after recent regulatory changes, the banking system should have ample lending capacity to meet the needs of borrowers who would have turned to pri- vate credit. Finally, it isn’t clear that the structure of private credit funds implies that these funds will have permanently higher funding costs, despite headlines about unmet redemp- tions at BDCs. Additionally, loans that have extended beyond their original maturity term also exhibit noticeably weaker performance (also Exhibit 10). We note that servicers in RTL deals can provide extensions subject to certain conditions, with the extension period being between three months to a few years. Loans requesting extension are more likely to experience delays in construction and/or unfavorable market conditions to sell the property. records.text: Latin America Outlook Spring of policy caution We spotlight how the region's central banks have reacted to the markedly high volatility in financial markets following the Iran conflict and its uncertain impact on energy prices. The first inflation readings affected by the conflict are coming through. This week we saw a more cautious approach from Brazil's central bank (BCB) that delivered a 25bp rate cut as anticipated, but with a somewhat hawkish tone, and from Chile’s central bank (BCCh) that kept rates unchanged while issuing a more direct and cautiously hawkish statement. However, in a more unexpected turn, Colombia's Banrep surprised by leaving its reference rate steady at 11.25%, contrary to our and consensus expectations for a 50bp increase. Nonetheless, it reinforced our view that the central bank was approaching the end of the hiking cycle and likely to tighten less than markets had been expecting. We also think the decision is consistent with underlying macroeconomic conditions. In the upcoming week, eyes will be on Mexico's Banxico where we expect a final 25bp cut to 6.50%, in line with recent remarks by board members signaling that they were comfortable with the, so far, muted pass-through from higher energy prices and the government's fiscal efforts to smooth any shock. records.text: 1 May 2026 US Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 29 How effective is Treasury’s forward guidance at anchoring issuance expectations? Steven Zeng, CFA | Strategist | +1-212-250-9373 In February 2024, Treasury began signaling that nominal coupon auction sizes would likely remain unchanged for “at least the next several quarters.” Since then, this message has been repeated at every quarterly refunding announcement, effectively becoming a form of forward guidance around coupon issuance. To assess the effectiveness of this guidance, we constructed a time series of average dealer expectations for coupon auction sizes using Treasury’s semiannual Primary Dealer Auction Size Survey (found here). The results are illustrated in today’s charts. records.text: Core vs. Trimmed vs. Median: What’s the Best Measure of the Inflation Trend? During his confirmation hearing last week, Fed chair nominee Kevin Warsh highlighted trimmed mean and median inflation as potentially helpful measures of the underlying price trend. These measures are statistically based alternatives to traditional “core” inflation, which simply removes food and energy. We describe each briefly, focusing on the PCE price index (as opposed to the CPI). Core PCE inflation: The core simply removes food and energy, whose price moves tend n to be more extreme and less persistent. Cleveland Fed median PCE inflation: Median inflation is the rate of change of the n category in the 50th percentile of categories sorted by their inflation rates and weighted by their index weights. Dallas Fed trimmed mean PCE inflation: The trimmed mean removes the categories that n account for the top 31% and bottom 24% weight of the index ranked by their monthly inflation rates. GS trimmed core PCE inflation: Our approach, based on earlier research, first drops all n food and energy categories and then trims out the top and bottom 25% of the categories by weight. Exhibit 1 shows that trimmed mean and median PCE inflation have run below core PCE inflation recently, though at a similar pace to core inflation excluding estimated tariff effects, a measure that Chair Powell and other Fed leaders have cited. One might expect statistical measures to outperform the core in forecasting future inflation

From a modeling perspective, score gaming reduces the predictive power of the resulting score (for more on that, see our work here and here). But it also means that originators may feel obliged to pull both scores in order to ensure they’re getting the lowest LLPA for the borrower. Pulling both scores statistically only makes sense if the first score pulled is ‘low’—one strategy would be to pull VS4 (which costs $6 for a two borrower tri-merge, versus $60 for classic FICO). If that score is low, then the originator could also pull FICO. Our work last week showed that, on average, that would result in enough LLPA savings to offset the cost of pulling the second score.

records.text: ta represents the average daily market spread based on quotes taken every 30 seconds in the order book aggregated across EBS and Reuters on a volume weighted basis. The spread signal is calculated as the ratio of the current spread relative to the prior one-year median spread. The values are then smoothed using a 20-day moving average. For example, a multiple of 1 indicates that the current average spread is equal to the historical median spread for that currency pair, whereas a multiple reading of 2 indicates that the current average spread for that given currency pair is twice as wide as its historical median. Turbulence is a price-based measure of the joint unusualness of G10 currency returns. It captures spikes in volatility in individual market components as well as correlation breakdowns – atypical co-movements – between these components. We apply a 5-day moving average and rank the current value over the prior one-year lookback window. * Historical data for EURHUF, EURPLN, USDTRY, and USDZAR is available from April 2019. ** When data first becomes available, we grow our percentile rank window from 6 months to 12 months. Page 15 Broadly speaking, the new eSLR calculation enables dealers to hold more Treasuries on balance sheet, which is supported by the weekly Fed data of dealer net positions which has shown a substantial increase since the rule change. Reduced eSLR constraints al so make dealers more likely to engage in swap spread trades directly or facilitate them for clients, which increases demand for Treasuries and resulted in wider swap spreads. On the flip side, these activities lead to crowded positioning and thereby increases the risk of large price changes during volatility shocks. (See: “Swap spreads: Waiting to re-enter wideners”.) Bank capital rules proposed in March could add to demand for Treasuries at the margin, though likely less impactful than the eSLR easing. Banks with freed -up capital can deploy them into Treasuries, although broader credit demand in the economy may ultimat ely determine whether banks expand into securities or loans. The GSIB surcharge proposal appears particularly beneficial for dealer banks with balance-sheet intensive business models and a low RWA base, which helps increase overall market -making capacity. GLOBAL OUTLOOK SPRING 2026 ▪ The duration and extent of the shock from the Middle East conflict will have a lasting impact on the global economy, regardless of what happens over the coming days and weeks. We now see lower GDP growth, higher inflation and more hawkish central banks than we did at the start of the year. However, we think this is a story of resilience dented but not derailed. Strong pre-conflict growth momentum and structural drivers such as AI and defence spending offer countervailing support. ▪ We expect monetary policy to move to a less accommodative stance. This does not automatically translate into higher rates everywhere, but it does imply tighter monetary conditions than we previously forecast. Between now and end-2026, we see the Fed on hold (albeit with a hike more likely than a cut in the near term), and the ECB, BoE and BoJ hiking by 50bp. ▪ We are bearish duration in the eurozone and US and expect curves to steepen. We expect a bear flattening in Japan and a bull flattening in the UK. We are bearish the USD, primarily reflecting global flow dynamics, and expect the currency to weaken broadly, with the JPY and some EM Asian currencies an exception.

Concerns over the Takaichi administration’s preference for high-pressure economy policies are also likely to remain a drag on the JPY. Since the administration took office last October, USDJPY has clearly risen above the fair value implied by our model (the high-140s; Figure 10). We believe the residual in the model reflects concerns over high-pressure economy policies – ie, an inflation risk premium. This interpretation is consistent with the fact that superlong JGB term premia, 10y BEIs and USDJPY have all risen in tandem since last October (Figure 11). While this inflation risk premium temporarily receded following the government’s landslide victory in the February general election, it has since turned higher again following PM Takaichi’s appointment of reflationist candidates to the BoJ board, and is currently accelerating further amid higher oil prices (see Japan Rates Strategy: Return of inflation risk premium). Looking ahead, inflation risk premia are likely to remain a headwind for the JPY, reflecting concerns over fiscal expansion (eg, measures against rising oil prices and defense spending) and administration's pressure on the BoJ to maintain accommodative policy. Different shades of patience Ten central banks we cover met this week and all remained on hold, outside of a 25bp ease in Brazil. Against a backdrop of rising inflation pressures and the historical tendency for cen- tral banks to hike through energy price shocks, the main mes- sage from these meetings is the differing degrees of patience for remaining on hold. • The Fed maintained its statement’s easing bias as it con- tinued to consider “additional adjustments.” Three dis- sents to this guidance and Chair Powell’s comment that the committee is moving towards a neutral bias sent a modestly hawkish signal that the Fed will likely remain on hold for some time to come (Figure 4). • When asked about policy rates this week, ECB president Lagarde said that “I think I know where we are heading” and did not push back against the broad market pricing, which currently has three hikes this year. For a month where the DXY squeezed 3%+ higher on the conflict in the ME, this jump in inflows – likely from the same region – highlights SG’s continued safe haven status for foreigners and locals alike. This structural, eastward shift in flows raises questions about its end destinations, with deployment of capital limited by the size of financial markets and a high hurdle for residential property. Our models suggest only small spillovers of foreign flows into SGD deposits thus far, but the risk is a renewed softening of the USD driving de- dollarization conversion into SGD, one that appears limited in May. On the policy front, the MAS continues to accommodate these flows, with MAS bills falling in Mar, suggesting a net liquidity injections and an easing of rates consistent with financial stability and an absence of tighter domestic price pressures. This continues to argue for a more typical FX-cen- tric tightening cycle, where rates fall to erode total S$NEER returns. With net carry -186bps in the front end negating a slope of +100bps, we continue to see SGD as a funder for more cyclically oriented trades and stay short SGDMYR. records.text: ion): CoreWeave develops and operates large-scale data center compute capacity that it leases to compute buyers (most notably Microsoft, OpenAI, and Meta, among others). While hyperscalers such as Microsoft contract portions of this capacity, those agreements do not always map to a single workload or end user. In Microsoft’s case, capacity procured through CoreWeave can be deployed flexibly, supporting internal model development, servicing external Azure customers, or extending capacity to partners such as OpenAI or Anthropic. As a result, CoreWeave’s capacity can surface first in infrastructure and power pipelines even as its ultimate utilization remains fluid across multiple layers of the AI ecosystem. The gap between visible project pipelines and longer-dated capacity targets is less a function of delayed demand and more a reflection of how data-center development is now sequenced. Power availability (discussed further below) has emerged as the binding constraint, with permitting timelines and long lead times for equipment increasingly dictating when and where capacity can be realized. As a result, hyperscalers and AI infrastructure buyers often move first on power contracting, securing capacity reservations and development rights well ahead of final site disclosure or end-customer alignment. Morgan Given the volatility in medium-term Fed expectations, we also use our fair value model to perform a scenario analysis in an attempt to forecast the evolution of the swap yield curve (Figure 6). We consider projections for the curve assuming what is priced into forwards is realized and under three alternative scenarios, reflecting different potential Fed policy paths. Specifically, in scenarios 1, 2, and 3, we assume that the 3Mx3M/1Yx1Y curve is equal to 25bp, 0bp, and -25bp, respectively, representing 1 hike, on hold, and 1 cut, respec- tively, becoming priced in. We also assume that the current residuals persist over the next three months. As the figure shows, if Fed expectations remain unchanged, then we expect near-forward curves to flatten and 2Y-forward curves to remain unchanged. Curves are like- ly to steepen more than what forwards are currently pricing in if oil reprices significantly higher and causes growth and recession concerns. Therefore, for investors who would like to position for such a scenario, we recommend steepeners in 1Y and 2Y forwards. For investors who would like to position for a more hawkish Fed, we recommend flatteners in near-spot sectors.

To our mind, especially ECB pricing of three hikes by year-end now looks very stretched. It is true that neither central bank has made any particular effort to push against market pricing. ECB President Lagarde has been fairly explicit in the signal that the ECB is on a path to deliver the hikes embedded in the March projections (via market pricing then) unless the data forces them not to. But remember the market was pricing c 40bp of hikes then, only. For the BoE, the signal was a bit less explicit. Scenario analysis similar to what the ECB delivered in March would suggest we should expect hikes from the central bank, though there is less certainty on timing, even if they deem policy rates still in restrictive territory today and might generally be less eager to hike than the ECB. We stick to our view that both central banks will hike in June and July (25bp each). In the case of the ECB, in particular, we think that is as far as they can go before things properly risk breaking in the Euro area. Cracks in the data are just too obvious today, already. We combine the FCI-G weights with Swanson’s asset response estimates to scale each policy shock so that it delivers 10bps easing in FCI-G. That is, we preserve the pattern of cross-asset moves from Swanson, and scale the rate, FG and QE shocks so that each would be expected to raise GDP growth by 0.1ppt. This scaling inevitably requires some judgment and assumptions given the Swanson paper does not include the exact set of financial assets that comprise FCI- G. Still, direct measurement is difficult, as this would require observing demand changes of individual consumers that each use a tiny fraction of refined products. Indirect measurement, which looks at tracked supply and inventory changes to back out what demand could be. 3. records.text: In Q2 2024, dealers expected “modest coupon increases beginning in 2025 or 2026”. By Q2 2025, those expectations had shifted “more definitively into 2026”. In Q1 2026, expectations moved further out again, with dealers pointing to “late 2026 or early 2027”. Our conversations with market participants suggest the consensus now centers around the February or May 2027 refunding window, with our forecast for coupon increases to begin in February. Overall, Treasury’s forward guidance has proven to be an effective tool at anchoring issuance expectations and helping contain near-term coupon supply. That said, given uncertainties around future borrowing needs, we anticipate Treasury may begin softening its guidance as soon as next week’s May refunding announcement. records.text: Q8. Has Asia been able to offset reduced Gulf imports with higher imports from elsewhere and reduced exports? Only partially, with especially large reductions in net imports for crude. Asia-Pacific (APAC) oil imports from the Persian Gulf plummeted by 11mb/d in April compared to a year ago, reducing the region’s total imports by over 40%. On the products side, APAC total net imports declined by only 0.7mb/d in April as a decrease in products exports offset 70% of the drop in imports from the Persian Gulf (although this lever is more powerful for countries with significant refining capacity such as China and South Korea than for large net importers). On the crude side, APEC net imports decreased by 7.0mb/d in April as alternative suppliers were able to replace just below 40% of lost Gulf crude imports. The lack of crude throughput will reduce domestic refined products supply. Refinery runs stayed strong, ticking up 0.08-m b/d w/w to 16.1-m b/d, while EIA estimated weekly crude output at 13.6-m b/d. The US SPR fell 7.1-m bbls to 397.9-m bbls, or just over 1-m b/d. Combined commercial and strategic stocks fell 13.4-m bbls, or 1.9-m b/d. US diesel inventories fell 4.5-m bbls to 103.6-m bbls, bringing stockpiles to the bottom end of the five-year range. This was as refinery supply fell slightly to 4.9- m b/d, and gross exports ticked lower but stayed high at 1.6-m b/d, well above usual levels this time of year. Thailand has been facing pressure from rising structural deficits. With an enlarging government, falling revenue to GDP ratio, rising interest share of the budget, and the need for the fiscal sector to absorb frequent economic shocks, debt consolidation is a challenge without ambitious government spending and revenue reforms. If the government cannot increase the tax base or introduce new taxes, a tax increase may prove inevitable. The Mathematics of Sustainability (r–g) The fundamental vulnerability of the Thai fiscal position is the narrowing spread between the nominal interest rate (r) and the nominal GDP growth rate (g). The debt sustainability equation, Δd = (r − g)d + pb, dictates that when borrowing costs exceed growth, the debt ratio rises automatically, even without new spending. At current debt levels (~67% of GDP), every 1% of positive r-g spread adds 0.67 percentage points to the debt ratio annually. Currently, Thailand’s r-g is close to zero, meaning structural deficits do not need to worsen for debt to drift higher; the mathematics work against consolidation on its own. Faced with a hiring stall, households have continued to spend at a solid pace by lowering sav- ings rates. The bottom line is that a strong earnings backdrop, which we expect over the next 12 months, is the main driver of upside in both outcomes. The near-term risk from the Fed is more related to liquidity tightness if they were to underestimate how much capital the real economy is now using for investment and the rolling recovery. Markets could periodically reflect this risk via higher bond volatility and/or tension in funding markets. A stronger dollar could also play a role in this dynamic. The Treasury (Buybacks) and Fed (Reserve Management Purchases) have tools in place to deal with tensions should they arise and are likely to do so in a reactive, rather than proactive manner.

One assessment by third-party analysts Kpler sees Iranian oil inventories at ~49-m bbls, out of 90-95-m bbls capacity, giving a range of 12- 22 days at ~1.85-m b/d of surplus, with the higher number including floating storage (Kpler 4/29/26). Another assessment by FGE sees Iran holding 32-m bbls of inventories out of 122-m bbls of onshore storage capacity at mid-April, leaving 90-m bbls available, or 60 days at 1.5-m b/d of surplus, or 90 days at 1-m b/d of surplus. If this storage effectively maxes out at 80% utilization, then that number could be 45 days at 1.5-m b/d, and a little over 60 days at 1-m b/d. Should Iran close production equal to exports, it would likely be able to manage its most vulnerable wells to minimize long term damage. There are concerns that extended periods of reduced production from Iran’s predominantly fractured carbonate reservoir geology could also cause its long-term production trajectory to suffer due to higher decline rates and lower recoverable reserves, though Iran has broadly been able to keep production capacity at around 4-m b/d despite more than a decade of sanctions. (See: “Reserve demand and deregulations”.) FRN maturity date For FRNs that do not mature on a business day, the lack of accrued interest is a major concern for 2a7 investors. As a result, many 2a7 funds sell such securities back to the dealers as the maturity month approaches, which add pressure to dealer balance sheets. Treasury should therefore consider changing stated maturity dates for FRNs, so they always occur on a business day. We do not see the same need for non-FRN securities, which generally have a broader and more diversified investor base that is less affected by this issue. The primary benefit would be stronger FRN liquidity and reduced need for dealers to warehouse affected securities on their balance sheet. A potential drawback would be increased fragmentation between FRNs and other Treasury securities, potentially resulting in similar but not identical maturity dates leading to pricing distortions in the front end of the curve. This would indicate a slight improvement in momentum, rather than a meaningful acceleration. The March reading of 54.0 masked considerable divergence across components: the new orders index remained strong at 60.6, while the employment index fell sharply to 45.2. Our forecast assumes that the March drop in employment overstated underlying weakness, which was partially reversed in April. Ongoing supply constraints that extend delivery times may have provided some mechanical support to the headline composite. We do not anticipate a significant pickup, as downside risks remain and broader survey evidence points to only incremental improvement. Adjusting for overstatement, we would estimate that pace is probably zero to +10K per month. We also would guess that even with the slowdown in immigration that is slow enough to over time put upward pressure on the unemployment rate. The bigger uncertainty for the path of the unemployment rate is labor force participation. The LFPR high or medium frequency moves can swamp whatever is happening in immigration and population growth. If we get a gain in NFP close to or ahead of our estimate, or a decline in the unemployment rate, that will interact with the inflation data and hawkish rhetoric and views would be likely to mount, and spread incrementally across the FOMC. The opposite, a weak report, would do the opposite. The report would need to be an unmitigated disaster and have large downward revisions to prior months to put rate cuts back on the table for June, however, so we do not think that is likely. The FOMC saw the -90K drop in employment in February and shrugged it off because January had been strong. The same would likely be said for a weak April report. As we mentioned in Headline Ping Pong the ‘Reflation trade (or Takaichi trade)’ regime for Japan markets really kicked off last year July, when following a bruising defeat of the LDP in the upper house elections, the odds of Sanae Takaichi as new PM started rising. The policy mix offered by the new candidate was perceived as expansive on fiscal and looser on monetary policy, meaning higher local equities, lower JPY, and steeper curve. The big LDP win in the lower house elections this year brought instead a (brief) shift towards a ‘buy everything Japan’ regime, on the idea that with a full majority in the lower house, the LDP would not need to compromise on fiscal policies proposed by the opposition (and thus remain expansionary but somewhat contained). FX rallied, curve flattened, and equities continued to trend higher. We represented the two regimes in Figure 4 below. The ‘Reflation trade’ is calculated as USDJPY, 2s10s, and NKY all above their respective 55 day moving average. While the ‘buy everything Japan’ is calculated as NKY above its 55dma, while USDJPY and 2s10s below. The reflation trade has made a comeback in recent weeks due to the war in the Middle East, given a cautious BoJ and potentially more fiscal on the government front, before the MoF intervened. In March, the latest data, exhaustions bounced back after declines in January and February. 26 weeks ago, in October 2025, claims were sawtoothing from week to week and still pushed around by a spate of fraudulent filings in the fall. The 4-week moving average of initial claims generally trended down from October through the rest of the fall, so in the coming weeks, there will likely be fewer claimants exhausting their benefits, possibly exerting less downward pressure on continuing claims. The plunge in initial claims in the week ending April 25 looks to be associated with mistimed seasonal factors as New York claims after spring break. Benefits exhaustions rose in March, possibly exerting downward pressure on continuing claims.

Volume data from July 2020 onwards represents the combined total traded volume across EBS and Reuters sources. Prior to July 2020, we aggregate total traded volume from EBS with estimated trading volume from Reuters, which is calculated as a product of total paid-given count and average trade size. To estimate average trade size prior to July 2020 we use all future data for total trading volume and trade count. We then apply a 20-day moving average and rank the current value over the prior one-year lookback window**. Spread data represents the average daily market spread based on quotes taken every 30 seconds in the order book aggregated across EBS and Reuters on a volume weighted basis. Global factors—risk and energy—remain in the driver’s seat, but where UK-specific themes do play a role, we think they are more likely than not to be marginal negatives for the currency. Our economists have stuck with their no-hike baseline for the BoE after this week’s meeting, and their relative modal views across central banks implies clearer dovish risks to market pricing for the BoE than anywhere else in the G10. This was also the case prior to the energy shock, and had been a core element of our Sterling underperformance view, but we think the weaker prevailing FX-rates relationship raises the hurdle for dovish BoE risks to dictate the trend in Sterling now. Elsewhere, this coming Thursday’s May local elections should keep focus high on the lingering risks of a flare-up in UK political or fiscal premium. We think options markets are right to price-in relatively limited vol premium for the day itself. The larger risks are likely in the form of either leadership challenges to the PM, or a shift in focus back to a constrained fiscal position on account of the evolution of energy prices and Gilt yields throughout the energy shock, and both of these are likely less immediate (Exhibit 5). Indeed, the 'full employment' part of the mandate distinguishes the Fed from other core central banks, which solely focus on 'price stability' . In the press conference, however, Powell was somewhat hawkish. He mentioned that the FOMC was in a holding pattern, given the upside risks to inflation, and that policymakers would need to see the 'backside' of the progress on inflation before thinking about reducing rates. He noted that the decision to keep the easing bias was a much closer call than at the March meeting. Powell stated that, once confirmed, Kevin Warsh would become the chair of the Federal Reserve Board and of the FOMC, while Powell would continue to serve as a 'low profile' governor 'for a period of time to be determined' , until the investigation about the Fed's building renovation is 'well and truly over with finality and transparency' . Powell's hawkish comments add to the risks that the FOMC will hold rates for an extended period. Our baseline outlook of a September cut relies on core PCE inflation prints moderating notably in the coming months. It then began to lose altitude as these tailwinds faded and as a surge in net immigration led to a sharp expansion of the adult population from 2022 to 2024. We have previously flagged that the rate at which immigrants form new households is lower than for the overall population. The more recent return to a higher headship rate likely reflects the reversal of this immigration surge, as the cohort with a lower-headship-propensity becomes a smaller share of the population. With immigration enforcement tightened under the current administration and net inflows running well below the 2022–2024 pace, we expect this compositional tail- wind to persist. Updated CBO projections estimate household formation of 1.2 million for full-year 2026, up from 1.1 mil- lion in 2025, even as population growth slows. With household formation remaining firm, new supply is unlikely to close a persistent structural deficit. Over the last 10 years, cumulative household formation has outpaced com- pletions by 2.3 million units (Figure 3). records.text: European Economics Presentation1 May 2026 ab 69 France outlook – key points • Growth is holding up well: moderate fiscal headwinds – GDP: 0.9% in 2025, 0.9% in 2026E, 1% in 2027E – vs trend growth of 1.2% – France less exposed to energy shock given low share of industry and large share of nuclear power in energy mix – Political uncertainty and moderate fiscal tightening is weighing on activity • Fiscal policy: Excessive Deficit Procedure (EDP) has been triggered – Persistent budget deficits (last surplus in 1974) reflect very high expenditures – We expect moderate declines in the budget deficit (-0.2pp to 4.9% of GDP in 2026), less than would be implied by the EDP • France has higher trend growth than Germany – More growth friendly demographics (higher fertility rate), past structural reforms (corporate tax cuts, labour reform), a smaller manufacturing sector, less exposure to high gas prices (nuclear power) • Next presidential election scheduled for 2027 – Pension reform likely to be a key topic – Key question: Will a unified centrist candidate emerge (e.g. Edouard Philippe?)

records.text: Europe was slowing even before the energy crisis The euro area Q1 GDP print came in at 0.1% q/q (0.148% q/q unrounded). This was somewhat below the consensus (0.2% q/q) and the ECB's March projections, which had anticipated a 0.3% q/q expansion. Geographically, growth dynamics continued to display significant divergence across major euro area economies. Spanish GDP growth maintained a strong pace (0.6% q/q), growth surprised to the upside in Germany (0.3% q/q) and Italy (0.2% q/q), but surprised significantly to the downside for France (0%). A large contraction from the highly volatile Irish GDP (-2.0% q/q in Q1) implies some downward distortion, but the details available so far suggest that domestic demand components for the euro area on aggregate may have begun to decelerate even before the onset of the Middle East conflict. Central banks: Wait and dissent Core central banks (Fed, ECB, BoJ and BoE) left policy rates unchanged this week, as widely expected. But the meetings were far from uneventful and the common 'holding pattern' came with significant differences between the central banks's communication, as well as dissent within their policy committees. records.text: Running Out of Oil? A Large But Still Mostly Local Products Risk We update and expand our analysis of the risks of oil shortages focusing on country-product markets. Because most non-OECD product stocks are not visible, we complement our tracking/estimation of stocks (approach 1) with an analysis of refined products supplied (approach 2), prices (approach 3), and news flow (approach 4). Approach 1: Tracking/Estimating Stocks Q1. You estimated that visible oil stocks are on track to reach record lows soon. Does that mean the world will run out of oil soon? Not exactly. We estimate that global visible oil inventories are likely to reach the lowest level on record since 2018 (when satellite data tracking most crude stocks became available) even if Hormuz flows started recovering soon, as any full normalization of deliveries would take at least several weeks (Exhibit 1). However, even modern lows for aggregate visible stocks are above estimated critically low levels. We expect OECD commercial oil stocks to decline to 57 days of demand (DoD) by June, also the lowest level since 2018 (Exhibit 2). But OECD landed commercial stocks were structurally lower before the US shale boom, averaging 53 DoD in 2000-2005 and below 50 days in February 2003.1 1 The structural increase in OECD commercial stocks can be explained by a shift from storage on water (given long-haul voyages from the Middle East) to landed crude storage in the US (and short-haul voyages). With Hor- muz effectively still closed, European policymakers can only try to improve the coordination of how existing sup- plies are used. The EC will try to coordinate the refilling of gas storage for next winter to avoid price spikes caused by simultaneous purchases by member states and it will allow more flexibility on the targets, both in terms of tim- ing (by 1 December versus 1 November) and level (80% and possibly 75% by next winter, versus the usual 90%). Storage levels have so far increased from a low of 28% to 32%, leaving a long way to go (Figure 1). Three other areas of coordination across member states are on (a) any releases from oil stocks (incl. jet fuel, diesel), (b) optimiz- ing existing refining capacity and distribution of fuels across member states and (c) purchases of energy from third countries. Such steps can help, up to a point, but will not solve the main shortage. Economic theory suggests that higher productivity of capital and labor should increase the real interest rate and wages in the long run, as capital owners and workers are compensated for their higher contributions to production. At the same time, inflation is largely the choice of the central bank over the long run. As it calibrates policy to achieve its inflation target, the central bank’s policy rate will average the real neutral interest rate—which is determined by non-monetary forces, including productivity—plus its inflation target. As shown in Exhibit 11, we find some evidence consistent with these economic principles: using long-run cross-country data as a proxy for different economic equilibria, we find that countries with faster productivity growth tend to have higher real interest rates and wages but find no relationship with inflation. That being said, other research has found little relationship between real output growth and long-term real interest rates over longer time horizons, so the strength of this mechanism could change over time.3 In the medium term, however, the transition to higher productivity growth is likely to weigh on prices, for at least a couple of reasons. First, wages typically take longer to adjust than prices, so businesses’ production costs can fall before higher wages offset the decline. This would be consistent with the official announcement that the UAE would be “bringing additional production to market in a gradual and measured manner, aligned with demand and market conditions”. Over the medium-term, rapid UAE production increases could risk spurring another price war as GCC countries compete for market share. An ensuant reduction in the GCC spare capacity could also have effects on the long-end of the oil price curve, all else being equal. Given how important AI has been for the move of the back to the highs, it is important to understand if the NDX outperformance is mostly due to a flight to safety, mixed with more favorable positioning, or whether the underlying US tech story is on track. With respect to the earnings, we got this week, the glass seems to be half full, according to our analysts. In the bigger picture, late last year, there were three stories hurting US tech. The first was linked to overinvestment and high capex fears, the second was linked to fears about OpenAI cash flows, which is of course related to the first reason, and the third was linked to AI disruption fears, especially in software. Capex fears mostly impact stocks negatively, if there is little to show for it. Overall, the hyperscaler basket has started to outperform the SPX again, as per Figure 8. While some of that was part of the flight to safety during the early days of the Iran war, it has continued even on days when Iran tensions lessened. Furthermore, the lesson from the earnings this week is that increasing capex can be a good thing for the market if revenues are rising too (as for GOOGL), or a bad thing, if the company is not able to show that much upside in business fundamentals (META). USD skew remains sticky, although the details suggest this is increasingly a story of a few holdouts rather than a broad-based repricing. The more notable feature is how subdued convexity pricing remains: with a continuing stale- mate, the path ahead can look deceptively linear right until it isn’t, and our analysts frame June as approaching “operational stress level.” That matters because the set of plausible cata- lysts is increasingly binary. A sharp regime shift could come from the Middle East either via escalation or resolution, while a second channel for wingy spot action could come from JPY and potential MoF intervention. Either (and especially both together) could be more than the current convexity pricing is set up to absorb. Yet we also acknowledge the other side of the distribution: the status quo can easily persist for weeks, consistent with our tactical pro-cyclical bias—so low cost of exposure is imperative. The UAE is second only to Saudi Arabia with regard to production flexibility, both for reducing output (discipline) and increasing it (spare capacity). Notably, the UAE also played a larger role in production cuts during the GFC than Qatar, another former "OPEC 'Core'" member, which exited in 2019. Therefore, with the UAE's absence from May, OPEC and the OPEC+ coalition will have a diminished ability to manage market surpluses and deficits. n The economic and fiscal motivations for the UAE's decision appear obvious, quite apart from the well-known political issues. The UAE stands out among much of its OPEC brethren due to its lower fiscal breakeven oil price. In fact, amongst oil-exporting countries surveyed by the IMF, the UAE (USD 45/bbl) is matched in its low fiscal breakeven only by Qatar (USD 43/ bbl) in 2026, while Iran (USD 165/bbl) is at the higher end of the spectrum. n In light of the UAE's pledge to "continue to act responsibly, bringing additional production to market in a gradual and measured manner", we anticipate that the UAE will most likely increase its production towards sustainable capacity over a period of a year following the end of commercial shipping restrictions. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 01 May 2026 13:20:52 ET │ 15 pages Canada Economics Weekly Opening the door for rate cuts... or hikes CITI'S TAKE BoC officials left policy rates and open-ended guidance unchanged as expected this week but took another small step towards adjusting rates again. Governor Macklem suggested that small policy rate changes could occur even in a scenario where the outlook evolves largely as expected, but gave no indication whether these adjustments would imply higher or lower rates. Markets pricing ~50bp of rate hikes this year are expecting a return to the mid-point of the neutral range. We think this is unlikely in the near-term given an unemployment rate stuck at 6.5-7% (including in our forecast for April data next week), an output gap that is more negative than in the 2015 oil price shock when policy rates were cut to 0.50%, two years of falling home prices, and core inflation around target. All of these conditions, if they persist, would suggest policy rates should be more accommodative, not less. In the first half of 2006, “Helicopter Ben” Bernanke led the Fed in a more hawkish direction than the market expected. The ques- tion becomes even trickier for Warsh. And that drives home another key point and our final observation: gradualism allows a good degree of control over interest rate expectation. In current circumstances, this is the most likely path taken by the ECB. For example, assuming that the desired policy stance by the ECB is current market pricing, i.e. three hikes this year (it is very likely less than that, as discussed above), a hike yesterday would have required a lot of additional communication to achieve the same market pricing. This points to a very likely sequence from here. A possible June hike is probably followed by a pause in July. Next to greater degree of control over short-term interest rate expectations, such a sequencing would also be in line with the lagged arrival of data and the availability of a new holistic assessment with the September projections. Much like in the case of an unlikely 50bp hike, speeding up the hiking cycle over the summer would require a fundamental change in the assessment of the situation by the Council. From today’s perspective that seems unlikely.

Food inflation has historically declined during El Niño episodes, providing a partial offset to the mining disruption. The net macroeconom- ic effect is therefore ambiguous, depending on the event’s intensity, spatial pattern, and the global copper price response. Ecuador: In the eye of the storm Ecuador shares Peru’s coastal geography and, consequently, its direct exposure to El Niño’s heavy rainfall, flooding, and agricultural destruction. The agricultural export base—banan- as, shrimp, cocoa, and cut flowers—is highly climate-sensi- tive. Flooding damages shrimp farms and banana plantations along the coast, while temperature anomalies affect cocoa quality. Ecuador’s vulnerability is compounded by its dollar- ized monetary framework, which eliminates the exchange rate as a shock absorber, and by limited fiscal buffers as recon- struction and social support add pressure on fiscal needs. There is, however, a partial offset: higher rainfall boosts hydroelectric generation, reducing reliance on imported fuels (with around 70% of electricity generated from hydro sourc- es). Yet, very intense El Niño events can disrupt power infra- structure and limit the ability to fully utilize increased hydro- electric capacity. We see large risks of jet fuel shortages in Europe already this summer, significant tightening in the European diesel market, but more buffers for crude and gasoline. Source: Citi Research, Citi Velocity Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg The week's economic data flow was uniformly tilted toward the "higher-for-longer" narrative. Q1 GDP rebounded at a 2.0% annualized pace, March PCE inflation rose 0.7% month over month and 3.5% year over year, ECI compensation costs rose 0.9% in Q1, and initial jobless claims fell to 189k. For Agency MBS specifically, the combination of resilient growth and sticky inflation reduces conviction in near-term Fed easing, keeping mortgage rates elevated and refinancing activity suppressed. Middle East uncertainty and energy price risk further complicate the Fed's reaction function, elevate inflation expectations, and reduce the market's willingness to treat any rate rally as durable. Strong tech and AI-related earnings provided a meaningful counterweight to macro headwinds. Major equity indices rallied sharply into month-end, improving broader risk sentiment and supporting demand for spread products — a marginal positive for Agency MBS. Prepared for Cayla Buettner
