records.text: We discuss several considerations for investors using analysts' price targets. First, price targets are more informative when normalised within a sector or an analyst's coverage universe. Second, the informativeness of price targets varies across firm characteristics: they are more informative among stocks with smaller market capitalisation, faster growth, higher quality, higher yield, lower past return volatility, and stronger momentum. Third, PTIR is more capable of predicting stock returns when conditioned on high analyst conviction, measured by the dynamics in analyst price target revision. Finally, including only the most recent price targets in the consensus calculation does not deliver superior results, as doing so aggressively reduces the number of price targets in the consensus measure and introduces noise. Appendix: Univariate portfolio sorts on price target revisions We want to ask: can analysts' price target revision alone predict stock returns? To address this question, we analyse the performance of quintile portfolios and the corresponding long-short portfolio formed on price target revisions. Figure 27 shows that although the top price target revision portfolio outperforms the bottom portfolio, the performance of the long-short price target revision portfolio, whether risk-adjusted or not, is significantly weaker than that of the long-short PTIR portfolio conditioned on high price target revisions. Prior volatility spikes were often dampened by policy support, whereas the Iran conflict introduces physical supply constraints in energy and commodities that are less responsive to policy intervention. This raises the risk that volatility shocks become more persistent. As a result, while current conditions justify maintaining short gamma exposure, the case for scaling positions aggressively is weak. records.text: Commodities: Forecasts and key views 1319 May 2026 ▪ Oil: While Brent prices have ebbed and flowed with geopolitical headlines, physical markets have priced steadily stronger, reflecting near-term supply shortages. We remain cautious on the prospect of a rapid normalisation of flows through the Strait of Hormuz, leading us to think prices may rise further before they fall. ▪ Gas: LNG prices have risen relatively modestly so far, mainly because spring sees low demand in both Europe and Asia. However, with gas having fewer supply offsets than oil, we expect significant price upside if disruption extends into the summer. ▪ Gold: We lower our price expectations modestly for the balance of 2026, reflecting the energy price shock’s negative impact on the precious metals complex. However, we remain bullish from current levels as a persistent de-dollarisation trend appears to be driving central bank accumulation of gold. ▪ Copper: We raise our price expectations, largely on continued speculative interest. This now reflects concerns that curbs on sulphur supplies could impact output from the Democratic Republic of Congo. ▪ Battery metals: Despite evidence of oversupply, we raise our lithium forecasts to reflect persistent supply risks and the prospect of prolonged Middle East tensions boosting global acceptance of electric vehicles and Battery Energy Storage Systems. records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 01 May 2026 3 Germany: budget holes, political tensions and confidence loss German budget planning has started. A more comprehensive discussion is on our “to do list” for next week, but so much up front: the very preliminary 2027 budget draft points to new borrowing of close to EUR 200bn, ie close to EUR 30bn more than the medium- term budget plans would have suggested. To our mind, this is largely down to cyclical deterioration from the significantly worsened growth outlook. There are two more crucial elements in budget planning discussions. First, large budget holes for 2027 need to be closed. With 2025 policy innovations having delivered fiscal easing, tightening is now in the making relative to that path. A healthcare reform (c EUR 16bn savings for 2027) is part of that, with the potential tow weigh on consumer confidence in the near term, on top of the effects of the energy crisis. Second, political tensions are running very high. Budget holes in 2028 look bigger than in 2027. Italy, by comparison, has been calm over recent years. But during our field trip to Rome last week, we sensed that relative stability – on growth, deficits and politics – coming to an end. records.text: During his press conference, Powell undid any dovishness that might have come out of the statement's retention of the easing bias, noting that the decision to retain the easing bias was a much closer call than at the March meeting. He favored keeping the statement unchanged for now, given the elevated uncertainty. As we had expected in our FOMC preview, Powell no longer emphasized that the base case involves additional rate cuts, while signaling that the FOMC is in a holding pattern, well positioned to address the risks on both sides of the dual mandate. Given the upside risks to inflation, he argued policymakers would need to see the "backside" of the progress on inflation before even thinking about reducing rates. Powell's hawkish comments add to the risks that the FOMC will hold rates for an extended period. In our baseline outlook in which the Strait of Hormuz reopens promptly and core PCE inflation prints moderate notably after the April reading, we think the FOMC would consider cutting rates in September. We view risks to our baseline view as skewed toward delayed rate cuts, with the conflict in the Middle East tilting inflation risks to the upside. Fed succession Powell provided more clarity about the Fed succession, suggesting that after his term ends on May 15, Kevin Warsh would likely become chair of both the Fed and the FOMC. records.text: US Economics Weekly1 May 2026 ab 43 Our models seem pretty happy with the current level of the unemployment rate (even those estimated in changes). The four-week moving average of initial claims was 211K in the April reference week, the exact same level seen in the March reference week. The level of continuing claims in the week ending April 18 was -31K lower than the week ending March 13. Some of the high frequency moves in the claims data could be noise related floating holidays and school breaks, when many public school workers file for the time off. Our models are concentrated around 4.25%-4.28% for April. We do not see much bias from seasonal adjustment this month. Slackening was evident on the margins in the March household survey data — household survey employment fell -64K, not in the labor force climbed 488K, and the number of unemployed individuals fell -396K. The number of discouraged workers rose, as people left the labor force. Added to that, the number of people working part-time for economic reasons, due to slack work conditions, climbed. Altogether, that offset the drop in the unemployment rate and pushed U-6, the broadest measure of labor under- utilization, up 0.1 pp to 8.0% in March. EU with continuous decline of WAM since 2022 - 11.3y ytd We provide the WAM of newly issued EU bonds (including taps) per year since 2020 and ytd compared with KfW, NRW and Berlin (BERGER) (Figure 104-Figure 107). With 11.3y ytd versus 14.8y in FY 2020, the WAM of EU supply has been on a continuous downward trend. This seems in line with the lower need for duration under the EU unified funding approach (UFA), for example, due to fewer RRF loans than originally expected and probably is also a result of trying to be more in line with core EGB issuers (e.g. Germany and France). In the cases of KfW and NRW, the WAM of ytd supply is at the lower end of the range since FY 2020 and is higher than the WAM in FY 2025. In the case of Berlin (BERGER), the WAM of ytd supply has risen significantly to 13.9y versus 6.8y in FY 2025 but is still lower than the high of 15.3y in FY 2020. In terms of outstanding volume of EUR benchmark bonds from these issuers, EU stands at EUR 758bn which is more than double the EUR 293bn from KFW followed by EUR 102.8bn from NRW and EUR 45bn from BERGER (Figure 108). The institutional response capacity remains weak despite recurring episodes. Flood defenses, early-warning systems, and urban drainage remain deficient, particularly in the most exposed northern coastal departments. The risk of compound- ing is high. If the El Niño Costero couples with a strong glob- al El Niño as forecast, coastal waters may not cool during the austral winter, extending the flooding season and prolonging the fisheries disruption through 2027. The inflation channel is also potent. Food prices in affected regions could rise by at least 30% during a strong event, compounding the already- challenging impact of higher oil prices and potentially fertil- izers, complicating the BCRP’s stance. Colombia: The hydro & food channels Colombia’s El Niño transmission operates through a distinct mechanism. Rather than flooding, El Niño brings reduced precipitation to much of the country, stressing the country’s hydroelectric-dependent energy matrix. With roughly 70% of electricity generated by hydropower, reservoir drawdowns force a costly shift to thermal generation, raising wholesale electricity prices and increasing the fiscal burden of energy subsidies. records.text: Modest EU underperformance on supply, but the curve is deepening. The EU n revised its H1 funding plan this week and now expects gross bond issuance to reach €100bn, vs €90bn previously. While modest in size, the revision is likely to be followed by ongoing upward revisions, with our economists expecting EU net bond issuance to reach about €125bn for 2026. Additionally, risks are firmly to the upside, depending on whether and how much NGEU disbursements and Ukraine funding accelerate, as well as the possibility of eventually repurposing unused spare financial capacity under the NGEU for other policy goals such as energy relief or security. In the upside scenario, EU issuance could reach €180bn (implying gross funding through bonds of ~€120bn in H2). We think this supply outlook presents the risk of underperformance of EU bonds against peers (including France, on which we have turned more positive). That being said, we note that the EU bond universe is deeper now compared to the last surge in EU issuance during the 2022-23 hiking cycle. With scope to increase its free float for 2026 and beyond, we see EU underperformance as a tactical supply-related risk, but think that the underperformance based on risk of lower liquidity in a period of elevated rate volatility is less relevant now than in 2022, which had seen EU trade at the higher end of the semi-core range (Exhibit 4). records.text: DM rates: Forecasts and key views 1119 May 2026 ▪ US: We see Treasury yields continuing to push higher, led by the long end and steepening the yield curve. ▪ Deficit concerns are driving term premiums upward and the curve steeper as the Middle East conflict prompts rates markets to price in both a ‘one- time’ cost to reflect recent hostilities and potential higher spending on defence going forward. ▪ Meanwhile, a Fed on hold with inflation above target should keep 2y yields oscillating near current levels, while adding more upward pressure on long-term yields and so steepening the curve. ▪ Eurozone: Yields have scope to push higher still, driven by oil prices normalising slowly, much higher inflation, likely rate hikes and a supply- demand mismatch for bonds in a context that remains pro-risk. ▪ As 2027 approaches, the market could start pricing in rate cuts, while the ongoing Dutch pension fund transition might also give more steepening impetus to the curve. ▪ UK: We think 10y gilt yields will remain elevated (staying above our fair value range) until Q4 2026, as rising inflation prompts rate hikes. A fragile political backdrop should also support a floor in the short term ▪ Japan: We expect higher JGB yields, with the 10y rising to 2.6% this year and 2.7% in 2027. The front end should lead this as the market prices in more rate hikes, so we expect 2s10s to flatten. EUR HICP forecasts We expect this week’s euro-area April HICP (ex-tobacco) release to show an increase of 2.98% (2.93%) year-on-year, which would be around 40bp above March and close to 1.1% above February. This is slightly below market pricing and the Bloomberg consensus. Uncertainty seems relatively high this month, given the confluence of rising oil prices, tax cuts and the volatility of travel prices around Easter and this is reflected in a comparatively wide distribution of consensus forecasts; individual forecasts range from 1.9% to 2.4% for core and from 2.8% to 3.3% for headline (removing the extremes). Energy is likely to have remained the main driver of higher prices, and we project HICP fuels to be up around 6% month-on-month, after 14.8% in March. Forecasts for the coming months have continued to rise as not only front-month brent prices are back at the highs, but end of the year and mid-2027 futures have also edged higher (Figure 83). This is expected to push HICP fuels to above 20% year-on-year (Figure 84). For HICP gas and electricity, uncertainty this month comes from the potential downward impact from tax cuts in Spain. For the former, we expect to see a pickup in price momentum from May, and overall HICP energy looks set to exceed 10% year-on-year from April, despite tax cuts in several countries. records.text: Special questions in the Dallas survey (link here) asked firms about the net impact of the conflict in Iran. 34.8% of manufacturing firms reported a net negative impact. Of those negatively impacted, 87.0% of firms cited higher fuel and transportation costs as a consequence of the conflict in the Middle East. As a response, 34.8% of manufacturing firms that report being negatively impacted said they increased selling prices, 26.1% adjusted supply chains, and 21.7% reported no response to the negative impacts. The supplier deliveries index could be giving undue strength to the composite index, rising on bottlenecks from geopolitical factors. The ISM headline was unchanged due to a rise in new orders, inventories, and supplier delivers being offset by a fall in production and employment. On an ISM-adjusted basis, all surveys except Kansas City and Philly improved, and all remain in expansion. The largest share of firms in the FRB Dallas survey reported no negative impact yet, with an expected negative impact if the Middle East conflict continues.

However, even if this headline appears soft, private domestic demand was resilient in Q1, with private domestic final purchases (PDFP) rising a solid 2.5% q/q saar. Notably, it was boosted by surging nonresidential fixed investment (10.4% q/q saar—its fastest since mid-2023), which reflect AI-related capital expenditure categories. With AI spending gaining further momentum during Q1, we estimate it contributed more than 1.0pp to growth in expenditure accounting terms. Given the strong indicators of capex demand from capital goods orders, and projections from the hyperscalers, this influence has room to run. Indeed, the upbeat earnings reports by hyperscalers this week, in particular Alphabet, confirm investor optimism on AI-related investment boom. China growth still driven by green-tech and AI-related exports Growth dynamics in China look similarly robust, even if lopsided. Following the better-than- expected 5.0% Q1 GDP print released earlier, this week's April manufacturing PMIs remained in expansionary territory, surprising slightly to the upside. records.text: as Chair Powell related this week, “we couldn't come up with anything that had really broad support on the Committee, and so we just moved on.” It seems that any modification to the SEP or the dot plot would require a committee vote. We suspect many on the FOMC are in favor of keeping the dot plot— despite mixed reviews from the public—because it allows them to have a say in the Fed’s overall suite of communica- tions. The modalities of the press conference, in contrast, are likely at the discretion of the chair. Given Warsh’s remarks that he would like to see less forward guidance, there has been spec- ulation as to whether Warsh would cancel the press confer- ences, reduce their frequency, or limit questions from the press. In the end, we suspect Warsh will keep the press con- ferences as they are. The press conference allows the chair to be the “first out of the gate” to shape the narrative of where policy is heading. Warsh’s experience with press conferences will get an early test with the June FOMC meeting. Part of the reason the press conference has received so much attention is that all the Fed chairs in the press conference era (Bernanke, Yellen, and Powell) were believed to be faithfully conveying the sense of the committee. If Warsh is opposed to keeping policy unchanged next month, this could complicate what he says. Any perception that his comments reflect some of his person- al bias could confuse markets and eventually diminish the power of the press conference.

We provide a regular update on the evolution of developed market (DM) rates markets in the recent past. We then analyse the distribution of outstanding bonds by investor type to assess the proportion held by price-insensitive investors, such as domestic central banks. Moving to market pricing, we examine pricing trends of major central banks, followed by recent market movements in key rates products. Surprises on both diminish the likelihood that Kevin Warsh will lead the FOMC in rate cuts soon, barring a signifi- cant weakening in the economy. This week we discussed fur- ther implications of Warsh’s upcoming chairmanship. The first surprise at the FOMC meeting was the decision by three regional bank presidents (Hammack, Kashkari, and Logan), to dissent on the language of the statement, noting that they “did not support inclusion of an easing bias in the statement at this time.” We believe this to be the first instance of dissent on the language when the Fed has not been at the zero lower bound. Those dissents highlight a growing cohort who see hikes as equally likely as cuts for the next move. Those three members have since outlined concerns about ris- ing uncertainty and the possible inflationary impacts of the Middle East conflict. Coming into the meeting, members would also have been aware that core PCE inflation was on track to hit 3.2%oya in March, which is the highest reading since late 2023—albeit by a small margin. The second surprise was that Powell said he would stay on as a governor “for a period of time,” and he replied affirmatively when asked if this was to serve as a “check and balance” on threats to Fed independence. LLC US Daily: Core vs. Trimmed vs. Median: What’s the Best Measure of the Inflation Trend? 1 May 2026 | 11:25AM CDT During his confirmation hearing last week, Fed chair nominee Kevin Warsh n highlighted trimmed mean and median inflation as potentially helpful measures of the underlying trend. These measures have recently run below core inflation in PCE terms, though at a similar pace to core inflation excluding estimated tariff effects, a measure that Chair Powell and other Fed leaders have cited. One might expect statistical measures to outperform the core in forecasting n future inflation because the core is a very simple measure that just removes two volatile categories, food and energy. But we find a more mixed track record: the core and trimmed mean have performed quite similarly in predicting year-ahead inflation, while the median has performed worse. Whether to trim is partly a judgment about the economic environment. n Trimming is appealing when one is confident that a key one-off factor has driven extreme moves in outlier categories and in calmer environments where outliers likely arise from measurement error or category-level idiosyncrasies. Balanced message with door open to modest hikes. No explicit guidance on June. • Base case: two hikes in June/July (with risks of one), followed by cuts in 2027. Risks of delay to hikes has increased. Active hold The BoE kept rates on hold as expected with a 8-1 vote (Pill voted for a hike). Overall, the messaging was balanced. The BoE kept the door open to modest hikes as we expected in its scenario analysis, and Bailey noted that market pricing of hikes is not in the wrong place, given the uncertainty. But Bailey didn’t explicitly pre-commit to hikes or give explicit guidance on June. The 8-1 vote was a bit more dovish relative to our expectations. It kept guidance unchanged that it stands ready to act as necessary to ensure that CPI remains on track to meet the 2% target in the medium term. Overall the MPC judged second round effects to be modest, which point to modest hikes but was alert to risks of stronger. The MPC judged that “while there were likely to be some second-round effects, continued weakness in activity would limit the strength of these. But these effects were likely to be stronger, the larger and more persistent the rise in global energy prices.” The BoE noted that strength of second round effects would depend partly on how long energy prices remain elevated, and nature of behavioural

That, along with our expectation for slightly better job growth, should help push real income growth higher in 2H 26. Last, the role of income in consumption is less important today than it was previously. We continue to see K-shaped dynamics driving resilient consumer spending. The saving rate fell again in March and is down 1.5pp from a year ago, as the stock market boom has allowed higher-income households to save less monthly. Equities remain near all- time highs, reducing the importance of income for activity. The consumer can weather the energy shock We also think the consumer and overall economy can weather the energy shock. To date, we estimate that gas prices have chipped away at nearly half the benefit of tax refunds (See our: Morning Market Tidbits: Tax refunds versus the “gas tax” 30 April 2026 ). To estimate the potential cost of the gas tax moving forward, we compare current futures prices for wholesale gas to prices on Feb 27, 2026 (prior to the war). Using various elasticities from the literature, we estimate the full year “gas tax” to be worth 0.3% - 0.5% of GDP. That is about equal to the boost we estimate to come from the One Big Beautiful Bill or from AI capex. To be sure, this drag could be much higher as we only focus on gasoline prices and the energy shock should drive up the costs of other goods and services. That echoes less of July 2024 and more of April 2024, when the MoF intervened amidst solid global growth, upbeat risk sentiment, and markets adjusting to higher-for-longer rates—a typically negative backdrop for the Yen. But even then, the intervention followed a dovish FOMC meeting, when Chair Powell emphasized that while there was still a high bar to cut, the bar was much higher to hike rates further. It had also come after a sharp rally in USD/JPY that looked clearly dislocated from fundamentals, in contrast to the latest episode that seemed aimed at defending the 160 level in USD/JPY (Exhibit 3). Overall, intervention often serves to buy time until macro conditions shift in the same direction. The prior interventions in 2022 and 2024 were successful in that sense, as the broader backdrop did evolve in a JPY-positive direction within subsequent months. records.text: US Economics Weekly1 May 2026 ab 4 Will the real unemployment rate please stand up? The real unemployment rate is 4.26%, or was in March, which we expect to be little changed in April in next week's employment report. However, given the disconnect between some labor market indicators we thought checking in on what other indicators implied for the unemployment rate might be insightful. Recent work by FRB of Chicago economist Bart Hobijn considers a range of labor market indictors, summarizes their information using principal component analysis and then fits the first two principal components onto the published unemployment rate. Hobijn finds that this fitted unemployment rate is ~0.5pp below the published unemployment rate, see here. Taking a page out of Hobijn's book we estimate a kitchen sink model — drawing on 18 indicators (1) of both labor supply and demand. Differing a little in our approach we fit these to the demographic adjusted (fixed-weight) unemployment rate and we find that when doing so the fit is much better historically where the demographic shifts will make the most difference. We also abstract from the pandemic noise by dropping March 2020 - March 2021 from the sample for the regressions. The gap between this measure of the unemployment rate and that implied by the kitchen sink model is smaller and is actually ~0.2pp below the demographically adjusted unemployment rate. Morgan The pace of real consumer spending growth in 1Q, at 1.6%, was decent though nothing special, and indeed it was the lowest rate of growth in a year. However, this softness wasn’t completely surprising as we’ve argued that with the drop in saving rates over time, we might start to see slower spending growth. The hit from higher gas prices in March didn’t help, but tax refunds were still about three times greater than the additional gas spending that month. Investment in equipment and intellectual property remained very strong as the AI boom kept lifting computer investment, OBBBA tax benefits for R&D kept lifting IPP, and what is probably noise in the software deflator lifted real software spending. records.text: as the FRBSF model. We start by overlaying a five-mile-by-five-mile grid across the contigu- ous United States and assign each grid point to its county. For each grid point, we compute inverse-distance-weighted aver- ages of daily weather measurements from all NOAA Global Historical Climatology Network stations within 50 miles, covering temperature, precipitation, snowfall, and extreme heat and cold. These grid-level daily values are then aggregat- ed to the county-month level with roughly double weight giv- en to weather in the first two weeks of the month, the period most relevant for the payroll survey which measures employ- ment in the payroll period containing the 12th of the month. We combine this weather data with county employment data from QCEW and estimate a dynamic panel data model of how deviations from seasonal weather norms affect local employment growth. The model measures five weather dimensions—average daily high temperature, precipitation, snowfall, the share of days above 90°F, and the share of days below 30°F—and allows their effects to vary by season and by Census region. The estimated coefficients are then applied to current weather data to produce real-time nowcasts of the weather effect on national payroll employment, with county- level effects aggregated nationally using employment weights. records.text: 4 May 2026 Hsueh On Oil Deutsche Bank AG/Singapore Page 3 Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, the UAE (joined in 1967) and Qatar (joined 1961, exited 2019) were considered to be OPEC 'Core' countries in the sense that they are "immediate neighbors of Saudi Arabia and have usually followed similar policies."4 In early 2008, the UAE's share of OPEC production was only 8%, yet it contributed 11% of the production cut (Figure 4). The UAE's "sacrifice" as a percentage of its own production was comparable to Saudi Arabia's (Figure 5), while non-Core countries generally made lesser sacrifices. By 2026, the UAE's share of OPEC production had risen to 12% just before the US-Iran war. While the UAE has typically produced above its quota, it has not been a remarkable standout in this regard (Figure 6), with Saudi Arabia and Kuwait also being similar or larger over-producers in recent years (2024-2025). This implies that to achieve the same impact in addressing demand shortfalls, other countries would need to sacrifice slightly larger shares of production and revenue. In 2020, the lower compliance demonstrated by OPEC+ coalition partners under the Declaration of Cooperation (shown as 'non-OPEC' in Figure 7), suggests there is more room for improvement here than within OPEC proper. Many analysts appear to be over- reading recent discrepancies between income and spending in the official estimates, which, in our view, reflect mechanical adjustments that one should always expect, as the BEA adjusts disposable income to changes in income tax policy at the beginning of each calendar year. Rather than tracking the flow of income to households from tax returns, the BEA level-adjusts estimated tax payments each January to reflect the expected average annualized rate of withholding over the coming year. Because of this, new income tax cuts will cause an abrupt jump in disposable income in January and a temporary jump in the saving rate as spending adjusts toward the new level of income. Deputy Governor Zamrazilova noted that the next policy move is more likely to be a hike, but stressed there is no urgency to act given CPI is expected to remain within the target band through the rest of 2026. This aligns with our baseline of a stable policy rate at 3.50%. She also flagged a potential acceleration in food inflation in H2 26. More detail should emerge from the updated staff forecasts due next week. In South Africa, implications from high energy prices are top of mind for the SARB: Governor Kganyago has said that the MPC would need to make a judgement call on potential second- round effects of the oil price increase, as it would be too late to act by the time they show up in the inflation aggregates. This week, the National Treasury extended the fuel levy cut for another month (May), and it plans to reinstate the levy over the two subsequent months (June-July). Adjusting for this, and pricing in some more upside from stickier-for-longer oil prices (both directly and indirectly via higher food and other prices), lifts our CPI trajectory further, with core CPI likely remaining above the 3% target in the period ahead. NYC schools' spring break moves around in timing from year to year, typically aligned with the Passover holiday. records.text: We see some risk that AI provides a more modest disinflationary impulse than our analysis suggests, for a few reasons. First, while we expect productivity gains to be sufficiently widespread to lower costs across a variety of industries, some AI-related product improvements—such as better software features—could be missed by the inflation statistics (as they likely are now). Second, the distribution of AI-enabled productivity gains is uncertain. While recent technological innovations have lowered consumer prices, the extent of the disinflationary impulse will depend on the degree to which competition forces businesses to lower prices, which remains highly uncertain. Third, the investment costs of AI are very high, and recovering those costs could keep prices high and counteract AI-driven declines in production costs. Fourth, the Fed could ease monetary policy in anticipation of the productivity benefits from AI, which could counteract the disinflationary impact of faster productivity growth. US Focus Taiwan lifers: Rewriting risks FX risk has shifted from earnings to capital for the Taiwanese life insurers, while TW ICS and IFRS 17 tighten capital constraints. We believe these changes explain increasing USD supply and USD credit allocations from Taiwan lifers. Following sector underperformance, we see value in select bonds. This is a reprint of Taiwan: Lifers: Rewriting of risks, published on April 27, 2026. We explore how FX exposures and regulatory reforms are shaping the credit trajectories of the Taiwanese life insurers. • FX exposure reduced P&L risk, but there are tail risks related to capital. Taiwan life insurers hold the highest share of overseas assets among Asian life insurance companies, with a growing portion of unhedged USD exposure. New FX accounting rules aimed to smooth the effects of currency fluctuations on earnings have also raised capital sensitivity to TWD moves, though this remains more of a tail risk. • Regulatory overhaul lifts capital needs. The transition to TW-ICS and adoption of IFRS 17 are making capital requirements more stringent and risk-sensitive for the lifers, driving structurally higher demand for capital replenishment. • Offshore USD supply to continue. The major lifers issued a total of USD3.3bn of bonds in 2024 and 2025, and we expect continued USD bond issuance as the insurers strengthen their capital buffers. • US credit remains a core allocation. Limited scalable domestic opportunities mean lifers’ portfolios are skewed

In contrast, the flows in April remain sizeable. Maybe the difference is no longer 80K, but mathematically it must be strictly greater than zero. However, the seasonal adjustment of private employment no longer estimates any difference. That may change when April 2026 is added, but we estimate it will take more than one additional year of a 5-week April to get the 4-5 week adjustment in April to adequately get back to capturing the difference in flows. The other difficult to assess question is whether and how much the flows have diminished post-Covid. The NSA changes certainly appear smaller in magnitude. The additional week probably does not add as much to the NSA change as pre-Covid. However, we attempted to evaluate a few counterfactuals, and comparing the revision patterns over time, and we estimate the 4-5 week adjustment adds ~40K jobs to the seasonally adjusted change in private employment, with a range from 30K to 80K. While most companies did not bake in the higher spot crude prices into their guidance, some offered commentary on the impacts that they are already seeing within their industry. At the industry level, we observed an elevated number of related transcript mentions within Semis, Chemicals, Metals & Mining and Machinery as many of these industries are directly impacted by the price spikes and potential shortages in raw materials. Below we highlight discussions from corporates around 3 themes: • Supply Chains: The conflict has caused significant disruption in certain chemical and petrochemical supply chains, surging freight costs, and warnings that normalization could take months or more even after a ceasefire. • Pricing Power: Most companies with oil-linked input costs moved quickly to announce price increases. Companies with pass-through contract mechanisms were better positioned, while those with fixed-price contracts faced margin compression. • Consumer Demand: As of Q1 2026, consumer demand remained broadly resilient, but companies and financial institutions widely flagged that a sustained period of high oil prices would divert some consumer spending from certain discretionary categories, particularly those with more concentration from lower income consumption. An unstable status quo: The challenge , however, is that disruption in the Middle East is entering its third month and, at least at the time of writing, there was little to suggest a resolution is imminent. The fact that Qatar Energy extended the force majeure on its LNG supplies by another month into mid -June may signal pessimism in the region about the possibility of a speedy de-escalation . The path of least resistance for oil prices is higher, should the status quo continue. After all, each day of reduced flow through the Strait of Hormuz implies a reduction in accumulated oil inventories that cannot be recouped. It is a matter of accounting that, absent a change in the supply dynamic, prices will have to be high enough to create the demand destruction that will bring the system into balance. While the UAE’s surprise exit from OPEC suggests a potential expansion in production that may help to lower prices in the medium term, we don’t expect any impact in the near term . Although the Strait remains closed and the Fujairah pipeline is at or near capacity – we expect more supply from the UAE from 2027 onwards (see UAE leaves OPEC – limited short-term impact, more supply in 2027 , dated 28 April). records.text: 1 May 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 60 Deutsche Bank AG Euroland Strategy EUR HICP market preview We expect April HICP ex-tobacco at 2.93% y/y, slightly below market fixings and Bloomberg consensus. Uncertainty seems relatively high this month, given the confluence of rising oil prices, tax cuts and the volatility of travel prices around Easter and this is reflected in a comparatively wide distribution of consensus forecasts. Looking further ahead, market pricing remains above our forecasts for 2026, with HICPxT accelerating to ~3.6-3.7% over the coming months/quarters, before falling back to ~2.2% in H2 2027. EUR HICP forwards have risen strongly recently implying some reassessment about the risk of indirect or second round effects; they have significantly outperformed USD CPI since the end of February. Given the strong increase in European natural gas prices in particular, the repricing of the near-term inflation outlook has been more pronounced in EUR. Still, several factors should work in favour of USD-EUR spread widening in 1y1y or 2y1y: downside risks to growth are likely to be more elevated in the euro area, US goods inflation momentum has been stronger going into the energy price shock and the ECB reaction has arguably been more hawkish. Against that, subdued US housing inflation is an important offset for upward pressures in other sectors. Still, on balance we would see scope for USD 2y1y outperformance. As noted in our research for months, the equity market correction began last fall with a tightening in funding markets. This is also when P/E multiples peaked for the S&P 500 and equities more broadly. The Fed noticed this stress at the time and decided to end QT earlier than planned to address it. records.text: 1 May 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 20 Deutsche Bank AG Appendix A: Definition and methodology Twin deficits and twin deficits score: Twin deficits are one of our preferred measures of fiscal policy space. In addition to the conventional twin deficit calculation, which is simply the sum of the projected Budget & Current Account deficit of each country data from the IMF's World Economic Outlook (WEO) database, we have also created a "twin deficits score”. For each year, the twin deficits score is a weighted average of the previous years' twin deficits. We assign a higher weight to this year’s Twin Deficit (t), followed by gradually lowering the weights of the past five years (t-1, t-2, …, t-5) twin deficits and finally adding some weight to the cumulative twin deficit up to year t-5. This allows us to create a synthetic twin deficit score which combines both the most recent flows and the historical stock of budget & current account deficits. Considering the fundamental difference between Norway and other G10 countries, we make adjustments to Norway's twin surpluses and NIIP when mapping with its market pricing. Net international investment positions (NIIP): NIIP is a measure of a country's reliance on foreign funding and, empirically, it is highly correlated with 10-year and 30-year government bond yields in cross-sectional regressions. Revisiting our GDP nowcasting model We formalize these signals through a new GDP nowcaster – a dynamic factor model in the spirit of Bánbura and Modugno (2014). This extracts common latent factors from a mixed- frequency indicators to generate a real-time estimate of quar- terly GDP growth. The framework begins with the assump- tion that GDP growth moves proportionately with an underlying unobserved set of latent factors (F) and an idio- syncratic error (ε): GDP = α + β'F + ε. The goal is to uncover F using observable data which – unlike GDP itself – need not be restricted to a quarterly frequency and, in our case, consists mostly of monthly indicators. Input variables are pre-selected using the Least Angle Regression (LARS) algorithm, which identifies the most informative pre- dictors while filtering out redundant ones. Rather than includ- ing ten similar indicators, it retains only the one that adds the most explanatory power. This matters: Bai and Ng (2008) show that selecting fewer but more informative predictors improves out-of-sample factor model accuracy by around 20%. Such an outcome would be in line with market expectations for the Riksbank, but slightly dovish for Norges, even if their communication remained hawkish. Central banks aside, we remain cautious on both SEK and NOK in near term, as we see energy markets pricing a best-case scenario and the FX market discounting the war’s impact on global growth. Assuming a gradual normalization around Hormuz in the coming weeks, we retain our bullish bias on SEK later this year: we count on renewed USD weakness, Germany’s fiscal push, and Sweden’s strong domestic position. In March, the US retail gasoline price from the EIA rose $1.05, but one-year ahead inflation expectations only rose 0.4 pp, less than the historical patterns would imply. In April, however, the gasoline price was more stable, up $0.13 over the month, but one-year ahead inflation expectations rose 0.9 pp, suggesting that the series was making up some ground. On net, over the two months, one-year ahead inflation expectations have risen a bit more than what the historical patterns would imply. That might suggest that consumers' inflation expectations have caught up to the run-up in gas prices, and in May, the series could remain more stable.  Upside: If inflation expectations continued to rise in May, it could signal a broader and more persistent shift in households' inflation views, especially if the increase in expectations continued to outpace the move implied by historical patterns.  Downside: If inflation expectations stabilized in May, it could suggest consumers had already largely absorbed the earlier run-up in gasoline prices. Consumers also remain concerned about the labor market in the University of Michigan survey. Economics Europe Blog Date 1 May 2026 Passthrough Playbook: Tracking the stages of energy transmission There are three stages in the passthrough or transmission of an energy shock into inflation: direct effects, indirect effects and second-round effects. At the current juncture, two months into this energy shock, the direct effects are in line with normal passthrough elasticities and there are some indications that indirect effects could be significant . Second-round effects generally take months/quarters to materialise. President Lagarde said the ECB sees no evidence of second-round effects yet . We are seeing one or two worrisome signs in our data. That said, for second-round effects to really take hold, the euro area economy will need to be more robust than we currently expect. In this Blog, we take a quick tour through what the passthrough data is showing – and what data to keep an eye on going forward. records.text: 1 May 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 39 Fixed Income Blogs The unequal effects of Fed rate and balance sheet policies? In his confirmation hearing last week, Kevin Warsh reiterated criticism of Fed balance sheet policy over the past 15 years. In doing so, he argued that, relative to policy rate adjustments, asset purchases fuel inequality by disproportionately impacting financial asset prices. Though it went unstated, a reasonable reading of the claim is that asset purchases have outsized effects on equity prices. Indeed, as shown in Figure 59, along with private business wealth, equities are the asset category that is most unequally distributed across household wealth percentiles. An important implication of this claim is that a growth-neutral shift in the mix of monetary policy tools, towards lower policy rates and a smaller Fed balance sheet, would be beneficial in reducing wealth inequality (or certainly not amplify it). This is not purely academic. Warsh has previously suggested that further shrinking the balance sheet would open a path for the Fed to cut its policy rate, and there is increasing focus, on the Committee and in markets, on steps the Fed could take to achieve a smaller balance sheet. records.text: DM economies: Forecasts and key views 319 May 2026 ▪ US: Our base case assumes a modest drag on GDP from the Middle East conflict, with a countervailing lift in 2027 as those effects fade and AI-related investments bear fruit. Unemployment is likely to edge down toward 4%, on average. All this leaves high inflation as a sticky problem for the Fed throughout 2026–27. ▪ Eurozone: The economy will prove resilient to the energy shock, in our view, delivering continued growth despite higher inflation. However, we no longer forecast a significant GDP acceleration. High energy prices are likely to curb consumption, limit productivity growth and reduce the return on German public investment. ▪ China: We expect broadly stable growth. So far this year, weak leverage demand, due to unattractive RV opportunity sets, has helped keep funding rates contained. However, improvements in returns on capital due to reduced margin costs could reignite leverage demand. Furthermore, movement in uncleared bilateral trades into FICC to capture the benefits of cross-margining could mechanically pressure SOFR higher as they become captured in the calculation. Given that widespread take-up by end-users may take a few months as dealers build out infrastructure and complete legal arrangements, the impact may not be realized until later this year. To assess this impact, we model the SOFR-RRP spread using bills outstanding (excluding Fed) alongside the difference in volume of sponsored reverse repo versus sponsored repo to approximate leverage demand. As we show below, plugging in our forecast for bill supply, current market pricing through the year embeds little risk of leverage returning and is primarily capturing the increase in collateral supply. Accordingly, we think SOFR/FF shorts for later this year make sense, though earlier passage of liquidity deregulation is a risk. records.text: Hyperscalers and neoclouds: One Big Beautiful Build- out Compute ambitions exceed the "visible" pipeline One way of tracking the data center pipeline is via hyperscalers and neoclouds themselves, as they are the point from which most of the spending emanates. Across this cohort, most companies provide some level of directional guidance about their data center goals. However, the specificity of guidance varies widely. Neoclouds tend to be more articulate with GW-level goals and timelines, while hyperscalers provide directional ambitions for scale and compute intensity. The presence of non-specific targets, such as Meta's target of "tens of gigawatts" and Amazon's and Microsoft's aims to double capacity without disclosing their current footprints, makes it difficult to quantify the aggregate target with precision. However, it is clear that ambitions from the cohort are very high. FIGURE 1. Our results imply that the timing of pass-through matters as much as the magnitude. A 10% q/q increase in fuel is insig- nificant contemporaneously but becomes statistically mean- ingful around three quarters later, lifting food inflation by roughly 0.4%pts. A 10% q/q rise in the FAO Index shows up mainly through the six-month lag, adding about 0.87%pts, while a 10% NEER appreciation materially offsets import pressures to reduce inflation by around 1.75%pts (1.3% in two quarters), broadly in line with the empirical literature. Finally, the significant lagged food inflation term confirms non-trivial inertia-so shocks that lift food inflation tend to carry into subsequent quarters, amplifying the cumulative impact even when the initial impulse is delayed. A key insight is the identification of a +10 to +20 volatility point regime in which the implied volatility risk premium remains positive but is insufficient to offset subsequent realized volatility. In this range, short gamma strategies exhibit hit rates comparable to the broader sample, but returns are negatively skewed. This unfavorable payoff asymmetry reduces the attractiveness of short gamma exposure, making the regime a practical signal to scale back or avoid such positions. Over the past five years, this regime has occurred on average 17 times per year, with an average duration of 3.5 days. Excluding short gamma exposure during these periods increases the Sharpe ratio of the TY option strategy to 0.57 (from 0.45) and that of the US option strategy to 0.72 (from 0.52). The relatively high frequency and short duration of these episodes make the signal operationally relevant for actively managed short gamma strategies. Uruguay: Agricultural tailwinds Uruguay’s macroeconomic exposure is predominantly posi- tive, though the mechanism operates through two distinct channels that have become increasingly important. First, El Niño typically brings above-average precipitation to the Río de la Plata basin during the austral spring and summer, which benefits soybean, wheat, barley, and rice yields. For an econo- my where agricultural commodities and agribusiness repre- sent roughly 70% of goods exports, this translates into a meaningful terms-of-trade improvement and current account support. Second, the electricity matrix—one of the most renewable-intensive in the world, with hydropower account- ing for approximately 55% of generation in normal years and wind contributing another 30%—benefits from higher inflows into the Río Negro and Río Uruguay reservoir systems during El Niño episodes. El Niño conditions can generate fiscal sav- ings of 0.3–0.5% of GDP through reduced thermal dispatch. The main downside risk is flooding. The 1997–98 and 2015–16 events triggered significant displacements and dam- aged infrastructure along the Uruguay River. records.text: US Economic Weekly | 01 May 2026 9 Core views Growth: to remain trendlike • The Iran conflict poses stagflationary risks as the oil shock is likely to weigh on consumer spending and business investment. But we still see several tailwinds supporting growth this year, including lagged benefits from Fed rate cuts, more supportive trade policy, ongoing AI-related investment, and favorable shutdown- related base effects. Taking these factors into consideration, we marked down our 2026 GDP forecasts. We now look for growth to come in at 2.1% on a 4Q/4Q basis and 2.2% on the annual average. Inflation: to remain stuck above the Fed’s target through 2027 • We now forecast headline PCE inflation to peak in 2Q 2026 at 4.1% and to remain above our prior forecast for the rest of this year due to higher oil prices. records.text: 2 Global Economic Weekly | 01 May 2026 Global Letter Claudio Irigoyen BofAS Antonio Gabriel BofAS Midterm incentives Two months have passed since the war started, with no clear end yet in sight. The longer the conflict continues, the closer it gets to the US midterm elections, and the more likely higher gas prices could impact the election outcome. This likely affects the calculus of the US administration around the conflict, as reflected in the US push to reach a deal and keep markets calm. However, the same factors that affect the US calculus also affect it on the Iranian side, as delaying any agreement could be punishing for the US and have a deterrent effect on potential future strikes. As a result, while our baseline scenario remains a resolution in the next few weeks, we continue to believe markets are underpricing the risks of escalation or of a more delayed resolution. Besides the war, the midterms are also likely to impact the calculus around trade policy. With Section 122 tariffs set to expire in July, the US administration is expected to announce additional tariffs under Sections 232 and 301. However, we think the decline in the effective tariff rate that we have already observed since the SCOTUS ruling on IEEPA could continue, and we see effective tariffs likely to end up in the 6-8% range. Recent ECB communication has indicated that a hike in April was highly unlikely. Having declined to 1bp priced, this has subsequently risen to 4bp priced at the time of writing. This highlights the sensitivity of pricing to newsflow, which is a key factor that might contribute to the pricing of 50bps. The commitment to not providing forward guidance, and a proven ability to surprise markets will also contribute. It is also worth highlighting that, beyond rate-hike pricing, broader financial conditions remain very well anchored, as proxied by the ECB's systemic stress indicator still being close to record-tight levels. whilst this will be viewed positively in the context of elevated uncertainty, it won't form an argument as why not to hike. However, the ECB’s approach of assessing the potential for second-round effects from the energy shock might imply that the risk of a single 50bp hike should be low. While surveys have pointed to rising inflation expectations, the BLS also points to tighter credit conditions in the face of elevated uncertainty. Such offsetting data should reduce the risk of larger hikes. In addition, the persistence of the shock is likely to be relevant in the ECB’s decision making. However, Fubon’s smaller amount of high guaranteed-rate legacy policies translates into a lower cost of liabilities than Cathay’s, resulting in a lighter negative-spread burden. (Figure 18) In fact, Fubon has a track record of a stronger investment portfolio management, delivering consistently better investment returns than peers (Figure 19). From a capital perspective, Fubon maintains the strongest capital buffer among its peers, with risk-based capital (RBC) ratio of 434% at end-2025, representing an improvement from 2024 after a volatile 2025 (Figure 14). In addition, Fubon strengthened its FX valuation reserves to the highest level among peers following the implementation of new regulatory calculation rules in 2025 (Figure 15). Nan Shan is smaller than Cathay and Fubon, and its capital position was more adversely affected by the 2025 FX shock – its RBC declined to around 270%. Nan Shan subsequently rebuilt its FX reserves after mid-2025, from TWD25bn in June 2025 to TWD68bn at year-end, but the reserve buffer remains smaller than the two market leaders’ buffers. Moving to the April reports, the Conference Board consumer confidence index sur- prised to the upside, rising to 92.8 from 92.2 in March, led by a rebound in expectations for the next six months. The survey’s gauge of current conditions ticked down just 0.3 points in April but is up 5.1 points over the past two months. Perhaps most notably, the labor market differential perked up to a four-month high of 7.5% in April, implying less risk of a larger rise in the unemployment rate (Improving labor signal lifts confidence in April, Bennett Parrish, 4/28/26). Meanwhile, today’s manufacturing surveys for April both pointed to strength in the sector; the PMI rose to 54.5 from 52.3 in March, marking its best level since May 2022, and the ISM index held at 52.7 m/m, which like the PMI is a cycle high. Lastly, echoing the positive tone from the labor market differential in the consumer confi- dence report, weekly jobless claims were very favorable, falling from 215k to 189k, which is not only the lowest reading this cycle but also the lowest since 1969. Given the recent choppiness in the employment data, it is possible we could still see a temporarily soft nonfarm payroll number in April, but the high frequency signals from claims and ADP point to healthy underlying conditions (A very good jobless claims report , Abiel Reinhart, 4/30/26). The Week in Review: the end of the Powell era Chair Powell said goodbye in a way Wednesday, despite announcing he would stay on the Board of Governors and thus the FOMC, pledging to keep a low profile and be deferential to the incoming Chair, Kevin Warsh. At the meeting, a surprising number of dissents to the FOMC statement punctuated a week of higher oil prices and stronger AI/ tech capex. records.text: m premia. Calibrating the shocks and a thought experiment The figure above showed the impact of one-standard-deviation policy shocks. For a cleaner comparison – one that puts the tools on more equal footing – and to speak directly to the question of substitution, we next re-scale the shocks so that each produces a similar easing in financial conditions and thus the growth outlook. To do so, we use the Fed staff’s Financial Conditions Impulse on Growth index (FCI-G), which aggregates changes in a set of financial variables – the fed funds rate, 10y UST yield, 30y fixed mortgage rate, BBB corporate bond yield, Dow Jones total stock market index, Zillow house price index, and nominal broad dollar index – using weights implied by FRB/US and other Fed models. The financial variables are weighted using impulse response coefficients that quantify the effects of unanticipated changes in each on real GDP growth over the subsequent year. We combine the FCI-G weights with Swanson’s asset response estimates to scale each policy shock so that it delivers 10bps easing in FCI -G. That is, we preserve the pattern of cross -asset moves from Swanson, and scale the rate, FG and QE shocks so that each would be expected to raise GDP growth by 0.1ppt. Naturally, these topics are interrelated. The president’s party tends to lose seats in the House, Senate is blurrier Historically, the president’s party tends to lose seats in the House in midterm elections (Exhibit 1). In this context, it is unsurprising that predictive markets see very large odds of a Democratic controlled House of Representatives after the elections (Exhibit 2). While this comes with several inputs, the clearest one to us is the oil chart (Figure 6). We would make 2 points. Firstly, with Scenario C peaking at $130 oil, we are not far from this in recent spot price terms. Secondly, while the key determinant of Scenario C is persistence, with the first condition close to being met already, every passing week is likely to push more MPC members into the Huw Pill camp of hawkish dissent. We have expressed increasing concerns of further delays in US-Iran negotiations as especially risky for fixed income, and our bias has turned more neutral on global rates, cutting rates risk in both our Asset Allocation (24 April) and GMS Hedge Fund portfolios (April 29). records.text: bs, on a non seasonally adjusted basis. This difference was not corrected for most of the history of the Current Employment Statistics program, until an adjustment was introduced in the 1990s. The adjustment for this was also not part of the usual X- 11, X-12, and now X-13 seasonal adjustment routines. The correction was made separately, and called the 4-5 week adjustment. The adjustment was originally designed by the labor economists on the staff of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, to better interpret the monthly changes in employment, was eventually adopted by the Bureau of Labor Statistics into its regular seasonal adjustment of the employment data. Today the BLS uses what they call "REGARIMA (regression with autocorrelated errors)" which uses time series models that fundamentally reduce to 11 indicator variables. Note there are not 12 because February has 28 days and thus the week including March 12 is always four weeks from February 12th (as an aside, it doesn't happen often but recall that a leap year and a late reference week in February has been shown to add to the seasonally adjusted increase in private employment in March.) The 11 coefficients estimated by the REGARIMA models attempt to capture the difference in NSA changes attributable to 4 versus 5 weeks in between the survey reference points. The coefficients are used to adjust payroll employment to remove the impact. Then the pre-treated series are seasonally adjusted using X-13ARIMA-SEATS.

records.text: US Rates Weekly 01 May 2026 Citi Research 4 Overview: US Rates Oil Strategy Chair Powell and NFP next week This week Chair Powell announced he would stay on as a Fed Governor after Kevin Warsh takes the Chair. Presumably, Powell will remain until the Fed’s Inspector General (IG) investigation is “well and truly over. ” We think there is a strong likelihood that he remains through the rest of his term, which expires in January 2028. Overall, this does not change the calculus for our rates forecasts. Chair Powell has leaned dovish, especially with respect to any weakness in the labor market, and our forecast expects some form of labor weakness ahead. This would be via seasonally weak data following the recent patterns around the summer months or through a growth shock following the short-term inflation shock. records.text: AI and (Measured) Inflation: Up Then Down We expect artificial intelligence to deliver large productivity gains over the next several years, boosting the economy’s potential growth rate and putting downward pressure on production costs. So far, however, AI is boosting US inflation. Three Input Cost Pressures from AI Spending We see three key channels through which AI is boosting inflation. First, strong demand for AI infrastructure has raised the prices of some key electronics inputs, including digital memory and batteries (Exhibit 1). Initially, AI-related demand caused sharp increases in the prices of a few specialized inputs like cutting-edge semiconductors. More recently, these cost pressures have broadened into a wider set of inputs that are key to electronics manufacturing, and they have boosted the prices of consumer electronics accessories like flash drives and other memory-related items. Second, AI-related spending has likely put some upward pressure on software prices over the last couple of years. For example, Microsoft raised the price of M365 consumer subscriptions for the first time ever in early 2025, and it is now including Copilot in all consumer M365 subscriptions (business subscriptions still feature it as a separate add-on). Others, like Adobe, have also raised prices and introduced new AI features into their software. records.text: The BoE meeting delivered a balanced message, with a nuanced set of analyses hinting at challenging trade-offs ahead. Our read of the meeting (see here) was that the MPC wants to maintain its tightening bias, albeit delivery of any hikes depends on the scale of upside risks to inflation. In its scenarios A and B, we would see the BoE on hold this year - albeit adopting an easing bias later in the year in scenario A and maintaining the tightening one in scenario B. In scenario C, which assumes a further rise in commodity prices - and one that persists for months - we think the BoE would hike 3 times. For now, our base case remains a hold in the near-term and a prolonged hold over our forecast horizon. Next week, with little market moving data, the focus will be on local elections on Thursday. Polling suggests the governing Labour Party could lose between 1500 to 2000 seats in England (see here), while also potentially coming in third in terms of the vote share in national parliament elections in Wales and Scotland. The results will come in overnight and during the day on Friday. The covering analysts didn't revise their price targets upwards in response to this price surge, which biases the consensus price target downward as of end of February (Figure 5). To address this timing mismatch, we calculate the implied return for each price target as the ratio of the price target to the previous-day stock price. We then aggregate these individual price target-implied returns at the stock level. Figure 6 shows that the signs of PTIRs are more aligned with their corresponding ratings: Buy ratings are generally associated with positive PTIRs, while Hold and Sell ratings are associated with negative PTIRs. Morgan Guess who’s back again Prior to the start of the Middle East conflict, vol-rate directionality had pretty much disap- peared. With yields range-bound and implieds headed lower for weeks due to carry-seeking gamma selling strategies, vol-rate directionality was near or below zero for most of 2025 and the early part of this year. However, the past two months of the Iran conflict resulted in vol-rate directionality turning significantly positive, reaching the highest levels since 2022, the start of a hiking cycle (Figure 9). While the correlation has declined some- what since reaching its peak in late March, it remains positive and elevated with respect to the past few years. Even more interesting is that the past few risk-off moves (we include the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the UK LDI crisis in 2022, the regional bank crisis in 2023, and “Liberation Day” in 2025) all exhibited the opposite dynamic: vol-rate correlations turned sharply negative following these events as a spike in implieds was met with a decline in yields (Figure 10). Paraguay: Hydro superpower The country derives virtually 100% of its domestic electricity from hydropower—primarily through its share of the Itaipú (binational with Brazil) and Yacyretá (binational with Argen- tina) mega-dams—and exports the majority of Itaipú’s output to Brazil. El Niño-associated precipitation in the Paraná River basin has historically boosted hydroelectric generation and royalty revenues, which constitute a material fiscal resource (approximately 1–1.5% of GDP). The agricultural channel is also strongly positive. The world’s fourth-largest soybean exporter, its Chaco and eastern regions benefit from El Niño precipitation patterns that alleviate the chronic drought risk associated with La Niña episodes. However, these benefits are not unconditional. Excessive rainfall can trigger flooding along the Paraguay and Paraná rivers, disrupt river-based export logistics (the bulk of soy exits via barge), and damage rural infrastructure. Bolivia: Main risk is food prices El Niño in Bolivia can generate severe economic and envi- ronmental impacts, typically through droughts in the high- lands and valleys and excessive rainfall and flooding in the eastern region. From a macro perspective, the transmission operates through three main channels. We estimate that the aggregate capacity of these projects is 40GW+, though only around 30GW of this has been disclosed/confirmed. Still, our tracking implies a large gap versus the capacity targets suggested by the hyperscalers. META is the clearest example of this; we see about 8GW of "visible" capacity in the pipeline, which, although large, pales in comparison to Mark Zuckerberg's goal of "tens of GWs" of capacity by the end of the decade. The presence of a gap is not surprising for a number of reasons. "Rented" capacity by hyperscalers is also likely contributing to the gap. As compute needs continue to outpace asset completions, these companies are turning to neoclouds (ie, Oracle, CoreWeave) to lease additional capacity from data centers, which leads to an element of double counting, as capacity included in the target for one participant is actually hosted by another. However, the biggest contributor to the gap is the fact that demand growth is outstripping the practical pace at which projects can be launched. Although we expect project announcements to roll in steadily, the gap between the pipeline and goals is likely to persist. records.text: 4 Bloomberg, Thailand Mulls Public Debt Ceiling Hike in Face of Energy Shock, 16 April 2026 We have previously noted fuel shortages in Thailand and Philippines, and gas shortages in India. In India, the prioritisation of LPG for households by the government meant gas production for industries such as petrochemicals, fertilisers, and ceramics was curtailed in March, leading to lower output and higher input costs in these sectors. The impact on industrial output is uneven though, and peak rationing has likely passed, with some normalcy creeping in from mid-April. Administered energy prices imply consumers are mostly protected from the inflation pass-through, but at the cost of growing fiscal strains if supply risks persist (see, India: Energy security's bill, 30 April 2026). Amidst persistent uncertainties surrounding the US-Iran conflict, we believe that growth considerations will likely remain a constraint for central banks in the region in terms of their overall hawkishness. records.text: US Economics Weekly1 May 2026 ab 29 US Economics Weekly UBS Research April employment report: hawkish We expect nonfarm payroll employment expanded 100K in April, with two sided risks from weather and significant support from seasonal adjustment, in particular the pandemic's influence on the pretreatment intended to account for additional distance between some monthly survey periods. The recent volatility poses risks too: we have a view on the underlying trend but the recent data has been sufficiently volatile to undermine the confidence in any such assessment. We expect private employment expanded 95K and government 5K, the latter benefitting from a waning of the 2025 efforts to trim the federal workforce. We expect cumulative downward revisions to prior months. We expect average hourly earnings climbed 0.27% in April, which absent revision would push the year-over-year change back up from 3.52% to 3.77%. We expect average weekly hours remained unchanged at 34.2 hours, though on an unrounded basis we would expect the workweek lengthened in April. We expect the unemployment rate held steady at 4.3%, little changed within the rounding, at 4.27%, representing more risk of a 4.2% than a 4.4%. We expect the labor force participation rate remains at 61.9%, at least when rounded. More unwinding of last month's 16.5 bp drop in LFPR poses an upside risk to the unemployment rate projection, given how much of the decline in the unemployment rate could be accounted for by that decline.

records.text: oming weeks. The revised trajectory of WTI has been marked up similarly, with the price peaking at $105/b in Q2 and averaging $93/b for the year. While the year average has moved up by $10 (WTI) for 2026, the persistence is higher in the current scenario relative to our prior baseline. Effects on inflation, activity and labor markets We expect the higher and more prolonged oil price trajectory to boost both headline and core PCE inflation measures, and to weigh somewhat on growth. As before, inflationary effects are mostly felt directly through energy prices, with headline PCE price inflation at 3.8% Q4/Q4 in 2026, 0.7pp faster than our prior projection. But with energy prices elevated for much longer, we now expect more noticeable spillovers to other consumer prices, with core PCE price inflation at 3.1% Q4/Q4 in 2026, 0.3pp faster than before. Although declining energy prices lead to rapid disinflation in headline inflation in 2027, core inflation remains somewhat above the target at 2.3% Q4/Q4. On the activity front, we expect higher energy prices to sap purchasing power from consumers, and we have marked down the trajectory of PCE accordingly. However, with the prolonged shock to energy prices boosting domestic energy exploration incentives, and AI-related investment surpassing our expectations in Q1, we expect a partial offset from somewhat stronger increases in business fixed investment (most notably from nonresidential structures). records.text: Deutsche Bank. Research Negotiations for a ceasefire in Ukraine will likely remain stalled during May. While there is ongoing diplomatic activity, no new rounds of ceasefire talks are publicly scheduled for May or June. Ukrainian President Zelenskyy has stated that the US wants Russia and Ukraine to reach a peace agreement by June. However, the specifics of how this would manifest in terms of scheduled meetings are unclear. While a ceasefire over the coming months is far from guaranteed, even credible steps toward a deal would have implications for markets. These could include a possible easing of some sanctions on Russia, the potential for increased Ukrainian agriculture exports, and for enabling reconstruction – with implications for investments in minerals, gas infrastructure, technology, city reconstruction, data centres and artificial intelligence. The UN-sponsored conference in New York is taking place against the backdrop of rising geopolitical tensions and the prospect of a new nuclear arms race. The expiry of the New STARTTreaty on 5 February marked the end of the last binding nuclear arms control agreement between the US and Russia. Both countries retain the world’s largest nuclear warhead inventories (see chart). While these have shrunk slightly in recent years, the unravelling of the New START deal could reignite nuclear competition. records.text: US Outlook Holding up, not calming down This week's FOMC signaled an extended hold, with the committee likely awaiting clear signs of disinflation before thinking about cuts. For now, activity measures point to resilience amid intensifying cost pressures, with markets awaiting signals from the April employment report. • Although the advance Q1 GDP growth estimate of 2.0% q/q saar was a touch softer than forecasts, the FOMC will likely see the 2.5% q/q saar increase in PDFP as an indication of solid underlying demand. Although slower consumer spending weighed on growth, strengthened AI-related capex more than picked up the slack. • With little sign that disruptions to key supply arteries in the Middle East will be resolved anytime soon, stagflationary risks are intensifying. Although a prolonged shock to energy prices would weigh considerably on consumers, we think that worries about March’s low saving rate are overblown. • The FOMC retained an easing bias in its latest statement, which triggered three hawkish dissents, with Powell stressing in his final post-FOMC press conference that this outcome was a close call. His language in the presser struck us as a hawkish hold, stressing that clear signs of disinflation will be needed before the FOMC even thinks about cutting rates. Barring a significant escalation in the Iran war, the summit between presidents Xi and Trump on 14-15 May will likely go ahead as planned – and deliver a package of tactical agreements. The meeting will likely coalesce around limited, but potentially more achievable, deliverables. These could include Chinese commitments to purchase up to 500 Boeing jets, US soybeans and energy, as well as Chinese requests for the US to ease export controls, including on chips and aircraft engine parts. Both sides could also agree to set up a ‘Board of Trade’ to increase bilateral trade in non-sensitive areas. Progress on a proposed ‘Board of Investment’ could be more limited owing to mutual national security concerns linked to investment, although the summit could still deliver a small number of investment deals. Despite recent signs of friction over Iran, both sides appear to be prioritizing bilateral stability. The threshold for another summit deferral is likely high. Even with the March deterioration, the 1Q26 trade surplus tracks around 0.6%pts of GDP higher in comparison to 1Q25. Exports rose 0.7% 3m/3m, led by gains in precious metals and mineral products. We suspect this reflects a recovery in PGM, gold and chrome production vol- umes. On the import side, the 5.9%m/m pullback in February set up for a payback in March, with the 12.1% rebound driven by firmer chemical products and vehicle imports. Mineral prod- ucts (crude oil and petroleum) were only marginally higher on the month (0.8%m/m), but import volumes remain materially weaker than a year ago (-14.8%oya). We anticipate momen- tum in the trade surplus to moderate in coming months, given disruptions to global trade activity, heightened uncertainty and a deterioration in terms-of-trade. Overall, data through March indicate a wider trade surplus of around 5.1% of GDP for 1Q26 (from 3.5%), which we think is sufficient to move the current account out of a deficit and into a surplus of around 1.6% of GDP. -30 -20 -10 0 10 20 30 40 -30 -20 -10

Political crisis in Romania weighs on macro and rating outlook PSD and AUR have agreed to submit a vote of no confidence11 . Together they control 219 MPs, slightly short of the 233 votes required for passage. However, we think they are likely to secure support from other ultra-nationalist parties and/or non-affiliated MPs12 , pushing the total comfortably above the threshold. The no-confidence motion is widely expected to be brought to Parliament early next week (possibly on Tuesday) and is more likely to pass13 (ie, exceed 233 votes). If so, PM Bolojan would continue as interim prime minister during the subsequent government-formation process. While PSD is tactically cooperating with AUR on the no- confidence vote, it has explicitly ruled out any formal cooperation with anti-EU parties, including AUR14 and other ultra-nationalist groups. In this situation, following consultations with parliamentary parties, the president will appoint a prime minister designate to attempt to form a new government. If two consecutive attempts to secure parliamentary confidence fail, the president may dissolve Parliament and call early elections. Realized volatility is computed using a 3-month lookback on 10y and 30y swap rates and compared to 1-month implied volatility. The horizon mismatch is intentional: the longer window stabilizes realized volatility estimates, while 1-month implied volatility aligns with the tenor at which short gamma is typically expressed. Prior QIS analysis finds that the 1-week implied–realized volatility spread has predictive power for subsequent short-gamma strategy returns across asset classes. We observe a similar relationship in OTC rates markets. Proxying Gamma Exposure via Systematic Short-Dated Option Strategies In practice, isolating pure gamma exposure is difficult, as short-dated option strategies embed both theta and vega exposure. To approximate gamma exposure, we use a tradable QIS strategy that systematically sells short-dated options and delta-hedges the position. For the 10y tail, we track a strategy that sells a strip of weekly TY options, delta-hedged daily and held to expiry. Since 2019, the TY short-volatility strategy has generated positive returns on 62% of trading days, with an annualized Sharpe ratio of 0.45. For the 30y tail, the analogous strategy using US futures options delivers an annualized Sharpe ratio of 0.52 ( Exhibit 3 ).
