records.text: Credit DNA of major issuers Cathay Life Market leadership and strong distribution. Cathay Life is the largest life insurer in Taiwan, with a well-established franchise and about a 20% market share in terms of total premiums. Total premiums in 2025 increased by 6.5%, strongest among the four issuers. It has a very strong distribution network, including the industry’s largest tied-agency sales force (which accounted for about 75% of the insurer's first-year premium equivalent (FYPE) in2025) and a supportive bancassurance arm via Cathay United Bank. Improving earnings quality and product mix. Cathay Life’s strategic focus on higher-margin, protection-oriented, and longer-term products has improved its earnings quality and new business margins. The insurer has been shifting away from low-margin, shorter-duration savings products, emphasizing protection (health and accident) and USD-denominated policies, which enhance profitability and reduce reliance on investment spread income. This improved product mix has helped stabilize the insurer’s earnings and value of new business. Negative-spread risk due to legacy policies with high guaranteed rates. Cathay Life’s average investment yield after hedging was 3.94% in 2025, marginally surpassing its cost of liabilities of 3.84%, after three years of negative spread between 2022 and 2024 (Figure 24). Real exports declined substantially in January and rebounded partly, but not completely in February. In February, real imports also rose substantially. While we would expect some normalization in imports in March, there is still likely to be a large mechanical drag on GDP in Q1. Of course, stronger imports would also suggest stronger investment, consumption, or inventory growth in Q1. Changes to some tariff rates following the Supreme Court ruling in late February could modestly boost demand for some Canadian goods, but most of the more meaningful tariffs on Canadian exports to the US were not affected by the Court ruling. We acknowledge that our eurozone growth forecasts have been revised lower as a result of the energy price shock, which, all else equal, does not bode well for the EUR. At the same time, we expect US growth to remain firm and corporate earnings strong. However, we think an end to the Middle East conflict would likely spark a shift in flow dynamics to a gradual but sustained diversification away from the USD by global investors. Therefore, we expect firmer economic growth in the US to end up slowing the pace of USD depreciation rather than driving USD strength. ▪ JPY to stay weak: We continue to expect the JPY to remain weak, with the Bank of Japan staying firmly behind the curve despite its ongoing tightening cycle. We keep our forecast for USDJPY to rise to 160 by end-2026. ▪ GBP to fall behind: We see the GBP lagging the wider USD-weakening move, as the energy price shock drags on already-lacklustre UK growth – and while sustained political uncertainty adds tail risk of fiscal imprudence. We think one reason the 20y bond may have been struggling in the past year could be the dearth of demand from foreign official investors. In general, foreign official demand for bonds (any paper longer than 10y) has been relatively paltry over the past few years, with very little increase in 20y allocation. That had been the case in 2021 through 2023 (Figure 12). Still, foreign private investors continued to buy the 20y sector, increasing from $286bn in June 2024 to $344bn in June 2025 (Figure 13). Which route for additional UAE crude oil exports? The UAE announcement raises uncertainty about the export route for additional crude oil exports against the backdrop of Iranian influence over the Hormuz Strait. Some UAE production increases could be directed through the Hormuz Strait post-war or occur once the UAE has been able to increase on an expedited basis its transport/loading capacity of the Habshan-Fujairah pipeline bypassing the Hormuz Strait. This decision will be a significant policy choice, in our view. records.text: ct With the increased volume of SASB deals, we have noticed the appraisal values used to calculate deal metrics more often including a clause which mentions certain premiums which are factored into them. We looked into the prevalence of these appraisal value premi- ums from 2023 and found they have generally increased since then. 75% of single borrower deals in 2026 contained appraisal value premiums, up from 59% in 2023. For single asset deals, 46% contained appraisal value premiums in 2026, up from 12% in 2023 (Figure 13A p p r a i s a l v a l u e p r e m i u m s i n S A S B d e a l s h a v e b e c o m e m o r e c o m m o n p l a c e s i n c e 2 0 2 3 ). Among the different types of appraisal value premiums, the most common are portfolio premiums in single borrower deals. Portfolio premiums reflect the added value assigned to a group of properties when sold together as a portfolio rather than individually. Single asset deals also contain appraisal value premiums, albeit at a smaller scale. The largest category for single asset deals in 2026 is “reserve / escrow adjustment”, which adjusts appraised val- ues upward by assuming that reserves for outstanding tenant improvements, leasing costs, and free rent obligations will be fully funded at loan origination. Interestingly, across SASB in 2025 and 2026, we have seen appraised values boosted by personal and intangible proper- ty, something that was not present in 2023 and 2024. records.text: Agency MBS Weekly 01 May 2026 Citi Research 2 Agency MBS navigated a challenging macro environment this week, defined by elevated rate uncertainty, a hawkish-leaning Fed hold, and sticky inflation data. Despite these headwinds, the sector demonstrated relative resilience — supported by constructive technicals, lower net supply, and healthy demand (Figure 1). Our stance remains neutral, though we note that valuations remain at the tighter range of our fair value range. The Federal Reserve held the policy rate unchanged at 3.50%–3.75%, but the tone of the accompanying statement leaned decidedly uncomfortable for rate bulls. Inflation was characterized as elevated, with global energy prices cited as a contributing factor, while Middle East developments were explicitly flagged as a source of "unusually high uncertainty. " The vote split was notably fractious — one dissenter favored a cut, while three officials opposed retaining any easing bias in the statement. The net effect is a wide distribution of rate outcomes, with the market pricing in ~10bp fewer cuts relative to the prior week (Figure 4). The 10-year Treasury yield rose from 4.31% on April 24 to a weekly high of 4.43% on April 29, before partially retracing to ~4.38% (Figure 2). Rate volatility — both vega and gamma — surged back to early April levels, though remained below the peaks observed in March (Figure 3). Figure 1. Closed for longer: Rethinking the Strait narrative From de-escalation to entrenchment Markets' narrative on the Iran war has fundamentally changed: expectations that the US administration would ultimately de-escalate in light of political considerations ahead of the midterm elections and the desire to lower US gasoline prices have given way to the acceptance that the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen anytime soon. US President Donald Trump's decision to enforce a blockade of the strait and Iranian ports has seemingly changed the US strategy from trying to quickly force Iran to the negotiating table through the threat of overwhelming military force toward an approach aimed at cutting off its key trade and energy lifelines. The latter may be 'somewhat more effective' , as Trump told Axios1 , but it could take much more time. Iran's economy is reportedly suffering shortages and very high inflation, but how long it can endure this depends on its pain threshold, which is not known ex-ante. The ener- gy crisis caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has overshadowed these efforts. They are, however, ongoing. Here we provide an update on recent progress and likely tim- escales. Overall, quick fixes are unlikely, but the ambition and urgency remain high, and gradual steps can cumulate. Energy: AccelerateEU and changes to ETS The energy crisis was already discussed at the European Council on 19 March and has now led to a communication by the European Commission (EC), called AccelerateEU. The “accelerate” refers to accelerated action towards an Energy Union that focuses on affordable energy and on energy secu- rity. The main mechanism is the green transition, which requires not only an expansion of renewables but also greater electrification so that more energy demand can be moved away from fossil fuels and imported energy. Nuclear power is also given a role as a lower carbon energy source. A few aspects of this stand out. • No silver bullet to the current energy crisis. records.text: Higher oil prices and international spillovers via imports point to higher US inflation: n Our model of domestic commodity price passthrough to consumer prices o implies a 0.35pp boost to core PCE and a 1.25pp boost to headline PCE inflation this year. But many countries are facing larger energy cost shocks than the US that will o spill over to US consumer prices via import prices. The impact should be modest in our baseline energy price scenario but § more serious in a more adverse scenario where global supply chain disruptions and shortages raise prices. The largest disruption so far is to air freight. Other key risks include diesel o shortages in Asia, fertilizer supply gaps in Europe and the Southern Hemisphere, and stress in petroleum-derived chemicals. Incorporating our new oil price path and larger foreign spillovers, we now o forecast 2.6% year-over-year core PCE inflation in December 2026 and 3.4% headline, with risks tilted higher. Indeed, this was a factor this week behind another hawkish repricing taking cumulative June pricing above 25bp. In our preview, we highlighted that there are few strong arguments in favour of a 50bp move at this stage. Although this appears asymmetric, the risk a continued rise in oil prices drags pricing further. Communications will clearly be the focus of tomorrow's meeting, gi ven policy is expected to remain on hold. Assuming the primary objective will be retaining full optionality, noting that this is not a repeat of 2022, or that there was time to assess the impact could help push back against 50s or back to back hikes being priced. Agreement would still require subsequent legislative steps, including at the country level. As before, the omnibuses and a number of other proposals (e.g. 28th regime, posting workers, European business wallet) are aimed at making the Single Market work better and cut- ting red tape. The motivation to reduce administrative and reporting requirements is large, but will need to be replicated at the national level, where the gold-plating of EU rules can often add to the fragmentation of the Single Market. This will take time to become effective. The 28th regime is a case in point as the proposal mainly focuses on establishing an “EU Inc.” through simplified digital processes. However, a start-up or existing company opting into this arrangement would still have to navigate 27 legal systems in terms of labour laws, product laws, etc. Hence, it is an important first step rather than an immediate gamechanger. On energy, the One Europe, One Market initiative is essen- tially part of AccelerateEU and the ETS review. It should also be viewed largely as a long-term project (e.g. in terms of elec- trification), rather than a very significant near-term change. Increased investment intentions were already a feature of the 2025 Budget, with some new measures also focusing on increased jobs training programs. This would be in line with the BoC’s latest estimate for 1.5% growth in both Q1 and Q2 this year. records.text: Japan Outlook BoJ's hawkish shift, JPY's ongoing weakness BoJ sounded more concerned about inflation upside than growth downside, and more hawkish in its guidance. Neutral PB member dissent was also a surprise. Yet JPY weakness has continued and spurred intervention. We stick to our June call, subject to the Middle East backdrop. The BoJ wrapped up its 27-28 April monetary policy meeting (MPM) with decision to keep policy rates unchanged at 0.75%, as expected. Three Policy Board members – Takata, Tamura, and Nakagawa – cast dissenting votes, arguing for a rate hike on concerns about upwardly skewed price risk. This was unusual. Indeed, the last time three dissenting votes were cast at a policy meeting was in January 2016, when the BoJ introduced its negative interest rate policy (NIRP). As such, this also marked the first such split under Governor Ueda's leadership since April 2024. Also, while Takata and Tamura were known hawks, Nakagawa had hitherto been viewed as neutral and closer to the governor and his deputies, suggesting the decision may have come under greater internal tension than implied by the 6-3 vote. Nakagawa’s term runs through end- June, and she will participate in the June meeting as well, so from here the outcome will arguably depend on the resolve of the governor and his two deputies. The transmission of stress from private credit to banks also appears limited. Banks do provide funding to private credit vehicles, but the exposure is comparatively small and low risk. Finally, the EL Niño’s strength outlook (April 9, 2026) assigns approximately equal probability (~25%) to moderate, strong, and very strong El Niño by November-January, with ENSO-neutral at ~10% (Table 2). Here is the key policy-rele- vant statistic: the combined probability of a strong-or-worse event (Niño-3.4 ≥ +1.0°C sustained) is approximately 50%. For Latin American risk management purposes, the planning horizon should treat strong El Niño as the central risk scenar- io rather than the tail. A super El Niño (Niño-3.4 ≥ +2.0°C)— comparable to 1997–98 or 2015–16—carries a probability below 5% but could represent a material shock to Andean economies. But an important caveat applies. These projections extend through the boreal spring predict- ability barrier—a well-documented period (typically March– May) during which ENSO forecast skill drops significantly. Even model ensembles with strong agreement at long lead times have historically exhibited large errors when forecasts are initialized during this time of year. records.text: 1 May 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 70 Deutsche Bank AG The ever-evolving relationship between EGB spreads & credit In our latest EGBs Relative Value Corner publication we’ve updated all our regular EGB valuation frameworks. A frequently used valuation tool for EGBs is to compare against iTraxx Main index. In last year’s detailed report EGB spreads: A shifting relationship vs credit & potential macro/market drivers we analysed the reasons behind EGB spreads’ outperformance vs credit and the subsequent weaker correlation between the two. Since the beginning of the Iran conflict though, EGB spreads have been underperforming vs credit and their correlation has become stronger (88% since March versus 67% in 2025). The jump in correlation is anticipated when an external shock becomes the main driver of risky assets, instead of idiosyncratic drivers in “ordinary” times. The relative EGBs’ underperformance can be attributed to a few factors. First, prior valuations at the beginning of the Iran conflict. EGB spreads have been outperforming vs credit since late 2024, and at the end of February they were looking quite rich, aided by their resilience to the latest AI-driven risk-off. Second, the vulnerability of Eurozone economies to energy and the impact of higher yields. The US is facing diminishing returns and increasing domestic and international pressure as the economic consequences of the crisis grow, which will likely push the administration towards a settlement. Iran is expected to emerge with enhanced influence, while Gulf states will likely re-evaluate their security posture and further diversify their international relationships beyond the United States. The median stock beating consensus EPS estimates has outperformed the S&P 500 on the day after reporting by just 20 bp, one of the slimmest magnitudes on record. As we discussed in our earnings season preview, the backdrop of macroeconomic uncertainty and elevated stock volatility creates a challenging backdrop for stock pickers attempting to generate alpha around earnings releases. Q1 2026 S&P 500 EPS is on pace for the strongest growth rate in five years even after adjusting for some one-time distortions. Combining realized results and consensus estimates, S&P 500 year/year EPS growth is tracking at 25%, more than twice the consensus estimate of 12% coming into the season. Much of this strength is attributable to the mega-cap technology stocks, some of whose earnings have been boosted by the appreciation of equity stakes in private companies (Exhibit 16). However, even excluding those figures, S&P 500 EPS growth would be on pace to register 16% in Q1, the strongest quarterly growth rate since 2021. Earnings growth for the median S&P 500 stock is tracking at 11%, compared with a consensus estimate of 8% ahead of the season. Out of the three main G10 central banks (Fed, ECB, BoE), the ECB is the only one so far to have seriously taken into consideration hiking rates in response to the energy supply shock. Of course, the key difference is that pre-conflict, the Fed and BoE were mid-way through a slow, data-dependent cutting cycle, while the ECB was already at neutral with their tone already shifting more hawkish (though no hikes were expected in 2026). While the bias of most G10 central banks so far has been to treat the shock as temporary, the ECB is worried that inflation expectations become once again un-anchored. In particular, as our economists note, the ECB’s President mentioned in the March meeting that inflation expectations “have a lot do to with the memory that people (…) have of inflation” and that economic agents’ reaction function to a price shock will be informed by fresh memories of a high level of inflation. In the latest April meeting, the President indicated explicitly that “directionally” the Governing Council knows where it is going (European Economics - ECB: Forward Hike(s)). Our economists therefore expect two rate hikes by the ECB in June and July, conditional though on a protracted war and a higher for longer oil regime. For rates, while a hike will likely cause more upside pressure on the front-end, it is important to remember that PC1 remains oil and the war. We use Barclays Equity Factor Scores as proxies for stock characteristics. Specifically, stocks are first sorted into quartiles based on equity factor scores. Within each equity factor score quartile, stocks are then further sorted into market-cap-weighted quintile portfolios based on PTIR. Figure 18 and Figure 19 present the excess returns over sector peers and the Fama-French six- factor alpha of the long-short (top-bottom quintile) PTIR portfolio across equity factor quartiles, respectively. We summarise key findings as follows. 1. Although the performance of the long-short portfolio strategy is stronger for smaller stocks (top size group), it also delivers solid performance for the largest stocks in the Russell 3000. 2. Performance is stronger for stocks with extreme value factor scores, both on the cheap and expensive ends. 3. Performance is stronger for stocks with faster growth, higher quality, higher yield, lower past return

We don’t think so, as both contemporary observers and historians would likely see this as a sign of a failed chairmanship. Simi- larly, while he has advocated for more dissent, we suspect that after he becomes chair, Warsh will begin to see the case for collegiality. A better reception on the balance sheet In his testimony, Warsh indicated he preferred to use interest rates over the balance sheet to steer the macroeconomy. Here he will find little debate from the rest of the FOMC, though he may want to hone his reasoning. Warsh said, “My view is the interest rate tool gets in the cracks. It's fairer. The balance sheet tool disproportionately helps those with financial assets.” The “cracks” reference seemed to be a misquotation of former Governor Jeremy Stein, who said that rate policy gets into the cracks of the financial system in places that reg- ulatory tools miss. Moreover, most Fed officials see balance sheet policy as just interest rate policy by other means when the short rate is constrained by being close to zero. Overall, quick fixes are unlikely, but the ambition and urgency remain high, and gradual steps can cumulate. Energy: AccelerateEU and changes to ETS The energy crisis was already discussed at the European Council on 19 March and has now led to a communication by the European Commission (EC), called AccelerateEU. The “accelerate” refers to accelerated action towards an Energy Union that focuses on affordable energy and on energy secu- rity. The main mechanism is the green transition, which requires not only an expansion of renewables but also greater electrification so that more energy demand can be moved away from fossil fuels and imported energy. This historic low underscores the region's overall resilience in the face of heightened geopolitical and economic uncertainty. That said, the decline in the unemployment rate masks soft underlying labour demand. The PMI employment index continues to point to positive, albeit modest, employment growth of 0.5%ar in the private sector in April. We are currently track- ing employment growth of 0.4%ar in Q1, based on available country-level data — a step down from 0.8%ar in Q4. It is also worth noting that the February unemployment rate was revised upward, and while April’s headline Euro area figure was additionally flattered by a withdrawal of workers from Italy's labour market. records.text: 1 May 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 44 Deutsche Bank AG Caveats We find the approach adopted here to be a useful way to gauge the relative impact of rate and QE shocks on equities and, by extension, inequality. That said, there we recognize several limitations to what we’ve done. First, it could be that the financial conditions-channel does not fully capture the transmission of these policies to the real economy. For example, there could be money supply effects that operate independent of asset price changes, and our calibration to FCI-G necessarily omits any impact on house prices. That said, incorporating these would likely widen the disparity between the effects of balance sheet and rate shocks on equity prices. This is because these additional channels are likely to be more impactful for balance sheet policy, and accounting for them would likely reduce, on relative basis, the size of the QT shock needed to deliver a 0.1ppt growth impulse, bringing down the impact on equities. Second, the estimates of asset price reactions that we use could be biased, due to state-dependent effects (e.g., QE has bigger impact when markets are stressed) or because they are based on policy shocks only through 2019. Third, in the substitution thought-experiment, we implicitly assume a QT and QE shocks are symmetric, with effects of the same magnitude but opposite signs. records.text: TRADE IDEA TRADE IDEA -2 -1 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 Sep-25 Nov-25 Jan-26 Mar-26 May-26 04/05/2026 1 FX: Going long BRLCOP We initiate a long BRLCOP position as conditions seem aligned for the trade to perform well due to the near proximity of a highly uncertain election cycle in Colombia and a negative asymmetry for the COP into the event. BanRep delivering a dovish surprise last week offers a good catalyst. Negative COP asymmetry into presidential election: The most important reason for initiating the trade is the proximity of the Colombian presidential election (31 May). We expect the COP to start reflecting heightened anxiety into the event as polls suggest a close race with sharply opposing potential market outcomes depending on the result (perceived as either market positive or negative). After the recent COP outperformance, risks for the currency look negatively skewed into the election (Figure 1). Given current conditions, we would expect a sharp rise in USDCOP if the outcome is viewed as negative, versus a relatively contained move lower in the opposite case. Regardless of the outcome, we expect the COP to correct its current skewness before the event. COP outperformance has been attributed to the accumulated government’s USD sales since Q4 2025, coupled with the peso’s high carry and positive sensitivity to the oil price shock. With Hor- muz effectively still closed, European policymakers can only try to improve the coordination of how existing sup- plies are used. The EC will try to coordinate the refilling of gas storage for next winter to avoid price spikes caused by simultaneous purchases by member states and it will allow more flexibility on the targets, both in terms of tim- ing (by 1 December versus 1 November) and level (80% and possibly 75% by next winter, versus the usual 90%). Storage levels have so far increased from a low of 28% to 32%, leaving a long way to go (Figure 1). Three other areas of coordination across member states are on (a) any releases from oil stocks (incl. jet fuel, diesel), (b) optimiz- ing existing refining capacity and distribution of fuels across member states and (c) purchases of energy from third countries. Such steps can help, up to a point, but will not solve the main shortage. For securitised products, we turn to Mortgage TBAs (To-Be-Announced), the most liquid and heavily traded instruments in the US mortgage market. These forward contracts allow market participants to buy or sell agency mortgage-backed securities (MBS) on a specific future date at an agreed-upon price. They are called “To-Be-Announced” because the actual pool of mortgages that will be delivered isn’t specified at the time of the trade – only a few key parameters are agreed upon upfront, such as the issuer (e.g., Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Ginnie Mae), maturity, coupon rate, face value, and settlement date. While TBA Futures do trade, liquidity is primarily in the TBA Forward market. These products are covered by our Securitised Products Research team with an Introduction to Agency MBS by Nick Maciu- nas. To replicate the benchmark (LD19TRUU) we choose three TBA for the FNMA 30y pro- gramme with coupons of 2%, 4% and 6% to reflect the type of mortgages that have been issued over the past few years and are represented in the benchmark. Our TBA replication strategy returned 11.0% compared to 11.3% for the benchmark with a monthly TEV of 7c (~1bp).

The program formally ended in May 2024 for households and ran through December 2024 for small businesses. Verbal intervention had been escalating since the coordinated rate check in January as the trade-weighted Yen gradually pushed to fresh multi-decade lows. The intervention size appears in the range of that on April 29, 2024, on the order of ¥5tn or roughly $30.3bn. But as we recently highlighted, the latest weakness in both the currency and JGBs reflects fundamental risks from rising inflation and constrained policy—suggesting that the impact of intervention may be short-lived. The most “successful” intervention episodes occurred around data releases or events that pushed USD/JPY in the same direction, such as a hawkish BoJ and dovish Fed. July 2024 was one such example, when the MoF intervened following softer-than-expected US inflation data in a broader backdrop of slowing US growth, rising expectations for Fed cuts, and unwinds of substantial short JPY positioning that combined for a “perfect storm” of sharp appreciation. The market is currently pricing in a default environment similar to Healthcare in 2022-2024 as opposed to the more draconian Telecom and Energy experiences. Indeed, bad PIK (sub $90) levels have yet to move across the sector as companies continue to perform. But we expect software and AI headlines to be inextricably linked with private credit going forward (see Credit Watch: Private Credit Uncovered - Time can heal a lot of wounds, Stephen Dulake, 4/30/26). We also think private credit risks to the broader economy and financial system remain limited. Private credit represents only about 10% of U.S. nonfinancial corporate debt, it doesn't fill a uniquely irreplaceable lending role, and banks have excess capital to absorb any gap if the sector pulls back. In terms of risks to financial stability, bank exposure to private credit funds is small and mostly senior-secured, BDC debt/equity ratios are modest, life insurers' holdings are largely investment-grade, and the limited maturity transformation in private credit structures reduces fire-sale risk. We view the current spread widening — driven partly by AI-disruption concerns in the software sector — as a natural repricing rather than a sign of a poorly functioning financial system (see US: Private credit isn’t a public problem, Abiel Reinhart et. al., 5/1/26)

records.text: 12 Global Economic Weekly | 01 May 2026 Risks of delays on hikes have increased after today’s lack of explicit guidance on June. The BoE is taking some comfort from tighter financial conditions doing some work for them as they wait for further evidence. But we think if higher inflation expectations are sustained, energy prices stay elevated and growth/labour market doesn’t worsen materially, then the BoE would need to lean against risks of second round effects as soon as June. The longer it waits the greater the risks that higher inflation persists for longer. Focus between now and June would be on price expectations in DMP, PMIs and Agents, wage expectations in DMP, evidence on margins as well as household inflation expectations. BoE’s scenario C implies much larger tightening in the optimal policy projection than our base case. While the recent move higher in energy prices increase risks of scenario C, it is worth noting Scenario C points to fairly strong second round effects which may not materialize given the weak labour market/ economic backdrop. We do think the bar for more than 50bps of hikes is high. At the same time if by mid-year, the shock subsides and it looks like energy prices are moving lower, the labour market/economy worsens materially or inflation/wage expectations fall, then chances will rise that the BoE looks through the shock and keeps rates on hold through 2026, with cuts in 2027.

In this situation, we believe that i) occasional negative payroll prints should not be viewed as alarming, ii) productivity w ill increasingly account for economic growth, enabled by AI/tech investment, and iii) the unemployment rate remains the best indicator of labor slack. In recent years, Warsh has indicated he’d also like to see a smaller balance sheet, saying it currently has too large an “imprimatur” on the economy. Although this issue has been debated before, we think many on the committee will wel- come giving the issue another look. The bigger challenge will be reducing banks’ demand for reserves such that reducing the size of the balance sheet does not lead to a disruptive shortage of reserves. The Fed has several options to reduce banks’ demand for reserves. See, for example, the compre- hensive list from Darrell Duffie. However, for almost all of these there would likely need to be a period of study and debate that could last at least several months. As such, we don’t see this as much of an issue for 2026 or even 2027. Communication: easier said than done At several points in his testimony, Warsh raised various issues regarding Fed communication. A common theme was a desire for less forward guidance, in part because it may lock in poli- cymakers' subsequent decisions. We believe the FOMC will be receptive to revisiting how they communicate, though it’s not easy to see where this debate concludes. We remain of the view that most scenarios have a neutral or better than expected (relative to targets) fiscal path. Direct or indirect investment related to data centers/ large load is likely approaching about 20% of sector capex overall. That said, we see only an approximate $10bn increase y/y in IG utility issuance needs to $140bn+ this year, in part because of diversification of issuance into alternative currencies/products (converts) and some greater utilization of equity. • Which power & utility subsectors are best positioned? Agreement would still require subsequent legislative steps, including at the country level. As before, the omnibuses and a number of other proposals (e.g. 28th regime, posting workers, European business wallet) are aimed at making the Single Market work better and cut- ting red tape. The motivation to reduce administrative and reporting requirements is large, but will need to be replicated at the national level, where the gold-plating of EU rules can often add to the fragmentation of the Single Market. This will take time to become effective. The 28th regime is a case in point as the proposal mainly focuses on establishing an “EU Inc.” through simplified digital processes. However, a start-up or existing company opting into this arrangement would still have to navigate 27 legal systems in terms of labour laws, product laws, etc. Hence, it is an important first step rather than an immediate gamechanger. On energy, the One Europe, One Market initiative is essen- tially part of AccelerateEU and the ETS review. It should also be viewed largely as a long-term project (e.g. in terms of elec- trification), rather than a very significant near-term change. Specifically, accommodative fed funds rate-shocks bull-steepen the curve, forward guidance shocks have their largest effect on belly rates (at horizons beyond which the ZLB is unlikely to bind), and QE shocks bull-flatten the curve. Looking across the other assets, QE has the most pronounced impact on corporate credit rates, in line with the bigger effect on longer -term benchmark (i.e., UST) rates. The shocks have broadly comparable effects on the euro -dollar and dollar-yen exchange rates. And, contrary to the suggestion that balance sheet policy disproportionately benefits equities, the increase in the S&P 500 from a one-standard-deviation funds rate shock is an order of magnitude larger than the impact from a QE shock. One potential explanation for this is that the effect on equities comes mainly through lower discount rates on future earnings, and for this the expected short-rate path matters more than term premia. records.text: 1 May 2026 UK Weekly Digest Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 Recent spending reviews have seen budgets topped up by near GBP 30bn on average. We assume the upcoming Spending Review to add at least GBP 15-20bn – a very conservative estimate. To be sure, there's upside to this estimate. But not all of this will have to come through higher borrowing. More allocated efficiency savings plus taxation will likely be needed to make the sums work. We pencil in a net GBP 10- 15bn to feature as part of borrowing projections in the medium term with the remainder funded by taxation and efficiency savings. We will come back to this later in the year as we make our way to the Autumn Budget. Where does this leave the public finances? On our estimates, this would see borrowing stick near 1pp of GDP higher through the OBR's forecast horizon – with borrowing sitting GBP 20bn/annum above the OBR's projections. This would see PSNB settling closer to 2.4% of GDP at the end of the decade (as opposed to the OBR's forecast of 1.6%). PSNFL, as a share of GDP, we expect will sit around 3pp higher than what the OBR forecasted in the Spring Statement. On these projections, our sums will likely test the Treasury's fiscal framework. More efficiency savings, spending cuts, or tax rises will be needed to square the fiscal circle and retain a similar amount of fiscal buffer to the last couple of years. A final important note is that such a substitution in tools would be difficult to achieve, beyond the challenges of calibrating it to be growth-neutral. Any of the balance sheet policies under consideration would take considerable time to decide and implement ; the Committee will approach this deliberatively and we keep saying the timeline should be measured in years not quarters or months . Caveats We find the approach adopted here to be a useful way to gauge the relative impact of rate and QE shocks on equities and, by extension, inequality. That said, there we recognize several limitations to what we’ve done. records.text: US Economics Weekly1 May 2026 ab 6 Tax tracking: refunds pick up the pace The tax filing deadline for individuals, April 15, has come and gone, but the IRS still needs to process returns and people also file late, so we're continuing to track the daily data from the Treasury. As we've noted, we expected that individual tax refunds would be cumulatively ~$50-60 billion higher this year versus last, equivalent to a ~15% rise. So far, tracking has been broadly consistent with that projection. Top left, the total dollar amount of refunds issued by the IRS, including both electronic and checks, year-to-date totalled $321bn, ~$46bn or 17% ahead of the same point last year in data to April 22. Top right, the outflow from Treasury for electronically transferred refunds year-to-date, stood at $308bn, ~$56bn or 22% ahead of the same point last year in data to April 22. In the latest weekly data from the IRS, see here, there was some catch up in filing and processing. The number of tax returns filed as of April 17 was down by 0.3% and the number processed was up by 0.4% lower than the same point last year. These lags in filing and processing widened as we approached tax day. The total amount refunded was up 17% according to that data with the average refund amount 11% higher. Tracking the impact of changes in withholding tables, which might be leaving more money in workers' pockets, withheld taxes look to be running 1.2% behind last year, relative to the ~3 ¾ % increase in nominal wages

Given the scale of the move and signs of corporate retrenchment, our intuition is that the closure of this gap may take longer than following the 12-day war last year. This component is a proxy for the BI’s ability to absorb FX pressures through intervention. In addition, when reserve depletion becomes pronounced, the tolerance for policy easing typically declines. • FX policy response is represented by the spread between the six-month SRBI yield and the policy rate. The spread captures the extent to which the BI is tightening monetary conditions through liquidity and FX-stabilization opera- tions rather than through the policy rate itself. Hence, it serves as a market-based proxy for the BI’s effective poli- cy bias. Such divergence is unlikely to be sustained over the long term, as it runs the risk of weakening policy transmission and blurring the policy signal. We assign a weight of 60% to FX pressures, which directly captures FX risks, and 20% to other components that provide additional insight into the implicit pressure for FX stability (Table 1). Construction spending in both the residential and non-residential sectors is an important input into the BEA's calculation of structures investment in GDP . We estimate residential construction spending edged up 0.2% in February and 0.7% in March. The March increase likely reflected an improvement in residential activity, supported by a rebound in housing starts, particularly in the single-family segment, with additional contributions from multifamily construction. Spending on residential improvements likely grew at a steady 0.7% pace in both February and March, following strong monthly gains of roughly 3% in Q4 and a 1.4% decline in January. In contrast, private non-residential construction spending is expected to have fallen 0.2% in February and remained unchanged in March. This sector continues to face headwinds, with recent strength concentrated in data-center investment (classified within office construction), while broader private non-residential spending has generally trended lower over the past two years. Public non-residential construction has remained volatile but, on net, largely stagnant over the same period.  Upside: A stronger-than-expected rebound in housing starts could translate into a quicker pickup in residential outlays, lifting total construction spending above our estimates. This week, Jens Eisenschmidt discusses what lies ahead for the ECB. Next week, the focus will be the Riksbank and Norges Bank meetings, ECB speakers and UK local elections on Thursday. This week in Europe: What's next for the ECB? This week is not only short – as the first of May is a public holiday in most of continental Europe – it was also a really busy one. It featured plenty of data releases and central bank meetings. Yesterday saw most of the action. First, we got data on euro area growth in the first quarter showing that the momentum of the economy already before the start of the Middle East conflict was lower than widely expected: 1Q26 GDP growth was reported at 0.1%Q. The ECB, for example, had expected 0.3%Q, the European Commission 0.4%Q (its forecast dates from November), and Consensus 0.2%Q. We expected a figure between 0.1%Q and 0.2%Q, with a sense it will round to 0.1%Q (see our PMI review last week here). These numbers may sound arcane, but they matter: 0.1%Q growth is clearly below potential, so the euro area output gap is widening. The second important release was euro area inflation in April (see our Watch here). Headline inflation increased further to 3.0%Y. Not surprising, higher energy prices were the main driver. Post-closure, Asia initially pulled ~100 Mcm/ day of US Gulf Coast LNG away from Europe; after a brief early-April reversal, the last ~10 days again favor Asia for mostly spot cargoes. Of ~110 USGC LNG vessels in transit, ~40% are headed to Europe vs a ~65% historical norm, and ~40% to Asia. JKM/TTF netbacks still favor Asia, and prices are expected to rise into 3Q, supporting faster European stor- age injections toward 80% by Nov 1. records.text: US Economics Weekly1 May 2026 ab 3 US Economics Weekly UBS Research Economic Comment: growth concentration From late February to last week we had marked up 2026 Q4/Q4 headline PCE inflation 0.4 pp to 3.2% and marked down real GDP growth 0.3 pp to 2.0%, some of which was softer real consumption than expected. This week we took headline inflation up another two tenths to 3.4%. Incoming real consumer spending data remains softer than we thought two months ago. GDP in Q1 was weaker than we expected. However, we are now going the other way and revising up Q4/Q4 real GDP growth on the back of ongoing strength in the outlook for AI/tech capex. In the first quarter, real personal consumption expenditures expanded 1.6% (saar), after 1.9% in Q4. records.text: US Rates Weekly 01 May 2026 Citi Research 9 Short-end: TGA evolution into May Yesterday, Treasury announced an increase to the size of the 6-week T-bill auction (to take place next Tuesday, 5/5) of $5bn, to bring the offering size to $75bn. This is in-line with what we had been expecting, and we are penciling in further increases to the 4-week through 8-week bill auction sizes over the coming weeks (see US Rates Weekly - May refunding preview – Will auction sizes ever be increased?). While we are also expecting to see a declining TGA balance through the next month (more on this below), we had been expecting Treasury to increase T-bill sizes to support larger funding needs in May. As we show in Figure 16, seasonal patterns in the past few years indicate that May tends to be a month of somewhat elevated deficits. Therefore, we expect net marketable T-bill issuance to reach $70bn in May (see Figure 17), which would bring marketable T-bill outstanding back above $6.7tn. This influx of T-bill supply would be relatively moderate, for example net marketable bill issuance in February was $212bn, hence we don’t expect to see significant pressure on funding markets in May on the back of this increase in collateral funding needs. Q3. What inventories are driving the visible draws in March and April? Oil in transit depletion accounted for most of the draws in global visible stocks in March as buyers rushed to secure oil tankers ahead of the drop in Gulf arrivals (Exhibit 4). With most of the on-water overhang (excluding Iran) absorbed by mid-April, draws in April moved to landed storage. While noisy and subject to revisions, global visible draws moderated in April to 2.4b/d from 4.5mb/d in March, likely reflecting higher draws in invisible refined products stocks and lower demand. Q4. How do you estimate invisible draws in general, and for non-OECD products? We estimate invisible non-OECD crude and product stocks using observable global stocks and econometric modeling. We estimate non-OECD product stocks as the product of 1) observed non-OECD crude stocks and 2) the products-to-crude stocks ratio modeled on country characteristics (see Appendix here). Overall, we estimate that the level of global stocks was just below 11 billion barrels at the end of 2025, with 1/4 of global oil stocks and 90% of non-OECD refined products stocks not observable (Exhibit 5). before this point. As a result, we view the utility sector as a more informative indicator of the forward data center pipeline than what is disclosed by the hyperscalers and neoclouds. Data center financing is evolving By now it is clear that cash flow is no longer sufficient to fund the compute build-out, even for the hyperscalers (see Hyperscaler Capex: Gonna Need A Bigger Boat). Public issuance of parent- level debt remains a large funding vehicle, but as the ownership structures have become more varied, so too has the funding mix. A growing share of development now occurs through leased facilities, powered shell developers, and project-level financing structures, allowing physical infrastructure and power to come online ahead of finalized leasing commitments. Smaller data center developers have accessed the high yield bond market to fund data center projects, with credit support from their hyperscaler or neocloud tenants operating the GPU cluster layer (now totaling ~$27bn in outstanding notes). Reflecting this shift, hyperscalers and AI infrastructure buyers are deploying capacity across three distinct data-center ownership models: 1) full direct ownership, where operators build and run facilities end-to-end; 2) leasing a powered shell while retaining control over power, cooling, and IT; and 3) pre-built capacity via leases from neocloud or third-party providers, which offer faster deployment but less customization and typically higher run-rate costs. Overall, the investment value of analyst price targets remains an open empirical question. Key findings • Using I/B/E/S data and a portfolio-based approach, we show that conventional consensus analyst price targets are weakly informative in the U.S. equity market (Figure 12 Panel A). One explanation for this weak performance is a timing mismatch: individual price targets included in the consensus are issued at different points in time, whereas the stock price used for scaling is common across all price targets. • To address this issue, we shift from consensus price targets (PT) to consensus price target- implied returns (PTIR). Instead of scaling the consensus analyst price target by the same stock price, we divide each individual analyst price target by the stock price at the time of issuance to get a price target-implied return (PTIR), and then aggregate individual PTIRs at the stock level. • We find that this price target-implied return (PTIR) measure provides stronger and more consistent predictability of stock returns than conventional price targets (PT). A PTIR- based long-short portfolio earns 9.7% p.a., with an information ratio over 0.5 (Figure 12 Panel B), and a Fama-French six-factor alpha of 7.8% p.a. (Figure 13 Section II). Risks of delays on hikes have increased after today’s lack of explicit guidance on June. The BoE is taking some comfort from tighter financial conditions doing some work for them as they wait for further evidence. But we think if higher inflation expectations are sustained, energy prices stay elevated and growth/labour market doesn’t worsen materially, then the BoE would need to lean against risks of second round effects as soon as June. The longer it waits the greater the risks that higher inflation persists for longer. Focus between now and June would be on price expectations in DMP, PMIs and Agents, wage expectations in DMP, evidence on margins as well as household inflation expectations. BoE’s scenario C implies much larger tightening in the optimal policy projection than our base case. While the recent move higher in energy prices increase risks of scenario C, it is worth noting Scenario C points to fairly strong second round effects which may not materialize given the weak labour market/ economic backdrop. We do think the bar for more than 50bps of hikes is high. The Treasury yield curve results are intuitive and in line with our thinking outlined above. Specifically, accommodative fed funds rate-shocks bull-steepen the curve, forward guidance shocks have their largest effect on belly rates (at horizons beyond which the ZLB is unlikely to bind), and QE shocks bull-flatten the curve. Looking across the other assets, QE has the most pronounced impact on corporate credit rates, in line with the bigger effect on longer -term benchmark (i.e., UST) rates. The shocks have broadly comparable effects on the euro -dollar and dollar-yen exchange rates. And, contrary to the suggestion that balance sheet policy disproportionately benefits equities, the increase in the S&P 500 from a one-standard-deviation funds rate shock is an order of magnitude larger than the impact from a QE shock. One potential explanation for this is that the effect on equities comes mainly through lower discount rates on future earnings, and for this the expected short-rate path matters more than term premia. Conversely, Freddie’s portfolio growth fell short of market expectations. The total retained portfolio subject to the PSPA cap now stands at $332bn, leaving $118bn of remaining purchase capacity. Duration gap widened across both GSE portfolios during March. Looking ahead, vol-rate directionality is likely to remain in positive territory for some time. Indeed, both our position indicators suggest that investors have extended duration in recent weeks and any unwind would drive yields higher (see Treasuries), and if this is due to geopolitical concerns, it will likely be followed by a move higher in implieds. However, in a scenario where oil reprices sharply higher, causing growth and recession concerns, vol/rate correlations could turn negative and risk-reversals could reprice higher. Therefore, for investors who would like to position for such a risk, risk-reversals in short expiries/ short tails could be an attractive option (see Interest rate derivatives). Against this backdrop, coupled with implieds not retracing to their March levels, higher MBS coupons outperformed into the selloff. During the March backup in rates, refi applications were lower than what we saw during the rally down below 6%; the average loan size of refis has also sharply dropped. Call it the loss of the media effect or some light burnout (we hesitate to say it would persist into a rally), but it does look like speeds could be a bit lighter in the coming prints than the pure rate level might imply. records.text: China Outlook Resilience holds firm The expansionary manufacturing PMIs – driven by exports – alongside contraction readings for services and construction reinforce a two-speed growth outlook. Ongoing energy shocks have supported China's green-tech exports, while robust global AI capex underpins demand for China's AI- related exports. PMIs point to a resilient economy China’s NBS manufacturing PMI remained in expansion territory for the second time this year, edging down to 50.3 in April from 50.4 in March. The print was slightly stronger than both consensus and our forecast (Bloomberg consensus: 50.1; Barclays: 50.2). We think the resilient April headline PMI – alongside continued improvement in new export orders and solid production readings – suggests that China’s economy remained relatively resilient despite the ongoing Middle East conflict and disruption risks around the Strait of Hormuz. In addition, both input and output prices began to stabilise in April following a sharp rise in March. The private RatingDog manufacturing PMI, which has greater exposure to exporters, surprised positively, rising to a multi-year high of 52.2 in April. In our view, it is encouraging that the NBS PMI new export orders index rose to a two-year high of 50.3 in April, reinforcing our view that exports will remain a key driver of GDP growth this year. Friday, May 8 University of Michigan consumer sentiment (May, prelim), 10:00 AM We expect University of Michigan consumer sentiment edged down 0.8 points to 49.0 in the preliminary May data. Sentiment fell 3.5 points to 49.8 in the final April data, a series low. The press release (link here) noted, "The Iran conflict appears to influence consumer views primarily through shocks to gasoline and potentially other prices. In contrast, military and diplomatic developments that do not lift supply constraints or lower energy prices are unlikely to buoy consumers." As of this writing, gasoline prices have not softened relative to the April data collection period. The all-grade average US retail gasoline price sat at $4.26 in the last week of April, up $1.18 since the last week of February and a high since the Middle East conflict began. From that vantage point, we see little scope for much improvement in sentiment in May.  Upside: If sentiment stabilizes or edges higher, it could suggest that consumers are becoming less sensitive to changes in gasoline prices.  Downside:Continued weakness or a further decline in sentiment could reinforce the message that high energy prices are persistently weighing on household outlooks, potentially amplifying concerns about consumer resilience and near-term spending momentum. In the final April data, the University of Michigan estimated that longer-run inflation expectations rose 0.3 pp to 3.5%.

records.text: ignals are being overshadowed by external shocks. Domestic conditions continue to diverge, but across economies we see a reluctance to signal imminent policy shifts, with central banks pushing back against market expectations. For the ECB and BoE that meant no April hike and some pushing back against aggressive hikes that were priced. For the Fed, the dissents and Powell’s press conference showed a trend away from an easing bias toward more two-way risk. The pivots are not over. Policymakers want to retain flexibility and data dependence in an environment of uncertainty arising from external shocks. We begin with the Fed. The April FOMC meeting marked a shift in tone, indicating the committee’s view that the easing cycle would be pushed further into the future. The dissents and Powell’s comment showed us that the bar for rate cuts got much higher. Given the strength of US growth and five years of above-target inflation, the global oil supply shock means the Committee is in no rush to cut rates. If the inflation path remains unchanged, with tariff inflation receding and oil-driven inflation largely excluded from core, we see cuts pushed from Sep-26 to 1Q27, when the disinflation will be more apparent. If inflation goes and stays higher, however, the cuts could disappear. Powell did retain optionality, describing policy as only mildly restrictive while explicitly not ruling out hikes. FX exposures, major differentiator among Asia insurers Large unhedged USD asset exposures. The Taiwan lifers have substantial investments in foreign assets (led by USD-denominated bonds) to back their TWD insurance liabilities. As of end-2025, overseas investments accounted for close to 70% of the Taiwan lifer sector’s total invested assets, which is the highest among Asia's major life insurance markets (Figure 6). A meaningful portion of the foreign currency assets are unhedged, and the degree of unhedged exposure has increased following the introduction of a new FX accounting rule earlier this year. This change allows lifers to amortize the effects of currency moves over the life of qualifying bonds instead of recording fluctuations on a mark-to-market basis, providing greater flexibility for them to manage their FX exposures. And since hedging is a currently a cost for them given USDTWD levels, the accounting change has given the lifers an incentive to operate with lower hedge ratios. According to FSC, the sector's average FX hedging ratio declined from around 59% as November 2025 to 45% in February, driven by an unwinding of FX hedging positions (Figure 7). records.text: Q2. What do we know about the minimal recommended/operational inventory levels? The IEA requires its members to maintain oil stocks of at least 90 days of their net oil imports (crude and refined products) while EU countries must hold oil stocks of at least 61 days of consumption (if this level is higher than what the 90-days of net oil imports imply). However, those levels are likely somewhat above operational minimum for inventories. Pipelines, refineries, and storage tanks must maintain minimum oil to operate. Storage tanks with a floating roof (most crude landed storage) need to be filled by at least 20% to support the roof. Pipelines must contain oil over their entire length and minimum technical throughput (likely around 20-30%). Refineries cannot run substantially below 65% of utilization rates for a long time and typically need at least 15 days of crude storage on site for smooth operations. records.text: the transmission operates through three main channels. First, it disrupts pro- ductive activity—particularly agriculture and livestock, which together account for close to 9% of GDP—via lower yields, herd losses, and operational constraints. Second, it puts upward pressure on food prices as supply declines; this is par- ticularly relevant given food’s 27% weight in the CPI basket. Third, flooding can damage infrastructure, raising logistics costs and disrupting supply chains. On inflation, a weath- er‑driven food shock would hit at a time of still‑elevated inflation, potentially complicating the disinflation process that has begun since the new administration took office last November. Finally, infrastructure impacts tend to concentrate on the transportation network, amplifying the economic costs through trade and distribution bottlenecks. JU18 auction size has been cut to JPY 400bn from JPY 500bn since July 2025, and further reduction by JPY 100bn is scheduled from May. Interestingly, JU14-18 spread has largely stopped flattening since mid-March even though generic 30s40s continued to flattened once nearly to 0bp. In other words, we interpret that the impact of flattening in generic has less impact on 36s40s flattening. Therefore, we think that it is a good time to take profit. We do not expect generic 30s40s to invert due to “BoJ behind the curve” theme is not completely over. As we look at the peripheral supply and absorption with Tap auction and rinban in Figure 3 overleaf, the visible bid through the tap auction only took place in October and December 2025. Nonetheless, we recommend buying CDX.EM protection (offer price: 97.28, spread: +162bp) to position for a spread sell-off environment. The 1-month carry cost of buying CDX.EM protection using the historical 2y beta relationship for sizing the trade would be similar to that of being UW EMBIGD, i.e. ~25bp. However, an expected improvement in the beta-profile would mean we could do it at a relatively lower size than implied by histori- cal levels. Assuming CDX.EM’s beta has improved to ~0.75x following the March roll, the 1-month carry-cost on this beta-adjusted sizing would reduce to ~18bp, i.e. only ~4-5bp higher than some of the higher-beta single-name CDS but more diversified exposure. Risks to this view include continued resiliency of credit spreads, lower correlated and beta move of CDX.EM versus the cash index. records.text: 1 May 2026 Japan Economic Notes Page 2 Deutsche Securities Inc. The most direct experience of the yen-related decline in purchasing power is foreign travel. I recently traveled on business to Copenhagen, known as a particularly expensive city, and could feel keenly the loss in purchasing power from the sagging yen. However, we suspect that the percentage of Japanese who have such experience is decreasing year by year. The ownership rate for passports in Japanese has trended downward as if in step with the decline in the real effective exchange rate, a measure of the yen’s value, to historic lows. Statistics by the Foreign Affairs Ministry show that the number of valid passports at end-2025 was around 22.82m, translating to an ownership rate of only 19%. That is a remarkably low level compared to other major economies like the UK (around 60%) and US (around 50%). In other words, the vast majority of Japanese have increasingly few opportunities to experience personally the negative effects of the flailing yen. For those who do not travel abroad, the yen’s drop may amount to little more than news from a distant land rather than something they feel directly. We believe this is one key to understanding public sentiment at present toward the weak yen. The next marker to confirm Warsh will be a vote in the full US Senate. The timing of a vote in the Senate is unclear, but we would expect Kevin Warsh to be confirmed and sworn in as the next Chair of the Board by the June FOMC meeting. We recapped takeaways from Warsh's testimony last week and the implications for monetary policy on page 10 of the US Economics Weekly, here. Debt to GDP surpasses 100%, Fitch raises concerns over fiscal sustainability The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget published a note this week highlighting that debt held by the public has surpassed the size of the economy (see here). As of March 31 debt held by the public totaled $31.27 trillion as of March 31 and the four-quarter moving average of nominal GDP was $31.22 trillion as of Q1, putting debt held by the public at 100.2% of GDP . The last time the series reached this level was in the aftermath of the COVID pandemic in 2020 and prior to that 1945. The rating agency Fitch, who downgraded the US debt rating in August 2023 to AA+, warned this week that the US debt burden is significantly higher than other sovereigns with this rating (see here). records.text: US Investment Grade Are we there yet? Recalibrating after the round-trip Since the onset of the Iranian conflict, index spreads are 4bp tighter, but the rapid sell-off into subsequent rally has created some dislocations. Curve flattening has left the front end more attractive, small caps have lagged but are playing catch-up, and noncyclicals look attractive. For our latest US High Grade company rating changes, click here. For our sector ratings, click here. The investment grade index trades tighter than its levels prior to the Iranian conflict. Despite the additional risks added to the market, on a net basis, credit markets have looked through the cons and focused on the pros (higher all-in yields) to maintain a risk-on tone. The conflict, though, in tandem with other concerns, such as private credit/AI-related worries, created volatility the market had not seen since Liberation Day last year. We look to identify pockets of the market that stick out following these sudden index moves. The front end has noticeably lagged, creating some opportunity. Performance recently has favored duration, with curves flattening across the board. More than 90% of 30y bonds trade tighter than they did at the end of February, while only about half of 1-4y bonds can say the same. Although high long-end Treasury yields will likely continue to drive interest in corporates with duration, given the drastic difference in moves, we believe 1-4y offers more relative value spread opportunities. Agreement would still require subsequent legislative steps, including at the country level. As before, the omnibuses and a number of other proposals (e.g. 28th regime, posting workers, European business wallet) are aimed at making the Single Market work better and cut- ting red tape. The motivation to reduce administrative and reporting requirements is large, but will need to be replicated at the national level, where the gold-plating of EU rules can often add to the fragmentation of the Single Market. This will take time to become effective. The 28th regime is a case in point as the proposal mainly focuses on establishing an “EU Inc.” through simplified digital processes. However, a start-up or existing company opting into this arrangement would still have to navigate 27 legal systems in terms of labour laws, product laws, etc. Hence, it is an important first step rather than an immediate gamechanger. On energy, the One Europe, One Market initiative is essen- tially part of AccelerateEU and the ETS review. It should also be viewed largely as a long-term project (e.g. in terms of elec- trification), rather than a very significant near-term change. The CPI details showed that energy price inflation increase 2.9%-pts to 10.1%oya (as measures announced by the government had not yet dampened fuel prices in April). ECB Outlook: Measured tightening to 2.50% Our main takeaway from the April ECB meeting and press conference is that the data and events now need to disprove the case for a hike in June. Avoiding hikes is still possible, but it needs a very rapid resolution in the Middle East and clear easing in energy prices. More likely than not, the ECB will be hiking – and the main question is whether it will be ‘measured’ tightening or ‘forceful or persistent’ tightening. We retain our baseline view that the ECB hikes to 2.50%. We continue to see 25bp hikes in June and September. ‘Measured’ tightening to 2.50%, the upper end of the range of neutral, feels like good risk management. It signals a commitment to price stability when there is a risk of persistent inflation. At the same time, keeping rates within the range of neutral means the ECB would not be overly burdening economic growth. records.text: Agency MBS GN buyout risk delayed: Trial payment loans temporarily excluded from delinquency calculations In our March 13th report, we highlighted the growing buyout risk in GNMA MBS, as D90+ rates climbed rapidly to 4% from less than 3% six months ago. One of the reasons for the rapid rise in delinquencies was the October 2025 change to FHA ’s modification program which now requires that borrowers enter into a three-month trial payment plan before a loan modification is approved. Subsequently, we forecasted that involuntary prepays for the GN universe could increase by about 1 CPR from current levels through year-end 2026 if recent roll rates prevailed for the rest of the year and lenders maintained their D90+ rates below 5%. However, a recent announcement from GNMA should largely neutralize this buyout risk, at least for the next several months. Late last week, GNMA announced that they would temporarily exclude any loans in a trial payment plan from the delinquency calculations that are used to determine issuer compliance with GNMA requirements. This would ensure that issuers are not in breach of GNMA requirements and can avoid any large-scale loan buyouts. While there is no precise reporting on the loans that are in trial payments, we estimate that D90+ rates would be about 1% lower if the roll rates experienced between October 2024 and March 2025 had persisted during the recent six-month period, all else equal (Exhibit 1). We see monetary policy as generally working by reducing interest rates faced by households and firms and easing broader financial conditions; e.g., a weaker dollar that spurs net exports and higher equity and house prices that have wealth effects. The most immediate difference between the interest rate and balance sheet tools is in the channels by which they lower longer-term rates: rate policy (including forward guidance) acts mainly on the expected path of short-term rates, while asset purchases primarily compress term premia and MBS spreads. However, it likely offsets the front-loaded tightening delivered in the previous meetings. Overall, the decision reinforces our view that the Bank was approaching the end of the hiking cycle and was likely to tighten less than markets had been expecting. While surprising, given the recently hawkish tone from board members, the decision is not inconsistent with underlying macroeconomic conditions. In our assessment, Banrep has already delivered most, if not all, of the tightening fundamentally required, and we had expected this to be the final hike of the cycle. Against a highly noisy backdrop, board members appear to have opted to contain rising tensions and build minimum consensus, reaching a unanimous decision. Nonetheless, they continue to acknowledge internal differences and have not fully closed the door to additional tightening should conditions warrant it, which should contain the risk of this being perceived as a politically motivated decision and concerns over the bank's independence. First, price targets are numeric and readily comparable across stocks, enabling efficient screening across a broad investment universe, even for investors primarily focused on qualitative narratives. Second, their numerical nature allows price targets to be directly incorporated into systematic and quantitative investment frameworks. Third, publishing price targets increases the transparency of around analysts' valuation views. Relative to categorical stock recommendations, price targets tend to be updated more frequently and covey more granular information .1 We focus on consensus price targets, which aggregate individual analyst views and reduce idiosyncratic noise. Despite the irregular timing of individual price target updates, consensus measures can be constructed at regular intervals, enabling systematic portfolio rebalancing. A brief literature review The literature predominantly focuses on price targets issued by individual analysts, with the aim of identifying the determinants of analysts' ability to forecast stock returns (e.g., Pope and Wang, 2023). This line of research documents substantial noise, bias and limited accuracy in individual analysts' price targets (e.g., Bilinski et al., 2013). While total global stocks—the sum of visible n and invisible, crude and products, landed and on water, and commercial and strategic stocks—are unlikely to hit minimum operational levels this summer, the speed of depletion and supply losses in some regions and products are concerning, with easily accessible refined products buffers approaching very low levels fast. Global oil stocks approaching their lowest level on an 8-year record is more n concerning from a depletion speed perspective than from an aggregate level perspective (for now). Growth in the quarter was a meagre 0.1% q/q (0.148% q/q unrounded), undershooting our forecast (0.2% q/q) and the ECB’s projection of a trend-like 0.3% q/q expansion. Across major economies, Spanish growth remained strong at 0.6% q/q, while activity proved relatively resilient in Germany (0.3% q/q) and Italy (0.2% q/q). By contrast, French growth surprised significantly to the downside, with real GDP flat at the start of the year. At the euro area level, a full assessment of the drivers of Q1 growth will be available on 5 June, when the expenditure-side breakdown is released. In the meantime, the details already available for France and Spain point to emerging signs of softening in domestic demand components (for more, see Euro area Q1 flash GDP: Slowing into the conflict). records.text: DM rates: Favouring structural steepeners over fundamental flatteners 1219 May 2026 GLOBAL OUTLOOK SPRING 2026 Source: BEA, Bloomberg, BNP Paribas Many sources of higher deficit risks ▪ We think the DM yield curve could steepen in scenarios of either further escalation or de-escalation in the Middle East: Escalation could see log-end yields rise due to deficit concerns driven by defense spending and fiscal stimulus. In case of de-escalation, front-end yields could decline with deficit concerns potentially lingering, steepening the curve. ▪ Fiscal risks look highly underpriced, especially in escalation scenarios: Most investors have seemingly paid little attention to deficits since the start of the Middle East conflict because (1) they think related one-time costs might be “manageable” and (2) many of them have been preoccupied with sharp market moves, headline volatility and inflation concerns. ▪ Overall, we think deficits might expand versus our current baseline by USD200bn (mild risk case) to USD1.0trn (worst case). Our model suggests that such wider deficits could be worth 20bp to 50bp in term premiums. The case studies below illustrate how these ownership structures can shape both the timing of capacity visibility and the attribution of infrastructure activity across the ecosystem. • Oracle/Crusoe (development and attribution timing): Oracle typically leases data centers from third-party operators that acquire land, develop powered shells, and secure grid access, while Oracle separately equips those facilities with compute infrastructure (chips, networking, servers racks, etc.) while marketing capacity to anchor customers such as OpenAI and Meta. In this structure, Oracle’s contracted capacity can overlap with developer-led project disclosures. In the case of Crusoe, early visibility into power procurement and site development may initially appear tied to Crusoe-branded initiatives, even as that same capacity ultimately supports Oracle offerings. In other words, Oracle and Crusoe represent different points along the development and monetization timeline of the same site, underscoring why infrastructure activity can surface prior to commercial announcements. • CoreWeave/Microsoft (flexible utilization): CoreWeave develops and operates large-scale data center compute capacity that it leases to compute buyers (most notably Microsoft, OpenAI, and Meta, among others). Exports continued to outpace imports, , coupled with strong investment and private consumption growth, drove headline GDP growth in Q1. We suspect part of the seeming resilience in trade and economic activity so far, despite EM Asia being a net oil importer, is due to destocking and diversification, as firms turned to inventories and other sources for oil imports: for instance, India increased its oil imports from Russia in March, along with a rise imports from the US, Nigeria and Angola. Thailand also increased oil imports from the US and Malaysia. The Philippines also imported Russian oil for the first time in five years. One key potential difference between March supply and May supply is new issue conces- sions (NICs), which have come down materially. NICs on a 10-day average basis have come back down to around 4bp lately, or less than half the 10bp+ levels seen in March (we calcu- late the aggregate NIC on a par weighted basis for deals where a reasonable NIC estimate is available). March's elevated NICs were driven by the likes of larger deals like CRM that came with significant concessions given both idiosyncratic issues as well the poor macro backdrop at the time, such that despite $235bn of supply, secondary spreads were about unchanged in March. This is sensible because NICs and new issue outperformance vs. the index are -71% correlated YTD: when concessions are sizeable, there is a much higher like- lihood of new issue outperformance in the first few days of trading and that oftentimes ensu- ing compression feeds back into a constructive technical loop for the broader secondary market. Short gamma strategies generate negative returns, as realized exceeds implied. This typically follows a volatility spike, when implied normalizes faster than realized. • Spread around zero (between -20 and +10 vol points, frequency = 67%) implied volatility reflects a broadly fair risk premium. This is the dominant regime, and short gamma returns are modestly positive. • Moderately high spread (+10 to +20 vol points, frequency = 20%) implied is elevated but not decisively rich. Short gamma returns are negative, as realized volatility tends to catch up. This regime often occurs after modest volatility shocks or in the early stages of broader risk-off episodes. • Sweet spot spread (+20 to +40 vol points, frequency = 9%) implied volatility embeds a substantial risk premium. Short gamma returns are strongest, as implied overcompensates for subsequent realized volatility. • Extremely high spread (>40 vol points, frequency = 1%) markets are in acute stress. Short gamma returns turn slightly negative due to large realized moves and gap risk, although the sample size is limited. We see a few potential measurement issues related to software’s contribution to PCE inflation, however. First, we suspect that the PCE weight on software is probably too large. The weight is based on a question in the Economic Census that asks businesses how much software they sell to individuals (rather than to companies or the government), which could inadvertently include software that households primarily use for work.1 By contrast, the CPI weights are based on the Consumer Expenditure survey, which explicitly asks households to exclude business-related purchases. This much higher weight in PCE creates an additional measurement problem. Software and accessories are a single component in the CPI. And while PCE uses different source data than CPI for the software and accessories weight, it uses the CPI itself as source data for prices. Since the CPI’s software weight is relatively small (compared to PCE), computer accessories likely make up a much larger share of the combined software and accessories price index in the CPI than in the PCE index. First, the Supreme Court overturned the use of IEEPA for broad tariffs, and the CIT then ordered the US Customs and Border Protection Office (CBP) to create a system to refund eligible importers for the $166bn of IEEPA tariffs that were paid. CBP created a portal to accept refund applications, and estimated in court filings that roughly $127bn would be eligible for refunds electronically, at an estimated timeline of 60-90 days from the time of application. We expect roughly $30bn of refunds to be paid in FY26, and $90bn in FY27, with the first wave of refunds paid over June and July.
