French Data Library, Barclays Research Price targets are more predictive of future stock returns when analyst convictions are high Analysts' price target revisions may reflect either passive responses to recent price movements or analysts' private information. A modest PTIR following an aggressive price target revision may indicate that the analyst is passively following price trends to avoid holding a price target that is mechanically misaligned with the current stock price. By contrast, a more extreme PTIR following an aggressive price target revision may suggest that the analyst is proactively incorporating private information into her views (i.e. high conviction).12 We examine this idea using portfolio double sorts. First, stocks are sorted into quartiles based on price target revisions, which are calculated for each price target issuance and then aggregated at the stock level. Within each quartile, stocks are subsequently sorted into quintile portfolios based on PTIR. Figure 20 reports differential performance of a long-short (top-bottom quintile) portfolio strategy based on consensus PTIR across price target revision quartiles. More than a meteorological curiosity, ENSO is the world’s most influential driver of year-to-year climate volatility, and its impact on Latin America is profound. The difference between El Niño and its counterpart, La Niña, reverberates far beyond weather forecasts: it determines the fate of harvests, swings commodity export revenues, strains fiscal balances, stirs inflation, and, in extreme cases, threatens the survival of entire industries. The region’s vulnerability is structural—its economies are deeply tied to climate-sensitive sectors, and chronic infrastructure gaps magnify the devasta- tion wrought by floods and droughts. This note provides an in-depth analysis of the evolving ENSO cycle and its macroeconomic implications for Latin America as the Pacific transitions from La Niña toward a likely El Niño in 2026. In his confirmation hearing last week, Kevin Warsh reiterated criticism of Fed balance sheet policy over the past 15 years . In doing so, he argued that, relative to policy rate adjustments, asset purchases fuel inequality by disproportionately impacting financial asset prices. An important implication of this claim is that a growth -neutral shift in the mix of monetary policy tools, towards lower policy rates and a smaller Fed balance sheet, would be beneficial in reducing wealth inequality (or certainly not amplify it). Dallas Fed economists also found that the trimmed mean has not been consistently better at forecasting future inflation, though they highlight two of its virtues—it is less prone to revision and more tightly tied to labor market slack than core inflation. We see two likely reasons why the statistical measures do not outperform: neither necessarily has the same average as the core or headline or even the same average gap with them over time, and sometimes outliers prove to be valuable early signals of broader trends. This makes whether to trim partly a judgment about the economic environment. Trimming is appealing 1) when one is confident that a key one-off factor has driven extreme moves in outlier categories and 2) in calmer environments where outliers likely arise from measurement error or category-level idiosyncrasies. But trimming is less appealing when the key drivers are unclear or the persistence of the key drivers is unclear, because in those cases outliers are more likely to signal a change in the trend. For example, during the pandemic period, the most extreme price increases and declines sometimes turned out to be leading indicators of economic disruption and recovery that eventually affected prices more broadly. records.text: We expect artificial intelligence to deliver large productivity gains over the next n several years, boosting the economy’s potential growth rate and putting downward pressure on production costs. So far, however, AI is boosting US inflation. We see three key ways in which AI is boosting consumer prices. First, strong n demand for AI infrastructure has raised the price of some key electronics inputs, which has increased computer accessories prices and will likely boost smartphone and computer prices in coming months. Second, the addition of new AI features to existing software has likely put some upward pressure on software prices over the last couple of years. Third, higher electricity demand to power data centers is increasing electricity prices in some US regions, and we expect it to continue boosting inflation over the next couple of years. Recent increases in computer software and accessories prices have boosted core n PCE inflation significantly, but we think much of that contribution is overstated. First, the software and accessories component receives about 30 times the weight in PCE as it does in CPI, but we think most of that gap reflects an overstatement of software sales to retail customers in the PCE source data. Second, PCE uses the same aggregate index of software and accessories prices as CPI despite putting greater relative weight on software, which has amplified and exaggerated the impact of the recent spike in computer accessories prices on the overall PCE

Our forecasts for April are for a trend -like print for nonfarm payrolls (65k) and a steady jobless rate at 4.3%. We also see firmer wage pressure at 3.9% y/y versus 3.5% prior, on the back of a 0.4% m/m gain. Such a print would be supportive of the Fed’s w ait-and-see stance and align with our call for an indefinite hold in the policy rate. Looking further out, our base case is for the unemployment rate to average 4.3% this year, then fall to 4.1% at the end of 2027, below consensus and FOMC estimates (Figure 3). Bidirectional risks to unemployment, but positive outcomes likely underappreciated: We suspect positive labor-market outcomes are underappreciated, even while acknowledging a high degree of uncertainty amid still -evolving geopolitical risks. If nascent signs of tightening translate to a falling unemployment rate alongside above-target inflation, we see a growing tail risk that the Fed might consider hiking later this year (see April FOMC: End of an era, dated 29 April). It would take only a few more months of above-trend job growth to push the unemployment rate to 4% or below, a level at which we think wage-price dynamics could creep back into the Fed’s thinking. Source: Bloomberg, Barclays Research Caveats in interpreting PTIR The sign and magnitude of price-scaled PT may change due to stock price movements. However, over short horizons, stock returns are close to independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables, and analysts' views should not be affected by the noise component of stock returns. By design, PTIR better preserves analysts' views, as it is immune to price movements between price target issuance and the formation of consensus. That said, when new information arrives, analysts' views may become outdated, as analysts tend to respond slowly or fail to fully incorporate new information in their revisions.2 Although a stale price target may no longer be indicative, the analyst's overall view (bullish vs. bearish) towards the stock should remain, assuming the analyst would update the price target when her view changes, making PTIR a more stable measure of analysts' views than PT . In the remainder of this paper, we conduct a large-scale empirical analysis to evaluate the investment value of PTIR and compare it with conventional aggregate analyst views, such as price targets and stock recommendations. Business development companies (BDCs) are another common struc- ture that offer more liquidity and have brought in retail inves- tors. These include private BDCs, which often provide equity investors the option to buy or sell investments monthly at NA V . Quarterly share sales are capped, usually at 5% of NA V , though funds may choose to honor additional withdrawal requests. In contrast, public BDCs have equity that can be bought or sold at any time on exchanges. Both extremes disrupt crop yields, supply chains, and place upward pressure on food prices. Heavy rains in Peru, Ecuador, and Chile trig- ger flooding, landslides, and infrastructure damage, imposing significant reconstruction burdens on public budgets. Mining operations in Chile and Peru face heightened risks from flooding, while Colombia’s hydroelectric reservoirs suffer from reduced precipitation. Public health systems are further strained as stagnant floodwaters and elevated temperatures foster disease outbreaks, including dengue, zika, and malaria, with past El Niño episodes linked to sharp spikes in cases across Peru and Brazil. A review of the empirical literature published since 2021 underscores El Niño’s measurable impact on inflation (Figure 2) and GDP growth (Figure 3) across Latin American econo- mies. For moderate to strong shocks, countries like Peru and Ecuador face the most pronounced effects, with headline CPI rising by 2.0–4.0%-pt in Peru and 2.5–4.5%-pt in Ecuador, while GDP growth contracts by as much as -4.1% and -4.4%, respectively. Colombia, Brazil, and Chile also see inflationary pressures and modest GDP slowdowns, particularly in agri- culture, hydropower, and mining, underscoring the vulnera- bility of primary industries to El Niño’s weather extremes. While FX intervention has limited effectiveness in exerting sustained JPY appreciation, it does tend to make it more difficult to break above the intervention level for an extended period. Indeed, it took roughly a year and a half for USDJPY to recover the October 2022 intervention level, while the 2024 intervention threshold held for about one year and nine months. In this sense, intervention appears to have a meaningful “line-in-the-sand” effect. Speculative positioning is also a key factor in assessing the likelihood of consecutive interventions. Movements in speculative JPY short positions are particularly important when evaluating the risk of follow-up intervention. While the JPY depreciation since March can be seen as reflecting fundamentals – namely the deterioration in Japan’s terms of trade driven by higher crude oil prices – conditions prior to the latest intervention were clearly conducive to action. These included the building-up of speculative JPY shorts, USDJPY breaking through key psychological levels, and growing concern about the adverse macroeconomic impact of JPY weakness (with the BoJ explicitly referring to a “yen depreciation shock” in its April Outlook Report). records.text: g at ~8.4 billion barrels, rebuilt after 2024–25 oversupply. Yet only ~0.8 billion barrels are realistically drawable without disrupting “working” oil circulation (pipeline fill, minimum tank levels, logistics). About 280 million barrels have already been used by April 23. Drawdowns occur in layers: (1) oil-on-water/floating stocks fell ~140 million barrels (2.7 mbd) and should slow; (2) OECD commercial stocks only recently started drawing (~74 million barrels since February); (3) strategic reserves are being released (~2.5 mbd; -61 million barrels since March 26). Next comes the pivot to demand destruction, with demand down ~2.8 mbd in March, ~4.3 mbd in April, and potentially ~5.5 mbd in May—implying OECD commercial stocks could near stress by early June if disruption persists. Even if demand destruction stabilizes at ~5.5 mbd, OECD commercial stocks could fall to operational floors by Septem- ber if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed (Oil Flash Note, Apr 30th). The Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed to LNG, shifting marginal supply flows and pricing power toward Asia even as intra-Gulf trade partially normalizes. Only one observable ballast crossing occurred (Apr 2), with 16 LNG ships still inside the Gulf, but Qatar’s continued cargoes to Kuwait (now an 8th en route) suggest some Qatari trains have restarted. records.text: M Idea 2 Interest Rate Derivative Strategy Is now a good time to short gamma? After rising by more than 40bp/year in March, 1m10y implied rates volatility has fully retraced to pre-Iran conflict levels ( Exhibit 1 ). A similar round-trip in implied volatility is observed across rates, equities, and FX (Exhibit 2 ). Clients have questioned whether both the spike in implied volatility and its subsequent normalization were justified by fundamentals. At its core, the question is whether implied volatility fairly prices the distribution of future rate outcomes. For positioning, the implication is binary: if implied volatility overstates realized risk, investors should be short gamma; if it understates it, they should be long gamma. This reflects a clear tension. On one hand, elevated geopolitical uncertainty argues for owning gamma, given the risk of large, discontinuous moves in rates. On the other, realized volatility, particularly at the long end, remains subdued by historical standards, supporting the carry from short gamma positions. Federal Reserve Commentary Outlook change: Inflationary pressures from higher energy prices delay FOMC cuts With energy prices expected to be elevated throughout 2027 amid the Iran conflict, we mark up the trajectory of core inflation and nudge down our growth forecasts. With the timeline for bringing down inflation elongated, we now expect only one 25bp Fed cut through end-2027, in March 2027. We are changing our Fed call, which had assumed the FOMC would deliver 25bp cuts in September 2026 and March 2027. With the latest baseline from our energy strategist now assuming that energy prices will remain elevated throughout 2026, we expect much slower progress in bringing down inflation and a somewhat slower growth trajectory. That leaves the short-lived March breakout as a likely bull trap and makes the market vulnerable to another bear leg this spring. The 1464 dual retrace- ment support has marked the lower end of the recent holding pattern. A downside break would seek next support at the 1444 200-day moving average and 1417-1420 medium-term support. That includes the 4Q25 breakaway gap, Jan-Feb lows, and Jul 2025 61.8% retrace- ment. Also note longer-term trend line support rising into that zone, which currently sits at 1398. Look to the 1502 bear gap as key resistance. A sustained break above that resistance would derail the bearish short-term setup. Leading employment indicators nonetheless point to improving labour market conditions. Job advertise- ments have turned a corner, picking up in proportion to labour force growth. Business surveys report rising difficulty in find- ing skilled labour and the proportion of the labour force seek- ing unemployment benefits has declined. However, the pass- through to the official employment data is yet to be fully established, with monthly filled jobs only showing modest signs of recovery. We look for a one-tenth decline in the unemployment rate to 5.3%, with a stable participation rate and 0.5%q/q employment growth. On wages (ex-overtime), we forecast consolidation at 0.4%q/q, consistent with the sequential run rate that has stabilized at a pace similar to 2018/19. While it would not be possible to respond via monetary policy, we think the probability of rate hikes would decline given the difficulty of raising rates if there was a prospect of negative growth. The BoJ may decide it is able to wait longer if the inflation rate is in the 2% handle. On the other hand, if it were to climb above 4% (spot) or 3% (forecast), there would be insufficient reason not to act. While it is only natural that attention focus on prices, we think that data such as the monthly GDP and the probability of economic downturn will grow in importance. The intervention itself has not had a significant impact on the pricing of rate hikes in June or July. Avoiding further yen depreciation or the time being could be a reason for continuing to wait and see in terms of monetary policy. However, accommodative monetary policy is behind the undercurrent of yen depreciation, and it is important to resolve this as soon as possible. In 2024, after intervening during the Golden Week holiday, the yen continued to depreciate, leading to a rate hike in July. Although we continue to expect a rate hike in June, it will still take time for that to become more probable. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: The AI hyperscalers reported sales, earnings, and capex guidance that again exceeded consensus estimates. Alphabet (GOOGL), Amazon (AMZN), Meta (META), and Microsoft (MSFT) reported aggregate year/year sales growth of 20% and EPS growth of 61% for Q1 2026. The hyperscalers’ post-report share price performance continued to reflect investor focus on signs of return on AI investment spending. GOOGL rose by 10% after reporting an acceleration in Google Cloud growth and AMZN rose by 1% after reporting above-consensus AWS growth. In contrast, MSFT declined by 4% as growth in Azure remained strong but did not accelerate meaningfully, and META fell by 9% as management guided 2026 capex higher despite disappointing user growth. The hyperscalers’ earnings growth this quarter was boosted by an unusually large contribution from equity stakes in private companies. Alphabet and Amazon generated “other income” totaling $53 billion in Q1 2026, which accounted for nearly 60% of those two companies’ income in Q1 and 34% of the total $155 billion in income this quarter across the five largest hyperscalers. This represents the group’s largest collective share of earnings attributable to “other income” in at least a decade. Of this $53 billion in “other income,” $49 billion was explicitly due to equity stakes in private companies. While this is a problem for investors in private credit vehi- cles, here we address whether this is also a problem for the broader macroeconomy. We see two major potential channels. The first is a reduction in credit supplied to non-financial businesses. The second is financial stability risks emanating from banks and other levered lenders to private credit. We see limited risks from either channel. Private credit accounts for only a small share of credit extended by the financial system to non-financial business borrowers. Perhaps more importantly, private credit doesn’t occupy a particularly unique role in credit extension. This contrasts with, say, the relation between community banks or CDFIs and the busi- nesses they serve. Moreover, after recent regulatory changes, the banking system should have ample lending capacity to meet the needs of borrowers who would have turned to pri- vate credit. Finally, it isn’t clear that the structure of private credit funds implies that these funds will have permanently higher funding costs, despite headlines about unmet redemp- tions at BDCs. We expect both the Riksbank and the n Norges Bank to remain on hold at their respective policy meetings next week. This model spits out returns that range from -1% to +12% across a range of liquidation prices ($98.25-$110.25). In a second scenario, we look at returns with +25bp widening in loan spreads to a 330bp WAS, which boosts returns to +6%-20% all else equal. In a print and sprint, the equity IRR relies on the principal component, making it essential to have an efficient ramp at cheap loan price execution and loan price ‘pull-towards-par’. Our analysis estimates indicative returns at a range of prices and holds debt and equity notional constant. As the portfolio notional is not changing, the iterative analysis solves for the equity purchase price, depending on the loan portfolio purchase price. The BoC noted a risk scenario that might require “con- secutive hikes,” which is new punchy language. But this is just a scenario, and is conditional on a more obvious jump higher in core which has been soft outright and relative to expectations of late, and excess capacity in the economy can help tamper that. Meanwhile they cited the risk of cuts should US-CA trade worsen, which remains a unique headwind for CAD. Overall the BoC meeting did little to alleviated CAD’s low carry headwind. US Credit Alpha Overview Index spreads remained in a tight range this week, even as oil and long-end Treasury yields traded at or above the Iran conflict highs. Strong 1Q earnings to date have underpinned credit valuations, but we see reasons to be cautious in the near term. The "don't worry, be happy" market Credit markets were little changed this week, despite a renewed rise in oil prices and Treasury yields. Investment grade and high yield cash spreads widened 1bp and 2bp, respectively, as of Wednesday's close, with similar performance in CDX. In contrast, crude prices surged this week amid persistent Middle East worries (although they were off the highs as of midday Thursday), and Treasury yields rose sharply, led by the front end, with yields largely appearing to move with crude. While crude and 30y Treasury yields reached new local highs this week, credit and equity markets remained relatively insensitive to the moves. In other words, investors appeared comfortable or, at a minimum, unbothered by elevated spot oil prices and 5% 30y yields, perhaps with the view that current levels are unlikely to be sustained. Despite this week's muted performance, April is on track to be the best month for credit since the post-'Liberation Day' rally. With one day left in the month (at the time of publication), both investment grade and high yield spreads have tightened meaningfully since the Iran conflict wides and are actually through levels that immediately preceded the conflict. Price indexes across both surveys reflect ongoing cost pressures. Most manufacturing surveys, except the FRB of Dallas, reported increases in prices paid indexes that outpaced prices received, suggesting firms are absorbing higher costs before passing them on to consumers. While hard activity data remain largely unavailable for the post-conflict period, mak- ing a precise quantification difficult, leading soft indicators such as confidence and business tendency surveys point to a meaningful softening in economic momentum. We have formalized this signal through our new GDP now- casting model, which delivers a meaningful improvement in predictive accuracy relative to its predecessor. Our new now- casting model currently tracks 1Q26 growth at 1.7% q/q saar, down from 3.0% prior to the Middle East conflict. This decel- eration prompts us to revise down our full-year 2026 GDP growth forecast to 3.4%, from 4.0% previously, reflecting weaker domestic demand and a less supportive external envi- ronment. Signs of slowdown Available soft indicators point to a broad softening in activity since the onset of the Middle East conflict. Where the FOMC lands (and any response from Treasury on issuance) will of course have big implications for markets. While a smaller balance could open the door to Fed rate cuts or guidance around them, the work here shows that if the policy mix is adjusted in a way that is growth- neutral it would significantly twist-steepen the curve. And contrary to the implicit claim, it would raise equity prices, though we suspect that that would go over fine. A final important note is that such a substitution in tools would be difficult to achieve, beyond the challenges of calibrating it to be growth-neutral. Any of the balance sheet policies under consideration would take considerable time to decide and implement; the Committee will approach this deliberatively and we keep saying the timeline should be measured in years not quarters or months. Forward guidance on future balance sheet actions could be used to bring market effects forward but there is relatively little experience with it and not much that lends itself to empirical analysis. records.text: Q1 2026 earnings season update Our Sentiment Indicator rose to 1.7 this week, the highest level since late 2024 but still well below previous extremes. The increase in the indicator, which combines nine measures of equity positioning across various investor types, was lifted by passive equity fund inflows and a decline in mutual fund cash balances. The current level of our Sentiment Indicator has typically signaled below-average subsequent equity market returns, but the signal following elevated readings is not as strong as the signal from depressed readings. We think it is appropriate for the BoJ to counter the recent rise in inflation with a rate hike rather than simply seeing it as temporary. The Bank says its outlook is based on policy decisions already made by members of the Policy Board, with reference also to market pricing of policy management. In other words, rate hikes roughly every six months will not be sufficient to reduce inflation. The problem is uncertainty regarding the growth rate. Moody's downgrades numerous senior bonds, CB not impacted Last Wednesday the finalisation of the CMDI regime was published and Moody’s completed its review of banks’ ratings linked to CMDI, expected to be implemented across the EU by 2028. Deposits will rank ahead of senior preferred debt whereas previously in most countries, the two were ranked the same. Moody’s upgraded 47 banks’ deposit ratings and the ratings outlooks on 14 of the institutions and downgraded 22 banks’ senior unsecured debt and issuer ratings and lowered the ratings outlooks of 34 banks’ senior or issuer ratings. For example, Moody’s downgraded the senior preferred or operating company unsecured bond ratings of ABN Amro, BNP Paribas Fortis, BPCE, Commerzbank, ING Bank, Kutxabank, Volksbank Wien and Rabobank. Most of the downgrades are based on the banks’ baseline credit assessment (BCA) and Moody’s views that these instruments “will be exposed to a higher loss severity as a result of the introduction of depositor preference”. As the topic and likely rating impacts had long been expected and/or there is limited focus currently on such details (at least if, for example, respective rating changes are only minor), there was no material impact on spreads of senior preferred bonds (for example, see Figure 117-Figure 118). We understand that the change of the creditor hierarchy is not a topic for CB. The respective changes take place “below” the counterparts risk assessments

records.text: US Economics Weekly1 May 2026 ab 52 Baked into our projection for the week ending May 2 is the assumption that seasonally- adjusted initial claims in New York State will normalize around the level prior to spring break after this week's pothole. A similar pattern unfolded in 2023 alongside a similar mistiming of seasonal factors, as the chart below shows. That year, seasonally-adjusted claims in New York returned to the normal range the week after falling back from the spring break peak. We expect continuing claims rose 20K to 1805K in the week ending April 25. In the week ending April 18, continuing claims fell 23K to 1785K, the lowest level since April 2025. Similar to initial claims, New York recorded a notable decline in continuing claims (down 16K SA and 21K NSA). That also appears to be a result of mistimed seasonal adjustment relative to the past two years. Similar to our initial claims projection, we've baked some normalization into next week's projection. Another potential contributor to the recent low level of continuing claims is an increase in exhaustions (final payment of unemployment insurance, when benefits run out after 26 weeks of benefits in any 52-week period). In March, the latest data, exhaustions bounced back after declines in January and February. 26 weeks ago, in October 2025, claims were sawtoothing from week to week and still pushed around by a spate of fraudulent filings in the fall. records.text: US Economics Weekly1 May 2026 ab 39 A number of these decisions are being challenged in court. About ~368K individuals, primarily from Haiti, currently maintain their status and authorizations while court cases proceed. For example, on February 2, 2026, the US District Court for the District of Columbia ordered that the planned February 3 termination of TPS for Haiti " shall be null, void, and of no legal effect " while litigation proceeds (link here). As a result, TPS status, protection from removal, and employment authorization remain in force for Haiti TPS beneficiaries during the stay. That said, these authorizations remain conditional on the outcome of the litigation, and the case was considered in the Supreme Court this week (link here). If the stay is lifted, work authorization could end quickly absent new relief or guidance. These court orders can quickly push around the employment authorization of hundreds of thousands of individuals, potentially opening up a larger downside risk to employment. For example, initially, district court orders temporarily blocked DHS from terminating the 2023 Venezuela TPS designation, allowing most Venezuelan TPS holders to continue working while the case proceeded. However, at the end of 2025, the Supreme Court permitted DHS to end the designation, stripping work authorization from the majority of beneficiaries despite ongoing litigation. records.text: Our thoughts on USD, JPY, EUR, HUF, CHF, GBP , AUD & NZD, and Frontier FX USD: The gap grows wider. As the conflict extends and the oil deficit grows—n about a billion barrels of lost production so far—markets have increasingly reflected that the path to a quick, benign resolution is fading away. Our rates strategists have noted this dynamic in front-end pricing, and in FX that is manifested by a still-growing gulf between energy importers and exporters (Exhibit 1). Despite a full slate of central bank meetings, this was the defining feature of price action over the course of the week; currencies such as BRL, CAD, and AUD were among the best performers (despite modestly dovish domestic news in all 3) while PHP , ZAR, IDR, INR and TWD—all energy-intensive importers—experienced some of the clearest currency weakness. This more persistent energy shock is the defining feature of our forecast revisions this week; our commodities team now assumes a slower normalization and a longer recovery, our European economists now expect headline inflation to remain elevated for longer, and our US team boosted their inflation forecast on increased spillovers. We expect this to continue to translate into a more divided Dollar than prior to the conflict (Exhibit 2). Cyclical winners, carry champions and commodity exporters should continue to do well, especially because—so far— the growth impact seems to be less extreme than feared. records.text: On balance, we have trimmed our GDP growth forecast for 2026 by 0.3pp relative to our last published outlook, to 2.1% Q4/Q4, and we maintain our growth outlook for 2027 at 1.5% Q4/ Q4. With aggregate demand on a somewhat softer trajectory, on net, we have also nudged down our expectations for job growth in 2026, which slows the pace of descent in the unemployment rate. Nonetheless, we expect the job market to remain resilient overall, providing little reason for the FOMC to believe that precautionary cuts are warranted on the grounds of managing risks to the labor market. Change to our policy call With core PCE inflation now projected above 3% y/y through the end of the year, with a monthly run-rate above 2.5% annualized and a resilient labor market, we no longer think the FOMC will be in a position to cut rates this year. While this year's policy undoubtedly will be influenced by incoming Fed Chair Warsh, we would not expect Chair Warsh to convince the committee that a cut would be warranted in the face of core PCE inflation prints above 3%. We maintain our expectation that the FOMC will cut rates when it sees clear evidence that inflation is returning toward its 2% inflation target. We time this cut in March 2027. At that point, headline inflation is projected to undershoot the target on a m/m annualized basis and core PCE inflation appears on its downward trajectory toward 2%. records.text: 1 May 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 52 Deutsche Bank AG Fed Notes April FOMC survey results This note summarizes responses to our pre-FOMC investor survey, which is designed to understand expectations for the meeting and how financial markets and market expectations are likely to respond to various potential outcomes. Expectations for policy at this week’s meeting (Figure 69-Figure 72) n Respondents attach an average probability of 87% to no change in the policy rate at this week’s meeting. There is some variation across asset classes and roles, with fixed income investors (94%) and those in research (93%) more confident about a hold than other roles. n A significant majority (75%) expect Chair Powell in his press conference to sound neutral relative to market pricing of the policy rate path through the June meeting. The remainder skew hawkish, with 20% expecting Powell to sound hawkish versus only 5% expecting a dovish tone. n Respondents were split on whether the FOMC statement would adopt explicit two-sided guidance on future rate decisions, with a slight majority (55%) expecting no inclusion of this language. If the market tests further JPY appreciation, key technical downside levels are 154.1 (the 200-day moving average) and 152.1 (the post-rate-check low). That said, near-term JPY moves will ultimately depend on developments in the Middle East, and should tensions intensify again and push oil prices higher, risks remain of renewed dollar strength and JPY weakness. A transition to a medium- to long-term JPY appreciation trend, as seen after past interventions, appears unlikely this time. Following the 2022 and 2024 FX interventions, the JPY ultimately shifted into an appreciating trend, but in both cases this reflected subsequent disinflation and declining rates in the US as well as broad USD weakness (Figure 8). By contrast, at this week’s FOMC meeting, while dovish guidance was maintained, three members voted against it and Chair Powell’s press conference struck a hawkish tone, emphasizing the need to confirm further progress on inflation before considering rate cuts, in light of upside inflation risks. Under these circumstances, a shift to a sustained JPY appreciation trend similar to past post-intervention episodes is difficult to envisage. Over the medium to long term, persistent depreciation pressure on the JPY is likely to continue, reflecting fragile FX supply-demand and inflation risk premia. Next week’s refunding announcement and long positioning skew risks toward higher yields, but Middle East and energy-price uncertainty temper conviction in duration shorts; our colleagues prefer 2s/5s/10s belly-cheapening butterflies. • For the week, HG muni yields closed higher by 10-9-7-6bps in 2-5-10-30yrs, tracking within 1bp of Treasuries in each spot. Fund flows continued to be a ballast, with Lipper showing a 21st inflow week in the last 23, adding $615mn over the week (ending 4/29) and bringing YTD inflows to $30bn, the 3rd fastest pace on record. • April extended the muni market’s 2026 playbook, with steady inflows offsetting elevat- ed supply and driving a 1.15% total return, the best April performance since 2014. • We expect May to be choppier on rate vol and technicals, with lighter reinvestment and heavier issuance

records.text: We think the internal decision, a 6-3 vote count, may have come under much greater tension than implied. Although Nagasawa's term will come to an end in June, she will participate in the June meeting. Thus, much will depend on the resolve of the governor and his two deputies. The policy guidance was revised substantially, due to the Middle East conflict, with a hawkish tone and increasing flexibility. In the March meeting, the guidance had explained that it would have become difficult to hike rates if the prices overshot, but the economy undershot. Now, the BoJ clarified that it intends to raise rates as long as underlying inflation keeps rising, albeit gradually, even if the economy weakens somewhat. In the Outlook report, the BoJ revised down its growth forecasts for FY 26 to 0.5%, while revised up its inflation projections (BoJ core CPI for FY 26 to 2.6%), the latter exceeding our expectations. We continue to expect the BoJ to hike in June. We then expect additional hikes in October and April 2027, with a terminal rate of 1.5%. We will also be watching for PM Takaichi's moves since, at this stage, measures to combat inflation are an urgent priority for her, and given that US Treasury Secretary Bessent has also indicated the need for rate hikes, we believe she will likely continue tolerating gradual raises, though perhaps reluctantly. 1 May 2026 8 Barclays | Global Economics Weekly: Closed for longer
